sections.text: A graph $z=f(x,y)$ has one height for each allowed planar input. A level set $F(x,y,z)=c$ may fail to be a graph in a chosen direction. A sphere has two $z$ values over most of its disk projection and needs upper and lower branches or surface charts.

sections.title: Read slices deliberately
sections.text: For $z=x^{2}-y^{2}$, fixing $y$ gives upward parabolas and fixing $x$ gives downward parabolas. Level zero is the pair $y=\pm x$; positive and negative levels give differently oriented hyperbolas. Distinguish a horizontal contour from a vertical slice.

exercise.prompt: Why is $x^2+y^2+z^2=1$ not globally a graph $z=f(x,y)$?
exercise.hint: Inspect the two points above $(0,0)$.
exercise.solution: Both $(0,0,1)$ and $(0,0,-1)$ lie on the sphere. A single-valued graph cannot assign both heights; separate hemisphere graphs are possible over appropriate domains.
rubric: Use an explicit repeated planar input.
Distinguish local representation from global representation.
exercise.solutionTex: (0,0,1),(0,0,-1)\in S\implies S\text{ is not a single }z\text{-graph}

contentBlocks.title: Openness and closedness are separate tests
contentBlocks.text: In $\mathbb R^2$, openness requires an interior ball around every member. Closedness requires every limit point to belong. One included boundary point can refute openness, and one excluded limit point can refute closedness.

contentBlocks.title: Classify with an interior ball and a missing limit point
contentBlocks.strategy: Test openness at an included boundary and closedness at an excluded accumulation point.
contentBlocks.setup: Consider $S=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:0<x^2+y^2\le4\}$ in the ambient plane.

steps.label: Test an included edge
steps.text: $(2,0)\in S$, but every open ball centered there contains points of radius greater than 2. Thus $S$ is not open.

steps.label: Test a missing limit point
steps.text: $(1/n,0)\in S$ for $n\ge1$ and tends to $(0,0)\notin S$. Thus $S$ is not closed.

contentBlocks.result: $S$ is neither open nor closed in $\mathbb R^2$.
contentBlocks.verification: The verdict uses the ambient Euclidean plane and treats openness and closedness as separate questions.

exercises.outcome: Give separate witnesses for openness and closedness in the plane.
exercises.prompt: In $\mathbb R^2$, classify $H=\{(x,y):x^2+y^2\le4,\ y>0\}$ as open, closed, both, or neither. Give a witness for each failed property.
exercises.hint: Inspect a point on the included circular arc and a sequence tending to the excluded diameter.
exercises.solution: It is neither. The point $(0,2)$ belongs to $H$ but no open ball around it stays inside the disk, so $H$ is not open. The points $(0,1/n)$ belong to $H$ and tend to $(0,0)$, which is excluded by $y>0$, so $H$ is not closed.
exercises.solutionTex: (0,2)\in H\text{ has no interior ball};\quad(0,1/n)\in H\to(0,0)\notin H
rubric: Use an included boundary point to refute openness.
Use an excluded limit point to refute closedness.
State the ambient space.

sections.title: Open balls encode all directions
sections.text: A ball $B(a,r)$ consists of points with distance less than $r$; its boundary sphere is excluded. A set is open when each member has some ball contained in it, and closed when it contains its limit points. A set can be neither open nor closed.

sections.title: Boundary depends on ambient space
sections.text: The disk $x^{2}+y^{2}<1$ is open in the plane, but the same disk embedded in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ has no three-dimensional interior. For limits on a restricted domain, only points belonging to that domain are admissible approaches.

exercise.prompt: Classify the annulus $1<\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\le 2$ as open, closed, or neither in $\mathbb R^2$.
exercise.hint: Test the included outer boundary and excluded inner boundary.
exercise.solution: It is neither: at an outer-circle point every ball leaves the set, while a sequence approaching the inner circle has a limit outside the set.
rubric: Name a witness against openness.
Name a missing limit point against closedness.

sections.title: One radius must cover every approach
sections.text: For a multivariable limit, every domain point with $0<|x-a|<\delta$ must meet the output tolerance. A separate $\delta$ for each ray is insufficient unless one common positive radius works uniformly.

sections.title: Use norm inequalities
sections.text: For $f(x,y)=2x-3y$ at zero, $|2x-3y|\leq \sqrt{13}\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$ by Cauchy–Schwarz. Choosing $\delta =\varepsilon /\sqrt{13}$ proves the limit zero over every approach, including curved paths.

exercise.prompt: Prove $x^2+y^2$ tends to zero at the origin with an explicit $\delta$.
exercise.hint: Write the function in terms of the Euclidean radius $r$.
exercise.solution: The output is $r^{2}$. Given $\varepsilon >0$, choose $\delta =\sqrt{\varepsilon }$; then $0<r<\delta$ gives $|f|<\varepsilon$.
rubric: Quantify over all domain points.
Use a radius independent of direction.

sections.title: Two paths can disprove
sections.text: For $f(x,y)=xy/(x^{2}+y^{2})$, the $x$-axis gives zero, while $y=x$ gives $1/2$ away from the origin. If a common limit existed, both admissible path restrictions would share it. Their difference proves nonexistence.

sections.title: Agreement cannot prove
sections.text: A finite or even infinite collection of selected paths can miss another obstruction. After path tests suggest a candidate, look for an estimate involving the full norm. The puncture and domain restrictions must hold along every path used.

exercise.prompt: For $x^2/(x^2+y^2)$, compare the two coordinate-axis limits at zero.
exercise.hint: Set $y=0$ and then $x=0$, excluding the origin.
exercise.solution: The $x$-axis gives 1 and the $y$-axis gives 0, so no limit exists.
rubric: Use two admissible paths approaching the same point.
State why distinct path limits contradict a common limit.

sections.title: Every line can agree
sections.text: For $f(x,y)=x^{2}y/(x^{4}+y^{2})$, along $y=mx$ with $m\ne 0$ the expression is $mx/(x^{2}+m^{2})\to 0$; along $y=0$ it is zero, and the vertical axis is zero. Thus every line through the origin suggests zero.

sections.title: A curve reveals the obstruction
sections.text: Along $y=x^{2}$ the same expression is $1/2$ for $x\ne 0$. The limit therefore fails. The denominator hints at the path: balance $x^{4}$ with $y^{2}$ by choosing $y$ proportional to $x^{2}$. Polar coordinates do not justify a limit unless the angular estimate is uniform.

exercise.prompt: What values occur along $y=kx^2$ for this function?
exercise.hint: Substitute and cancel $x^{4}$ for $x\ne 0$.
exercise.solution: The value is $k/(1+k^{2})$, independent of nonzero $x$. Different $k$ give different path limits and exhibit the hidden family of obstructions.
rubric: Balance denominator terms.
Cancel only away from the puncture.

sections.title: Squeeze with the full radius
sections.text: For $x^{2}y/(x^{2}+y^{2})$, use $|y|\leq r$ and $x^{2}/(x^{2}+y^{2})\leq 1$ to obtain $|f|\leq r$. Defining the value zero at the origin makes it continuous. This uniform estimate handles all paths at once.

sections.title: Composition has a target condition
sections.text: If $g$ tends to $b$ and $f$ is continuous at $b$ through the relevant domain, then $f\circ g$ tends to $f(b)$. Check that $g$’s nearby values lie in $f$’s domain; continuity of a formal expression outside its domain is not a usable theorem.

exercise.prompt: Does $xy/\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, extended by zero, become continuous at zero?
exercise.solution: Its absolute value is at most $r/2$ and therefore tends to zero. The extension is continuous.
rubric: Bound the absolute error by a quantity tending to zero.
Match the extension value to the limit.

sections.title: Every escape route counts
sections.text: A limit at infinity means for each $\varepsilon >0$ some $R$ makes the output error smaller than $\varepsilon$ whenever the input norm exceeds $R$ within the domain. Either coordinate can diverge; one cannot test only $x=y\to \infty$.

sections.title: A uniform decay estimate
sections.text: For $f(x,y)=1/(1+x^{2}+y^{2})$, if $r>R$ then $f<1/(1+R^{2})$. Choosing $R>1/\sqrt{\varepsilon }$ suffices to prove limit zero. The function $x^{2}/(x^{2}+y^{2})$, by contrast, retains values 1 or 0 on the coordinate axes even arbitrarily far away.

exercise.prompt: Does $x/(1+x^2+y^2)$ tend to zero at infinity?
exercise.hint: Bound $|x|$ by $r$.
exercise.solution: For $r>0$, its absolute value is at most $r/(1+r^{2})\leq 1/r$. Taking $R>1/\varepsilon$ proves the limit zero.
rubric: Use the full norm.
Give a single $R$ for every escape route.

supplementalBlocks.title: Slice slopes give only a candidate map
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Restrict the piecewise function to each coordinate axis before taking a quotient.

steps.label: Horizontal slice
steps.text: $q(h,0)=h$ for nonzero $h$, so $q_x(0,0)=1$.

steps.label: Candidate
steps.text: If a total derivative exists, it must send $(h,k)$ to $h$. This conclusion names the only possible map; it has not established a uniform remainder estimate.

supplementalBlocks.result: The candidate is $L(h,k)=h$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The next step tests $|q(h,k)-L(h,k)|/\sqrt{h^2+k^2}$ along all approaches.

exercises.outcome: Distinguish coordinate slice slopes from continuity and total differentiability.
exercises.prompt: Extend $u(x,y)=xy/(x^2+y^2)$ by $u(0,0)=0$. Find both partials at zero from the definition, then test continuity along $y=x$.
exercises.hint: Both axis restrictions vanish, but the diagonal denominator is $2x^2$.
exercises.solution: Both axis restrictions are zero, hence both partials at zero equal zero. Along $(t,t)$ for $t\ne0$, $u(t,t)=1/2$, which does not tend to $u(0,0)=0$. It is discontinuous and cannot be totally differentiable there.
rubric: Use the actual axis restrictions at the piecewise point.
Give an admissible diagonal path.
Do not infer continuity from two partials.

sections.title: Hold the other input fixed
sections.text: For $f(x,y)=x^2y+\sin y$, $f_{x}=2xy$ and $f_y=x^2+\cos y$. The constant-held-fixed operation defines a coordinate slice derivative; it does not describe arbitrary combined input changes by itself.

sections.title: At a special point use the definition
sections.text: For a function defined by one formula away from zero and another at zero, differentiate the actual one-variable slice through zero. An off-origin derivative expression need not extend correctly by substitution at the missing point.

exercise.prompt: Find both partial derivatives of $f(x,y)=xe^y$ at $(2,0)$.
exercise.hint: In the $x$ derivative $e^y$ is constant; in the $y$ derivative $x$ is constant.
exercise.solution: $f_{x}=e^y$ gives 1 and $f_{y}=xe^y$ gives 2. These are the slopes of different coordinate slices at the same point.
rubric: Name which variable stays fixed.
Evaluate after differentiating.

sections.title: Cross product and rank
sections.text: For $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$, the ordered product $u\times v$ is perpendicular to both vectors and has magnitude equal to the parallelogram area. If $u$ and $v$ are dependent, the product is zero and gives no normal direction. Reversing the order reverses the normal: $u\times v=-(v\times u)$.

sections.title: The algebraic laws have limits
sections.text: The cross product is anti-commutative, distributes over vector addition, and is compatible with scalar multiplication. It is not associative: $(u\times v)\times w$ need not equal $u\times(v\times w)$.

sections.title: Write a plane from its normal
sections.text: For $p_0\in\mathbb R^3$ and a nonzero normal $n$, the unique plane through $p_0$ perpendicular to $n$ is $n\cdot(x-p_0)=0$. Two nonzero nonparallel directions $u,v$ determine such a normal $u\times v$.

sections.title: Graph slices give a candidate tangent plane
sections.text: If $f$ is defined on an open set and its two partials exist at $p=(a,b)$, the coordinate-slice tangent vectors are $(1,0,f_x(p))$ and $(0,1,f_y(p))$. Their cross product is $(-f_x(p),-f_y(p),1)$, so the plane through $(a,b,f(p))$ has equation $z=f(p)+f_x(p)(x-a)+f_y(p)(y-b)$. This is the source-defined candidate tangent-plane function; the differentiability supplement treats whether it is a linear approximation.

exercise.prompt: Find a normal and plane through the origin spanned by $(1,1,0)$ and $(0,1,1)$.
exercise.hint: Compute the ordered cross product.
exercise.solution: A normal is $(1,-1,1)$, giving $x-y+z=0$. Its dot product with each spanning vector is zero.
rubric: Check both orthogonality conditions.
Avoid confusing plane coefficients with a point on the plane.

contentBlocks.title: Magnitude gives area; orientation gives a normal
contentBlocks.statement: For nonzero, nonparallel $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$, $u\times v$ is perpendicular to both, has magnitude $\|u\|\|v\|\sin\theta$ where $\theta\in(0,\pi)$ is their angle, and points in the right-hand-rule direction. If either vector is zero or they are parallel, $u\times v=0$.
hypotheses: $u,v$ are vectors in $\mathbb R^3$.
The angle formula uses nonzero, nonparallel vectors; the dependent cases have zero product.
prerequisites: Dot products and the right-hand rule

contentBlocks.title: A nonzero normal fixes one plane through a point
contentBlocks.statement: For $p_0\in\mathbb R^3$ and $n\in\mathbb R^3$ with $n\ne0$, the set $\{x:n\cdot(x-p_0)=0\}$ is the unique plane through $p_0$ perpendicular to $n$.
hypotheses: $p_0\in\mathbb R^3$.

contentBlocks.title: Two independent directions fix one plane
contentBlocks.statement: For $p_0\in\mathbb R^3$ and nonzero, nonparallel $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$, $n=u\times v\ne0$. The unique plane through $p_0$ parallel to both directions is $p_0+s u+t v$ and equivalently $n\cdot(x-p_0)=0$.
hypotheses: $p_0\in\mathbb R^3$.
$u,v$ are nonzero and nonparallel, so $u\times v\ne0$.

contentBlocks.title: Expand an ordered cross product
contentBlocks.strategy: Expand the determinant along its first row, keeping the alternating sign in the middle component.

steps.label: First component
steps.text: Use the minor from the first coordinate.

steps.label: Second component
steps.text: The middle component has the negative determinant sign.

steps.label: Third component
steps.text: Use the minor from the third coordinate.

steps.label: Check orthogonality
steps.text: The result is perpendicular to both inputs.

steps.label: Dependent inputs
steps.text: If one input is a multiple of the other, the parallelogram is degenerate and the cross product is zero.

contentBlocks.result: $u\times v=(8,-4,-7)$; its magnitude $\sqrt{129}$ is the parallelogram area. The dependent pair has zero cross product and zero area.
contentBlocks.verification: Reversing the independent inputs gives $v\times u=(-8,4,7)$, so the oriented normal changes sign while its length stays the same. For the dependent pair, the zero cross product supplies no nonzero normal direction.

contentBlocks.title: Check the laws and the failed converse
contentBlocks.strategy: Evaluate basis-vector products to test each algebraic claim directly.
contentBlocks.setup: Let $i,j,k$ be the standard unit vectors, with $i\times j=k$, $j\times k=i$ and $i\times k=-j$.

steps.label: Order
steps.text: Swapping the inputs reverses the result.

steps.label: Distribute
steps.text: The product distributes over a sum in the second input.

steps.label: Scale an input
steps.text: For $u=i+2j$, compare scaling the first input with scaling the result.

steps.label: Associativity fails
steps.text: The two parenthesizations give different vectors.

contentBlocks.result: These instances agree with anti-commutativity, distributivity and scalar compatibility; associativity fails for the displayed triple.
contentBlocks.verification: The unequal results $0$ and $-j$ are a counterexample to associativity, not a failure of distributivity.

contentBlocks.title: Build a plane from its point and normal
contentBlocks.strategy: Substitute the point and normal into $n\cdot(x-p_0)=0$, then simplify.

steps.label: Use the point-normal equation
steps.text: The displacement from $p_0$ must be orthogonal to $n$.

steps.label: Simplify
steps.text: Collect the coordinate terms and constants.

contentBlocks.result: The plane is $2x+y-2z+3=0$.
contentBlocks.verification: The point $(2,-1,3)$ satisfies the equation; the coefficient vector $(2,1,-2)$ is its nonzero normal.

contentBlocks.title: Use two directions to find a plane
contentBlocks.strategy: Take the ordered cross product to get a normal, then use the point-normal plane equation.

steps.label: Find a normal
steps.text: The directions are nonzero and nonparallel, so their cross product is nonzero.

steps.label: Write the plane
steps.text: Use the normal and the point $p_0$.

contentBlocks.result: The plane is $z=x+y+2$; its parametric form is $(0,0,2)+s(1,0,1)+t(0,1,1)$.
contentBlocks.verification: The normal has zero dot product with each direction, and the plane contains $p_0$.

contentBlocks.title: Derive the graph plane from its slice directions
contentBlocks.strategy: Take the cross product of the two coordinate-slice tangent vectors, then apply the point-normal plane equation.
contentBlocks.setup: Let $f$ be defined on an open set, let $p=(a,b)$, and suppose $f_x(p)$ and $f_y(p)$ exist. Set $P=(a,b,f(p))$.

steps.label: Read the slice tangents
steps.text: Vary one coordinate at a time.

steps.label: Take their cross product
steps.text: The first two coordinates make these vectors independent, so the normal is nonzero.

steps.label: Use the point-normal equation
steps.text: Set the normal dot the displacement from $P$ equal to zero.

contentBlocks.result: The source-defined candidate tangent plane function is $z=f(p)+f_x(p)(x-a)+f_y(p)(y-b)$.
contentBlocks.verification: This derives the source-defined candidate plane from the two coordinate-slice directions. The separate differentiability lesson treats whether the candidate is a linear approximation.

contentBlocks.title: Apply the formula to a quadratic graph
contentBlocks.strategy: Evaluate the function and partials at the base point, then substitute into the candidate formula.

steps.label: Find the base value and slopes
steps.text: Differentiate each coordinate slice.

steps.label: Write the candidate plane
steps.text: Use the base point and the two slice slopes.

contentBlocks.result: The candidate tangent plane function is $z=4x+2y-3$.
contentBlocks.verification: At $(1,1)$ it has height $3$ and coordinate slopes $4$ and $2$, matching the graph there.

exercises.outcome: Compute and interpret an ordered cross product.
exercises.prompt: For $u=(2,-1,0)$ and $v=(1,3,4)$, compute $u\times v$, verify it is perpendicular to both inputs, find the parallelogram area, and state $v\times u$. Then take $p=(1,-2,3)$ and $q=-2p$; compute $p\times q$ and explain what its magnitude says about the parallelogram and its normal.
exercises.hint: Use the signed component formula; the area is the norm of the cross product. In the second pair, substitute the scalar multiple into the formula.
exercises.solution: $u\times v=(-4,-8,7)$. Its dot products with $u$ and $v$ are $-8+8=0$ and $-4-24+28=0$. Its norm is $\sqrt{16+64+49}=\sqrt{129}$, and $v\times u=(4,8,-7)$. Since $q=-2p$, $p\times q=p\times(-2p)=-2(p\times p)=0$; the parallelogram area is zero and this product gives no nonzero normal direction.
exercises.solutionTex: u\times v=(-4,-8,7),\quad \|u\times v\|=\sqrt{129},\quad v\times u=(4,8,-7),\quad p\times(-2p)=0
rubric: Compute the middle component with the correct sign.
Check orthogonality with both vectors.
Interpret the norm as area and reverse the orientation when the order is swapped.
Identify that dependent inputs give zero area and no nonzero cross-product normal.

exercises.outcome: Distinguish the valid cross-product laws from associativity.
exercises.prompt: Let $u=(1,0,1)$ and $v=(0,1,1)$. Verify $(-2u)\times v=-2(u\times v)$, compute $v\times u$ to compare the order, and verify $u\times(v+w)=(u\times v)+(u\times w)$ for $w=(1,1,0)$. Finally compare $(i\times i)\times j$ with $i\times(i\times j)$ using $i\times j=k$ and $i\times k=-j$.
exercises.hint: Use the component formula for the vector calculations. For the last comparison, preserve both sets of parentheses.
exercises.solution: $u\times v=(-1,-1,1)$, so $(-2u)\times v=(2,2,-2)=-2(u\times v)$. Reversing order gives $v\times u=(1,1,-1)=-(u\times v)$. Also $u\times w=(-1,1,1)$ and $u\times(v+w)=(-2,0,2)=u\times v+u\times w$. But $(i\times i)\times j=0$ while $i\times(i\times j)=i\times k=-j$; this counterexample shows associativity fails.
exercises.solutionTex: (-2u)\times v=(2,2,-2)=-2(u\times v),\quad v\times u=(1,1,-1),\quad u\times(v+w)=(-2,0,2)=u\times v+u\times w,\quad (i\times i)\times j=0\ne-j=i\times(i\times j)
rubric: Evaluate both sides of the scalar-compatibility identity.
Show reversing the input order negates the cross product.
Evaluate both sides of the distributive identity.
Keep the parentheses in the associativity test and use unequal vectors as a counterexample.

exercises.outcome: Construct a plane from a point and two nonparallel directions.
exercises.prompt: Find the plane through $(1,2,0)$ parallel to $u=(1,0,1)$ and $v=(0,1,1)$. Give both a point-normal equation and a parametric form.
exercises.hint: Compute $u\times v$ in the stated order, then use the point-normal equation.
rubric: Check the directions are nonzero and nonparallel.
Use a nonzero cross product as the normal.
Verify the point and both direction vectors satisfy the plane.

exercises.outcome: Derive a candidate graph plane from its coordinate-slice slopes.
exercises.prompt: For $f(x,y)=x^2+2xy+3y^2$ at $(1,-1)$, find the two slice tangent vectors, their cross-product normal, and the candidate tangent plane function.
exercises.hint: Compute $f$, $f_x$ and $f_y$ at the point, then use $(-f_x,-f_y,1)$.
rubric: Evaluate the base value and both partials.
Use the ordered cross product as a nonzero normal.

supplementalBlocks.title: Build the candidate, then test it
supplementalBlocks.text: When $f_x(a,b)$ and $f_y(a,b)$ exist, the supplement calls $L_{f,(a,b)}(x,y)=f(a,b)+f_x(a,b)(x-a)+f_y(a,b)(y-b)$ the tangent plane function. This formula defines the only possible affine first-order model. It is a proven linear approximation only if $|f(x,y)-L_{f,(a,b)}(x,y)|/\|(x-a,y-b)\|\to0$ as $(x,y)\to(a,b)$ through the domain.

supplementalBlocks.title: Read the arrows from total differentiability
supplementalBlocks.text: The source lists three necessary consequences: total differentiability at $p$ implies continuity, both coordinate partials exist, and the tangent-plane function is the unique linear approximation. It separately lists neighborhood existence and continuity of the partials as sufficient. The following derivation proves the three consequences without reversing any arrow.

supplementalBlocks.title: A total derivative forces its necessary properties
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Start from one full-radius remainder expansion; then restrict to continuity, coordinate slices, and competing linear maps.
supplementalBlocks.setup: At an interior point $p$, write $f(p+h)=f(p)+L(h)+r(h)$, where $L$ is linear and $r(h)/\|h\|\to0$.

steps.label: Continuity
steps.text: A linear map is bounded, so its contribution and the normalized remainder both vanish as $h\to0$.

steps.label: Coordinate partials
steps.text: Set $h=te_i$ and divide by $t$. The remainder quotient tends to zero because $\|te_i\|=|t|$.

steps.label: Unique linear approximation
steps.text: If $M$ is another linear approximation, then $(L-M)(h)=o(\|h\|)$. Put $h=tv$ for each fixed $v$; linearity makes the quotient constant, so it must be zero.

supplementalBlocks.result: Total differentiability implies continuity, existence of both coordinate partials, and uniqueness of the first-order linear map. These are necessary consequences, not converses.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The source page states each implication but gives no proof. The derivation uses its full-distance remainder definition; the guide checks the three consequences independently.

supplementalBlocks.title: A derivative forces the slice slopes
supplementalBlocks.statement: If $f$ is totally differentiable at an interior point $a$, each coordinate partial exists and the derivative map is $Df(a)h=\sum_i f_{x_i}(a)h_i$.
hypotheses: $a$ is an interior point of the domain.
$f(a+h)=f(a)+Lh+o(\|h\|)$ for one linear map $L$.

supplementalBlocks.title: Restrict the approximation to basis directions
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Set the full increment to a coordinate direction and read off each coefficient of the linear map.

steps.label: First coordinate
steps.text: Use $h=te_1$ and divide by nonzero $t$; $r(te_1)/t\to0$ because $|r(te_1)|/|t|\to0$.

steps.label: Other coordinates
steps.text: Repeat with every basis vector $e_i$; each partial equals $L(e_i)$.

steps.label: Linearity
steps.text: A linear map is determined by its basis values, so $Lh=\sum_i f_{x_i}(a)h_i$.

supplementalBlocks.result: The partials force a unique candidate; they do not prove its residual is small.
supplementalBlocks.verification: This is a one-way implication. The next lesson supplies a continuous function with all direction slopes but no total derivative.

supplementalBlocks.title: The full-radius remainder test
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Expand at an arbitrary base point and divide the residual by the full input distance.

steps.label: Expand
steps.text: The linear part is $2a_1h+2a_2k$ and the residual is $h^2+k^2$.

steps.label: Normalize
steps.text: For $r=\sqrt{h^2+k^2}>0$, the residual divided by $r$ equals $r$, independently of direction.

supplementalBlocks.result: $Df(a)(h,k)=2a_1h+2a_2k$ and the tangent plane is $z=f(a)+Df(a)(h,k)$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The bound covers every nonzero increment in the disk $r<\delta$, not selected lines alone.

exercises.outcome: Prove a candidate derivative with a full-radius bound.
exercises.prompt: For $f(x,y)=x^2+y^3$ at the origin, find the only candidate linear map and prove or disprove total differentiability using $r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$.
exercises.hint: Both partials vanish. Bound $|x^2+y^3|/r$ with $|x|,|y|\le r$.
exercises.solution: The coordinate partials at zero are both zero, so $L=0$. For $0<r<1$, $|f|/r\le x^2/r+|y|^3/r\le r+r^2\to0$. Thus $f$ is totally differentiable at zero.
rubric: Identify the unique candidate map.
Use one norm bound valid for every direction.
Conclude from the normalized residual, not a plot.

exercises.outcome: Use a verified total derivative to infer continuity and recover coordinate partials.
exercises.prompt: For $F(x,y)=1+2x-3y+(x^2+y^2)^{3/4}$ at the origin, verify total differentiability from its remainder, then use the necessary-consequences argument to state continuity and both partial derivatives.
exercises.hint: With $r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, the nonlinear remainder is $r^{3/2}$, so its quotient by $r$ tends to zero.
exercises.solution: $DF(0)(h,k)=2h-3k$ because $r^{3/2}/r=\sqrt r\to0$. Thus $F$ is totally differentiable and therefore continuous at zero. Restricting the linear map to the coordinate axes gives $F_x(0)=2$ and $F_y(0)=-3$.
rubric: Normalize the nonlinear remainder by the full Euclidean distance.
Use the verified total derivative to conclude continuity.
Read both partials from the coordinate directions.

exercises.outcome: Prove that two first-order linear approximations at one point must coincide.
exercises.prompt: At the origin let $G(x,y)=4+3x-2y+x^2+y^2$. Verify that $A(h,k)=3h-2k$ is a linear approximation, then prove that any other linear approximation $B$ equals $A$.
exercises.hint: The residual of $A$ is $h^2+k^2$. Subtract the two small remainders, then test the difference on $(t,0)$ and $(0,t)$.
exercises.solution: $G(h,k)-G(0,0)-A(h,k)=h^2+k^2$, whose quotient by $\sqrt{h^2+k^2}$ tends to zero. If $B$ is also an approximation, then $(A-B)(h,k)=o(\sqrt{h^2+k^2})$. Restricting to $(t,0)$ and $(0,t)$ shows both coefficients of $A-B$ vanish; hence $B=A$.
rubric: Verify the first candidate with its normalized remainder.
Subtract the two approximation conditions.
Use coordinate directions to prove equality of linear maps.

sections.title: One linear map for all increments
sections.text: At $a$, differentiability means $f(a+h)=f(a)+Lh+r(h)$ with $r(h)/\|h\|\to 0$. For scalar $f$ with existing partials, the only candidate is $Lh=\nabla f(a)\cdot h$. The candidate still needs an all-direction remainder check.

sections.title: Work a polynomial remainder
sections.text: For $f(x,y)=x^{2}+y^{2}$ at $(a,b)$, the exact increment is $2ah+2bk+h^{2}+k^{2}$. Dividing the remainder by $\sqrt{h^{2}+k^{2}}$ gives $\sqrt{h^{2}+k^{2}}\to 0$, proving differentiability. The affine tangent plane includes the base value $a^{2}+b^{2}$.

exercise.prompt: Find and justify the derivative of $f(x,y)=xy$ at $(a,b)$.
exercise.hint: Expand $(a+h)(b+k)$ and bound |hk|.
exercise.solution: The linear map is $L(h,k)=bh+ak$. The remainder is hk, with $|hk|/\sqrt{h^{2}+k^{2}}\leq \sqrt{h^{2}+k^{2}}/2\to 0$.
rubric: Identify a linear map, not just two numbers.
Prove a uniform remainder bound.

supplementalBlocks.title: Keep the implications one-way
supplementalBlocks.text: The one-page supplement lists four failed implications: continuity at $p$ does not force total differentiability; two partials at $p$ do not force continuity or make their candidate a linear approximation; and partial derivatives continuous at $p$ do not suffice without clarifying where they exist. The continuous example below separates continuity from differentiability and refutes the candidate. A zero extension supplies a distinct discontinuous example with two existing partials. The pointwise-continuity bullet needs a domain qualification: if both partials exist throughout an open neighborhood and are continuous at $p$, the MVT proof in the next route makes differentiability follow. The supplement does not state a counterexample or resolve this wording.

supplementalBlocks.title: One continuous function defeats its candidate plane
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Use axis slices to find the candidate, then one diagonal to disprove its full-radius remainder condition.
supplementalBlocks.setup: $q(x,y)=x^3/(x^2+y^2)$ off zero, extended by $q(0,0)=0$; this is distinct from the final-review numerator $x^3-xy^2$.

steps.label: Continuity
steps.text: $|q(x,y)|\le|x|\le r$, so $q\to0$ as $r\to0$.

steps.label: Candidate
steps.text: The axis slices give $q_x(0)=1$, $q_y(0)=0$, forcing $L(x,y)=x$.

steps.label: Diagonal obstruction
steps.text: At $(t,t)$, $q=t/2$ and $L=t$; normalize their difference by $\sqrt2|t|$.

supplementalBlocks.result: $q$ is continuous with all directional derivatives, yet not totally differentiable at zero.
supplementalBlocks.verification: For $v=(a,b)\ne0$, $D_vq(0)=a^3/(a^2+b^2)$ is not additive in $v$; a total derivative would be linear.

supplementalBlocks.title: Two existing partials do not force continuity
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Use the axis slices to find both partials, then test the diagonal.

steps.label: Find the coordinate partials
steps.text: Both coordinate-axis slices vanish, so $u_x(0,0)=u_y(0,0)=0$ and the candidate affine model is zero.

steps.label: Approach diagonally
steps.text: For every nonzero $t$, the diagonal value is $1/2$, while the value at the origin is zero.

steps.label: Separate continuity from approximation
steps.text: The function is discontinuous, and its candidate residual divided by distance grows without bound on this path.

supplementalBlocks.result: Existence of both coordinate partials at one point gives neither continuity nor a linear approximation there.
supplementalBlocks.verification: This distinct zero extension complements the continuous counterexample: together they separate the two failed implications listed on source page 1.

supplementalBlocks.title: Continuity on a partial's domain is not neighborhood existence
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Make the derivative functions continuous on their actual domains while leaving a line where the partials do not exist.

steps.label: Find where the partials exist
steps.text: At the origin both axis slices are zero. Off the line $y=x$, the function is locally zero. At a nonzero point of that line, each coordinate slice has a jump, so neither partial exists. Thus both partial functions are defined on $D=\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(t,t):t\ne0\}$.

steps.label: Check relative continuity
steps.text: Each partial function is identically zero on its domain, hence continuous at the origin relative to $D$.

steps.label: Check the function itself
steps.text: Along the omitted line, $w(t,t)=|t|\to0$, so $w$ is continuous at the origin. Its candidate is zero, but the normalized residual stays nonzero; the partials also fail to exist on any full neighborhood.

supplementalBlocks.result: The source pointwise-partial-continuity warning is valid when partial derivatives are continuous only on sparse domains that omit nearby points. With both partials defined on an open neighborhood and continuous at the point, the standard sufficient theorem applies.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The one-page source labels this implication false but gives no witness. This counterexample uses continuity on the derivative functions' domains; it does not contradict the neighborhood theorem stated in section :03.

exercises.outcome: Disprove total differentiability after computing the unique candidate and a normalized path residual.
exercises.prompt: Extend $p(x,y)=x^2y/(x^2+y^2)$ by zero at the origin. Find its coordinate partials and test total differentiability along $(t,t)$; also decide continuity.
exercises.hint: Both axis slices vanish. Along the diagonal, $p(t,t)=t/2$. Bound $|p|$ by a constant times $r$ for continuity.
exercises.solution: Both partials are zero, so $L=0$. For $t>0$, $|p(t,t)|/\sqrt{2t^{2}}=1/(2\sqrt{2})$, so no total derivative exists. Since $|p|=|y|x^{2}/r^{2}\leq |y|\leq r$, $p$ is continuous at zero.
rubric: Use definitions on the axes.
Normalize the diagonal remainder by Euclidean distance.
Prove continuity with an all-direction bound.

exercises.outcome: Disprove the implication from existence of two coordinate partials to continuity.
exercises.prompt: Define $v(x,y)=\frac{2xy}{x^2+3y^2}$ away from the origin and $v(0,0)=0$. Find both partials at the origin, then test continuity along $y=x$.
exercises.hint: Restrict to each coordinate axis for the partials. On the diagonal, simplify before taking the limit.
exercises.solution: Both axis restrictions are zero, so $v_x(0,0)=v_y(0,0)=0$. But $v(t,t)=1/2$ for $t\ne0$, so $v$ is not continuous at the origin. The partials at the point do not imply continuity.
rubric: Compute each partial from its coordinate slice.
Use a path limit to decide continuity.
Separate pointwise partial existence from continuity of the function.

exercises.outcome: Distinguish continuity of partial functions on their domains from their existence throughout a neighborhood.
exercises.prompt: Let $g(x,y)=2|x|$ when $y=2x\ne0$, and $g(x,y)=0$ otherwise. At the origin, determine where $g_x$ and $g_y$ exist, whether each partial function is continuous there on its domain, and whether $g$ is continuous or totally differentiable.
exercises.hint: Check the axes, an off-line point, a nonzero point on $y=2x$, and then the path $(t,2t)$.
exercises.solution: Both partials at the origin are zero. At every point off $y=2x$, the function is locally zero; at each nonzero point on the line, the coordinate slices jump, so the partials do not exist. Their domains omit that line except the origin, and both partial functions are zero on those domains, hence continuous at the origin relative to their domains. The function is also continuous at the origin because $g(t,2t)=2|t|\to0$. However, $|g(t,2t)|/\sqrt{t^2+4t^2}=2/\sqrt5$, so it is not totally differentiable.
rubric: Find the natural domains of both partial-derivative functions.
State the topology used for continuity at the origin.
Use the missing neighborhood and the diagonal path to reject differentiability.

sections.title: Directional existence is weaker
sections.text: For the displayed $f(x,y)=x^{3}/(x^{2}+y^{2})$, extended by zero, every directional derivative along $v=(a,b)$ exists and equals $a^{3}/(a^{2}+b^{2})$. This dependence on $v$ is not linear, so it cannot be a total derivative. The final-review lesson studies the distinct numerator $x^{3}-xy^{2}$.

sections.title: Test the only possible map
sections.text: Coordinate partials give $L(x,y)=x$. Along $(t,t)$, $f=t/2$ while $L=t$, so $|f-L|/\sqrt{2t^{2}}=1/(2\sqrt{2})$. The normalized error does not vanish. Yet $|f|\leq r$, so $f$ is continuous: continuity is another distinct property.

exercise.prompt: For the displayed $f$, compare directional derivatives in $e_1$, $e_2$ and $e_1+e_2$.
exercise.hint: A linear derivative must preserve addition.
exercise.solution: They are 1, 0 and $1/2$ respectively. Since $1/2\ne 1+0$, the directional-derivative map is not additive, ruling out total differentiability.
rubric: Use directional vectors consistently without silently normalizing.
Test linearity explicitly.

supplementalBlocks.title: Continuous partials are sufficient (imported)
supplementalBlocks.statement: If every first partial derivative exists near $a$ and is continuous at $a$, then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$.
hypotheses: $a$ is an interior point.
All first partials exist on a neighborhood of $a$ and are continuous at $a$.
prerequisites: Mean value theorem applied to coordinate increments

supplementalBlocks.title: Choose the proof route
supplementalBlocks.text: The $C^1$ criterion is sufficient, not necessary. If its neighborhood hypotheses fail, it gives no verdict; compute the unique candidate from partials and test the normalized residual directly. The exact final-review pair lets you compare a successful all-direction bound with a failed diagonal bound.

supplementalBlocks.title: Why the neighborhood criterion works
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Split the increment into coordinate moves, apply the one-variable mean-value theorem, and normalize the remainder.
supplementalBlocks.setup: Assume both partial derivatives exist on an open neighborhood of $p=(a,b)$ and are continuous at $p$. Let $r=\sqrt{h^2+k^2}$.

steps.label: Split the increment
steps.text: For small increments, both axis-parallel segments stay inside the neighborhood.

steps.label: Apply the mean-value theorem
steps.text: For some $\theta,\eta\in(0,1)$, the two changes use partial derivatives at points that approach $p$.

steps.label: Subtract the candidate linear map
steps.text: The candidate is $Df(p)(h,k)=f_x(p)h+f_y(p)k$. Continuity at $p$ makes both coefficient errors tend to zero.

steps.label: Bound every direction
steps.text: Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the error by the Euclidean size of its two coefficient errors, uniformly over all increments.

supplementalBlocks.result: The neighborhood existence plus continuity-at-$p$ hypothesis proves total differentiability. Continuity throughout the whole neighborhood is stronger than necessary.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The source states the sufficient criterion but supplies no proof. This guide derivation fills that gap and explains why the adjacent pointwise-continuity claim needs its partial-derivative domains stated.

exercises.outcome: Distinguish a sufficient $C^1$ criterion from the definition of differentiability.
exercises.prompt: Let $f(x,y)=|xy|$. At the origin, show differentiability directly. Can you apply the theorem requiring first partials throughout a neighborhood?
exercises.hint: Use $|xy|\le(x^2+y^2)/2$. At nearby points on an axis, check the partial in the transverse direction.
exercises.solution: Both coordinate partials at zero are zero, so $L=0$. Since $|f|/r\leq r/2\to 0$, $f$ is differentiable at zero. At $(0,y)$ with $y\ne 0$, the $x$ partial of |xy| does not exist, so the continuous-partials neighborhood theorem is unavailable. Its failure does not reverse the conclusion.
rubric: Prove differentiability with a uniform norm bound.
Identify a failed neighborhood hypothesis.
Do not treat a sufficient theorem as necessary.

exercises.outcome: Use neighborhood existence and pointwise continuity of partials to certify a candidate plane.
exercises.prompt: For $f(x,y)=e^{xy}+x^2$ at $p=(1,0)$, find its candidate tangent plane function and decide whether the continuous-partials theorem certifies total differentiability. State which neighborhood hypothesis you checked.
exercises.hint: Compute $f(p)$, $f_x(p)$ and $f_y(p)$. The formula is smooth on an open neighborhood of $p$, so both partials exist there and are continuous at $p$.
exercises.solution: $f(1,0)=2$, $f_x(x,y)=ye^{xy}+2x$, and $f_y(x,y)=xe^{xy}$, giving $f_x(1,0)=2$ and $f_y(1,0)=1$. Thus $L_{f,p}(x,y)=2+2(x-1)+y$. Both first partials exist on a neighborhood of $p$ and are continuous at $p$, so the sufficient theorem proves this candidate is the unique linear approximation there.
rubric: Calculate the base value and both partial derivatives correctly.
Check existence of both partials on an open neighborhood and continuity at the point.
Distinguish the candidate formula from its certification by the theorem.

exercises.outcome: Compute a first-order measurement estimate and test it against the exact worst-case change.
exercises.prompt: For $W(x,y)=x^2y$ measured at $(2,3)$ with $|\Delta x|\le0.05$ and $|\Delta y|\le0.1$, find the first-order absolute error estimate. Then expand the exact change and determine the exact maximum absolute error over the uncertainty box.
exercises.hint: Use $W_x=2xy$, $W_y=x^2$. On this positive box, check whether $W$ increases with both inputs.
exercises.solution: $W_x(2,3)=12$ and $W_y(2,3)=4$, so the first-order estimate is $12(0.05)+4(0.1)=1$. With $u=\Delta x,v=\Delta y$, the exact change is $12u+4v+3u^2+4uv+u^2v$. Both partials stay positive, so the extreme values occur at corners. The upper corner gives $1+0.0075+0.02+0.00025=1.02775$; the lower corner has absolute error $0.97275$. Thus the exact maximum is $1.02775$, larger than the linear estimate.
rubric: Evaluate both partial derivatives at the measured point.
Use absolute input tolerances in the first-order estimate.
Retain every nonlinear term in the exact expansion.
Justify the endpoint comparison using monotonicity on the box.

sections.title: A useful sufficient theorem
sections.text: If both first partials exist throughout an open neighborhood and are continuous at $a$, then $f$ is differentiable at $a$. This is sufficient, not necessary. Partial functions continuous on sparse domains do not meet the existence hypothesis, while neighborhood existence makes continuity at $a$ alone sufficient.

sections.title: Finite versus asymptotic error
sections.text: If a twice continuously differentiable $f$ has Hessian operator norm at most $M$ along the segment from a to $a+h$, Taylor gives $|f(a+h)-f(a)-\nabla f(a)\cdot h|\leq M|h|^{2}/2$. This finite bound needs an actual $M$; little-o alone does not provide one.

sections.title: Linearization estimates change, not finite error
sections.text: If $f$ is totally differentiable at an interior point $p$, then $f(p+h)=f(p)+Df(p)h+o(\|h\|)$. For measurement limits $|h_i|\le\varepsilon_i$, the derivative gives the first-order estimate $|Df(p)h|\le\sum_i|f_{x_i}(p)|\varepsilon_i$. The little-o term tends to zero relative to $\|h\|$; by itself it gives no fixed finite error bound.

exercise.prompt: Bound the tangent-plane error for $f=x^2+y^2$ at any base point when $|h|\le 0.01$.
exercise.hint: The Hessian is twice the identity.
exercise.solution: $M=2$, so the error is at most $|h|^{2}\leq 0.0001$. Here the remainder equals $|h|^{2}$ exactly.
rubric: Control the Hessian along the whole segment.
Distinguish a guaranteed bound from a sampled error.

contentBlocks.title: The linear error estimate assumes total differentiability
contentBlocks.statement: If $f:D\to\mathbb R$ is totally differentiable at an interior point $p$, then $f(p+h)-f(p)=Df(p)h+o(\|h\|)$ as $h\to0$. Componentwise measurement limits give a first-order estimate by maximizing the linear term over those limits.
hypotheses: $p$ is an interior point of the domain, so all sufficiently small increments remain in $D$.
$f$ is totally differentiable at $p$; partial derivatives at $p$ alone do not suffice.

contentBlocks.title: Separate the cone estimate from the exact error
contentBlocks.strategy: Check differentiability, apply the derivative to the measurement tolerances, then expand the exact change to test whether the estimate is a bound.
contentBlocks.setup: The cone volume is $V(r,h)=\frac{\pi}{3}r^2h$ for $r,h>0$. The measured values are $(10,25)$ with $|u|=|\Delta r|\le0.1$ and $|v|=|\Delta h|\le0.1$.

steps.label: Check the approximation hypothesis
steps.text: The domain $r>0,h>0$ is open and both partial derivatives are continuous there, so the continuous-partials criterion makes $V$ totally differentiable at $(10,25)$.

steps.label: Compute the first-order estimate
steps.text: At the measured point, weight each absolute input error by its sensitivity.

steps.label: Expand the exact change
steps.text: Keep the quadratic and mixed terms that the differential omits.

steps.label: Find the exact worst case
steps.text: Both partials are positive throughout the uncertainty box, so the maximum and minimum occur at opposite corners.

contentBlocks.result: The source’s $20\pi$ is a first-order estimate. The exact maximum absolute error over the stated box is $60.451\pi/3\approx20.1503\pi$, so $20\pi$ is not a guaranteed upper bound.
contentBlocks.verification: The conclusion uses monotonicity on the whole positive uncertainty box and compares both endpoint errors; little-o alone does not certify the finite maximum.

supplementalBlocks.title: Composition multiplies the linear parts
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Apply one differentiability expansion to the path and another to the field.

steps.label: Path increment
steps.text: $k=r(t+h)-r(t)$ is $O(|h|)$ because the path is differentiable.

steps.label: Field increment
steps.text: Substitute that $k$ into the field expansion. Since $\|k\|=O(|h|)$, the field remainder is $o(|h|)$.
steps.usesHypothesis: $f$ totally differentiable at $r(t)$; coordinate partials alone are insufficient.

steps.label: Linear coefficient
steps.text: The remaining first-order term is $Df(r(t))r'(t)h$.

supplementalBlocks.result: $(f\circ r)'(t)=Df(r(t))r'(t)=\nabla f(r(t))\cdot r'(t)$ for scalar $f$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: For $f=x^2+y^2$ and $r(t)=(t,t^2)$, both direct differentiation and the dot product give $2t+4t^3$.

exercises.outcome: Compute a composed rate with both coordinate contributions and verify it directly.
exercises.prompt: For $f(x,y)=xy$ and $r(t)=(t^2,t^3)$, compute $(f\circ r)'(t)$ by the multivariable chain rule and by first composing. Name the differentiability assumptions.
exercises.hint: Use $\nabla f=(y,x)$ and $r'=(2t,3t^2)$.
exercises.solution: The dot product is $(t^{3},t^{2})\cdot (2t,3t^{2})=5t^{4}$. Directly, $f(r(t))=t^{5}$ also differentiates to $5t^{4}$. Both $f$ and $r$ are polynomial maps, hence differentiable everywhere.
rubric: Evaluate the field derivative along the path.
Include both coordinate rates.
Check the composed expression and assumptions.

sections.title: Do not hide cancellation
sections.text: For $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$ and $r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$, the output is constant and its derivative zero. To see nonzero contributions, take $r(t)=(t,t^2)$: $f(r(t))=t^2+t^4$ and derivative $2t+4t^3$.

sections.title: Multiply derivative maps
sections.text: Along that path, $\nabla f(r(t))=(2t,2t^{2})$ and $r'(t)=(1,2t)$, whose dot product is $2t+4t^{3}$. More generally $D(f\circ g)=Df(g)Dg$, with matrix dimensions determined by the input and output spaces. Differentiability of both maps is a sufficient hypothesis.

exercise.prompt: For $f(x,y)=xe^y$ and $r(t)=(t,t^2)$, find $\frac{d}{dt}(f\circ r)$.
exercise.hint: Compute the two partial contributions separately.
exercise.solution: The derivative is $e^{t^2}\cdot 1+t e^{t^2}\cdot 2t=e^{t^2}(1+2t^2)$, agreeing with direct differentiation of $t e^{t^2}$.
rubric: Evaluate partials on the path.
Include both coordinate rates.
Check using the composed formula.

sections.title: Which variable can be solved for?
sections.text: For a $C^1$ equation $F(x,y,z)=0$, if $F_z(p)\ne0$ then a local $C^1$ graph $z=g(x,y)$ exists near $p$. Its derivatives are $g_x=-F_x/F_z$ and $g_y=-F_y/F_z$. This existence theorem is imported; differentiating a presumed graph alone does not prove its existence.

sections.title: Choose another chart when needed
sections.text: On the unit sphere at $(0,0,1)$, $F_z=2$ and a local $z$ graph exists. At $(1,0,0)$, $F_z=0$ but $F_x=2$, so $x$ can instead be expressed locally as a function of $y,z$. The surface remains smooth even though a chosen graph direction fails.

exercise.prompt: Find the tangent plane to $x^2+y^2+z^2=9$ at $(1,2,2)$.
exercise.hint: Use the nonzero gradient as normal.
rubric: Verify the point is on the surface.
Use a nonzero gradient.

supplementalBlocks.title: The gradient formula needs one linear map
supplementalBlocks.statement: If $f$ is totally differentiable at $p$, then $D_uf(p)=Df(p)u=\nabla f(p)\cdot u$ for any fixed vector $u$.
hypotheses: $p$ is an interior point and $f$ is totally differentiable there.
$u$ is fixed; choose $\|u\|=1$ for rate per unit distance.

supplementalBlocks.title: Restrict the full error to one line
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Substitute $h=tu$ in the full differentiability expansion.

steps.label: Restriction
steps.text: $f(p+tu)-f(p)=tDf(p)u+r(tu)$ by linearity.

steps.label: Divide
steps.text: $r(tu)/t$ tends to zero because $|r(tu)|/|t|=\|u\| |r(tu)|/\|tu\|\to0$.
steps.usesHypothesis: The remainder condition holds for all small vectors, hence this line.

supplementalBlocks.result: $D_uf(p)=Df(p)u$. Unit normalization changes interpretation, not existence.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The reverse implication is false; the preceding counterexample has every directional derivative but no total derivative.

exercises.outcome: Check total differentiability before replacing a directional limit by a gradient dot product.
exercises.prompt: For $q(x,y)=x^3/(x^2+y^2)$ off zero and $q(0)=0$, compare $D_{(1,1)}q(0)$ from its defining limit with $\nabla q(0)\cdot(1,1)$. Why may they differ?
exercises.hint: Along $(t,t)$, $q(t,t)=t/2$; axis partials are $(1,0)$.
exercises.solution: The defining limit gives $D_{(1,1)}q(0)=1/2$. The axis partials form gradient $(1,0)$, whose dot product with $(1,1)$ is 1. The dot-product theorem requires total differentiability, which fails for this $q$.
rubric: Use the unnormalized vector consistently.
Compute the directional limit directly.
Name the missing total-differentiability hypothesis.

sections.title: Normalize when measuring slope per distance
sections.text: For a differentiable scalar field, $D_{u}f=\nabla f\cdot u$. A unit $u$ measures change per unit distance; an arbitrary velocity $v$ includes its speed. For $f=x^{2}+3y^{2}$ at $(1,1)$, the gradient is $(2,6)$, so direction $(1,1)/\sqrt{2}$ gives slope $4\sqrt{2}$.

sections.title: Existence of the gradient is not the whole hypothesis
sections.text: Coordinate partials define a vector when they exist, but the dot-product formula for all directions is guaranteed by total differentiability. At singular examples, compute the directional derivative from its limit rather than assuming the formula.

exercise.prompt: Find the directional derivative of $f=x^2+y^2$ at $(1,2)$ in direction $(3,4)$.
exercise.hint: Normalize $(3,4)$ to length one.
exercise.solution: The gradient is $(2,4)$, so the unit-direction derivative is $(2,4)\cdot (3/5,4/5)=22/5$. Using velocity $(3,4)$ instead would give 22 per unit time.
rubric: Declare whether the vector is a direction or a velocity.
Evaluate the gradient at the requested point.

supplementalBlocks.title: Maximal first-order slope
supplementalBlocks.statement: At a totally differentiable point, the largest directional derivative over unit $u$ is $\|\nabla f(p)\|$.
hypotheses: $f$ is totally differentiable at $p$.
$u$ has unit length; if $\nabla f(p)\ne0$, normalize the gradient to identify a maximizing direction.

supplementalBlocks.title: Bound every unit direction
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Optimize the linear first-order response using Cauchy–Schwarz.

steps.label: Upper bound
steps.text: Cauchy–Schwarz gives $D_uf(p)\le|D_uf(p)|\le\|\nabla f(p)\|$.
steps.usesHypothesis: Total differentiability supplies the dot product formula.

steps.label: Equality
steps.text: If the gradient is nonzero, choose $u=\nabla f/\|\nabla f\|$; its dot product equals the norm.

steps.label: Stationary case
steps.text: If the gradient vanishes, all first-order directional slopes are zero, with no distinguished maximizing direction.

supplementalBlocks.result: The maximal first-order slope is $\|\nabla f(p)\|$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: This local linear statement does not promise globally increasing values along a finite step.

exercises.outcome: Interpret a zero gradient without inventing a unique ascent direction.
exercises.prompt: At the origin for $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$, what is the maximum unit directional derivative and which unit directions attain it? Does that say nearby values cannot increase?
exercises.hint: Compute the gradient at zero, then compare actual function values at nonzero nearby points.
exercises.solution: The gradient is zero, so every unit direction has first-order directional derivative zero; the maximum is zero and every unit direction attains it. Yet $f(x,y)=x^{2}+y^{2}>0$ at every nonzero nearby point, a second-order increase.
rubric: State the maximum slope and all maximizing unit directions.
Separate first-order slope from finite nearby values.
Do not claim a unique direction at zero gradient.

sections.title: The maximum slope is a norm
sections.text:
Cauchy–Schwarz gives $
abla f\cdot u\leq |
abla f|$ for unit $u$, with equality for $u=
abla f/|
abla f|$ when $
abla f
e 0$. At a stationary point all first-order slopes vanish, so the gradient picks no unique steepest direction.

sections.title: Contours and tangency
sections.text: If a differentiable curve lies in $f=c$, chain rule gives $\nabla f\cdot r'=0$. A nonzero gradient is normal to the level set. A zero gradient does not establish a smooth contour or a normal direction; inspect the geometry separately.

exercise.prompt: At $(1,1)$, find the steepest ascent direction for $f=x^2+2y^2$ and the maximum slope.
exercise.hint: Use gradient $(2,4)$.
exercise.solution: Its norm is $2\sqrt{5}$, and the unit direction is $(1,2)/\sqrt{5}$. The opposite direction gives steepest descent.
rubric: Normalize the direction.
Distinguish maximum slope from the direction vector.

sections.title: Use the domain in the definition
sections.text: A local minimum compares values in some neighborhood intersected with the domain. Interior differentiable extrema require zero gradient; boundary extrema do not. A saddle has nearby values on both sides of the point’s value.

sections.title: Stationarity admits every outcome
sections.text: At the origin, $x^{2}+y^{2}$ has a strict minimum, $-x^{2}-y^{2}$ a strict maximum, and $x^{2}-y^{2}$ a saddle. The zero function has non-strict maxima and minima everywhere. All have zero gradient at the origin.

sections.title: Coordinate restrictions prove necessity
sections.text: At an interior local extremum $p=(a,b)$, each coordinate slice through $p$ has a one-variable local extremum. If its derivative exists, Fermat’s theorem gives $f_x(p)=f_y(p)=0$. The converse fails: a zero gradient is only a candidate. The source also counts an interior point where a partial derivative fails to exist as critical.

sections.title: Critical is a candidate, not a verdict
sections.text: At $f(x,y)=y^2-x^2$, the origin is the only critical point but the $x$-axis gives negative values and the $y$-axis positive values arbitrarily close. Its zero gradient does not yield an extremum.

sections.title: A saddle needs two signs
sections.text: For a smooth stationary point, exhibit values both above and below $f(p)$ in every neighborhood to establish a saddle. A boundary point can be a domain-relative extremum without being an interior critical point.

sections.title: A missing partial is critical too
sections.text: For $f(x,y)=|x|-y^2$, the origin is interior but $f_x(0,0)$ does not exist. It is critical under the source definition even though its gradient is undefined. Along the axes, nearby values have opposite signs, so the point is neither a local minimum nor a local maximum.

exercise.prompt: Classify $f(x,y)=x^2-y^2$ at zero directly.
exercise.hint: Compare its coordinate axes.
exercise.solution: Along $(t,0)$, $f=t^{2}>0$; along $(0,t)$, $f=-t^{2}<0$ for nonzero $t$. Arbitrarily close values lie above and below $f(0,0)=0$, so the point is a saddle.
rubric: Produce both signs arbitrarily close.
Do not identify a saddle from stationarity alone.

supplementalBlocks.title: A boundary extremum uses the domain
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Check source hypotheses, calculate, then compare with the contrasting case.
supplementalBlocks.setup: On $D=[0,1]^2$, $f=x+y$ has a domain-relative local and absolute minimum at $(0,0)$.

steps.label: Reasoning
steps.text: For every $(x,y)\in D$, $x+y\ge0=f(0,0)$. The comparison quantifies only over $D$; $(0,0)$ is not interior, so the gradient condition is inapplicable.

supplementalBlocks.result: For every $(x,y)\in D$, $x+y\ge0=f(0,0)$. The comparison quantifies only over $D$; $(0,0)$ is not interior, so the gradient condition is inapplicable.

supplementalBlocks.title: Restrict before differentiating
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Check source hypotheses, calculate, then compare with the contrasting case.
supplementalBlocks.setup: Suppose $f$ has an interior local maximum at $(a,b)$ and both partials exist.

steps.label: Reasoning
steps.text: The slices $g(t)=f(t,b)$ and $h(t)=f(a,t)$ have local maxima at $a$ and $b$. One-variable Fermat gives $g'(a)=f_x(a,b)=0$ and $h'(b)=f_y(a,b)=0$.

supplementalBlocks.result: The slices $g(t)=f(t,b)$ and $h(t)=f(a,t)$ have local maxima at $a$ and $b$. One-variable Fermat gives $g'(a)=f_x(a,b)=0$ and $h'(b)=f_y(a,b)=0$.

supplementalBlocks.title: A critical point need not be an extremum
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Check source hypotheses, calculate, then compare with the contrasting case.

steps.label: Reasoning
steps.text: The only solution is $(0,0)$. Yet $f(t,0)=-t^2<0$ and $f(0,t)=t^2>0$ for $t\ne0$, so it is a saddle, not an extremum.

supplementalBlocks.result: The only solution is $(0,0)$. Yet $f(t,0)=-t^2<0$ and $f(0,t)=t^2>0$ for $t\ne0$, so it is a saddle, not an extremum.

supplementalBlocks.title: Classify a critical point without a gradient
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Check interior status, one-sided partials and nearby signs.

steps.label: Criticality
steps.text: At $(0,0)$, the $x$ partial has right quotient $1$ and left quotient $-1$, so $f_x$ does not exist. The point is interior and therefore critical.

steps.label: Classification
steps.text: $f(t,0)=|t|>0$ and $f(0,t)=-t^2<0$ for $t\ne0$. Nearby values have both signs, so no local extremum occurs.

supplementalBlocks.result: The origin is critical with an undefined gradient and no extremum.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The source definition on physical page 19 includes an undefined partial; the two axis comparisons verify the classification.

exercises.hint: Compare over $D$; inspect interior status.

exercises.prompt: For $f(x,y)=|x|+y^2$ on $\mathbb R^2$, is the origin critical? Does it have a local extremum?
exercises.hint: Compute the two one-sided $x$ quotients, then compare $|x|+y^2$ with zero.

sections.title: Order and notation
sections.text: Here $f_{xy}$ means differentiate first in $x$ and then in $y$. For $f=x^{2}y^{3}$, $f_{xy}=6xy^{2}=f_{yx}$. State the convention because subscript and operator notation are sometimes read in different orders.

sections.title: When swapping is justified
sections.text: Continuity of the second partials on a neighborhood is a sufficient condition for equality of mixed partials. Merely existing at one point is insufficient. Higher-order cancellation identities likewise need appropriate smoothness rather than formal rearrangement alone.

sections.title: Read the subscript order
sections.text: In this source, $f_{xy}=(f_x)_y$: first differentiate in $x$, then in $y$. The four second partials may have smaller domains than $f$.

sections.title: Equality needs neighborhood hypotheses
sections.text: Clairaut’s theorem requires both mixed partials to exist and be continuous on an open neighborhood of the point. The analogous third-order reorderings require the third partials to be defined and continuous nearby. Equality seen in an example is not itself a proof of the theorem.

exercise.prompt: Compute both mixed partials of $f=xe^y+y \sin x$.
exercise.hint: Differentiate in the stated order each time.
exercise.solution: $f_x=e^y+y\cos x$, so $f_{xy}=e^y+\cos x$. Also $f_y=xe^y+\sin x$, so $f_{yx}=e^y+\cos x$. Smoothness justifies equality.
rubric: Show both orders.
Name a sufficient regularity condition.

supplementalBlocks.title: Compute every second partial
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Check source hypotheses, calculate, then compare with the contrasting case.

steps.label: Reasoning
steps.text: First $f_x=2xy+1/x$ and $f_y=x^2-3y^2$. Hence $f_{xx}=2y-1/x^2$, $f_{xy}=2x$, $f_{yx}=2x$, $f_{yy}=-6y$. The formula is valid only for $x>0$.

supplementalBlocks.result: First $f_x=2xy+1/x$ and $f_y=x^2-3y^2$. Hence $f_{xx}=2y-1/x^2$, $f_{xy}=2x$, $f_{yx}=2x$, $f_{yy}=-6y$. The formula is valid only for $x>0$.

supplementalBlocks.strategy: Check source hypotheses, calculate, then compare with the contrasting case.

steps.label: Reasoning
steps.text: $g_{xy}=6xy^2=g_{yx}$. Also $g_{xxy}=6y^2=g_{xyx}=g_{yxx}$. Polynomial partials are continuous on an open neighborhood of each point; mere pointwise existence would not supply this justification.

sections.title: Quadratic forms decide second-order shape
sections.text: For a $C^{2}$ scalar field at a stationary point, the quadratic Taylor term is $h^{T}Hh/2$. A positive-definite Hessian gives a strict minimum, a negative-definite one a strict maximum, and an indefinite one a saddle. In two dimensions, determinant positive plus $f_{xx}>0$ or $f_{xx}<0$ distinguishes the two definite cases.

sections.title: Mixed terms can rotate the shape
sections.text: For $f=x^{2}+4xy+y^{2}$, $H=[[2,4],[4,2]]$ has eigenvalues 6 and $-2$. Coordinate-axis slices both rise, yet along $y=-x$ the value is $-2x^{2}$, so it is a saddle. A zero determinant is inconclusive; compare $x^{4}+y^{4}$ with $x^{4}-y^{4}$.

sections.title: Use the determinant with hypotheses
sections.text: At a zero-gradient critical point, first check that all second partials are continuous on an open neighborhood. Then $D=f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2$: $D>0$ and $f_{xx}>0$ means local minimum; $D>0$ and $f_{xx}<0$ local maximum; $D<0$ saddle; $D=0$ gives no classification.

sections.title: Solve the complete stationary set
sections.text: For $f=\sin(xy)$, $\nabla f=\cos(xy)(y,x)$. Thus critical points include the origin and every hyperbola $xy=(k+1/2)\pi$. At the origin $D=-1$; on each hyperbola $D=0$, so use the global range $-1\le f\le1$ to classify the latter.

sections.title: Zero determinant asks for more
sections.text: A zero determinant cannot be read as a saddle or flat extremum. On $xy=(k+1/2)\pi$, $\sin(xy)=(-1)^k$: even $k$ gives absolute maxima and odd $k$ absolute minima. Their nonisolated nature does not prevent an extremum.

exercise.prompt: Classify $f=-2x^2-2xy-2y^2$ at zero.
exercise.hint: Compute the Hessian determinant and one diagonal entry.
exercise.solution: $H=[[-4,-2],[-2,-4]]$, determinant $12>0$ and $f_{xx}<0$, so it is negative definite and zero is a strict local maximum. Completing squares also shows global maximality.
rubric: Retain the mixed-term contribution.
State local classification and justify any global claim separately.

supplementalBlocks.title: Apply the full two-variable test
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Check source hypotheses, calculate, then compare with the contrasting case.

steps.label: Reasoning
steps.text: Compute $q_{xx}=2$, $q_{yy}=2$, $q_{xy}=4$, so $D=4-16=-12<0$. It is a saddle, confirmed by $q(t,0)=t^2>0$ and $q(t,-t)=-2t^2<0$.

supplementalBlocks.result: Compute $q_{xx}=2$, $q_{yy}=2$, $q_{xy}=4$, so $D=4-16=-12<0$. It is a saddle, confirmed by $q(t,0)=t^2>0$ and $q(t,-t)=-2t^2<0$.

sections.title: Existence then candidate search
sections.text: A continuous function on a nonempty compact set attains maximum and minimum. Search interior stationary points, smooth boundary stationary points, corners, and singular locations. A local Hessian test does not compare all candidates.

sections.title: A disk example
sections.text: For $f=x^{2}+y^{2}-2x$ on the closed unit disk, the unconstrained stationary point is $(1,0)$, on the boundary. On the boundary $f=1-2x$, so its values range from $-1$ at $(1,0)$ to 3 at $(-1,0)$. Completing the square $f=(x-1)^{2}+y^{2}-1$ confirms the minimum.

sections.title: Existence comes before searching
sections.text: A continuous function on a nonempty closed bounded domain in Euclidean space attains both absolute extrema. Without closedness or boundedness, existence requires another argument; a gradient calculation alone cannot supply it.

sections.title: Search every part of the domain
sections.text: On a rectangle, solve interior critical equations, restrict to each of four edges, include their endpoints, and compare all values. The Hessian test classifies local interior shape but is unnecessary for the global value comparison.

sections.title: Compare values, including ties
sections.text: For the source rectangle $[0,3]\times[0,2]$ and $f=x^2-2xy+2y$, the interior value is 1 at $(1,1)$. The four edge restrictions are $x^2$, $9-4y$, $(x-2)^2$, and $2y$. Their endpoints and edge stationary points reveal two global minimizers and one maximizer.

exercise.prompt: Find extrema of $f=x+y$ on the square $[0,1]^2$.
exercise.hint: There are no interior stationary points; inspect the boundary and corners.
exercise.solution: The minimum is 0 at $(0,0)$, maximum 2 at $(1,1)$. Monotonicity in each coordinate proves these global bounds.
rubric: Include boundary candidates.
Explain attainment on the closed bounded set.

supplementalBlocks.title: Check the theorem hypotheses
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Check source hypotheses, calculate, then compare with the contrasting case.

steps.label: Reasoning
steps.text: The polynomial is continuous; the rectangle is closed and bounded. Thus absolute minimum and maximum exist. This gives existence, not locations; interior and boundary checks follow.

sections.title: Tangency is a necessary condition
sections.text:
For a smooth constraint $g=c$ with $
abla g
e 0$, a constrained extremum has $
abla f=\lambda 
abla g$. Both gradients are normal to the same tangent directions. Solve the multiplier equations together with the original constraint.

sections.title: A singular constraint can hide candidates
sections.text: For $g(x,y)=x^{3}-y^{2}=0$ at zero, $\nabla g=0$. The usual regular multiplier condition cannot be assumed there. Keep such feasible singular points as separate candidates instead of dividing by a gradient component.

sections.title: Regularity gives a necessary equation
sections.text:
On an open neighborhood of the feasible level curve, continuous gradients and $
abla g
e0$ imply that a constrained extremum, if it exists, satisfies $
abla f=\lambda
abla g$. The equation alone neither proves existence nor selects a maximum or minimum.

sections.title: Candidates need a global certificate
sections.text: Solve $g=k$ together with both component equations, retaining branches where a coordinate is zero. Compare all resulting $f$ values. On a closed bounded feasible curve, continuity and the Extreme Value Theorem certify the largest and smallest candidate values as global extrema.

sections.title: Do not divide away a branch
sections.text: For $f=x^2+2y^2$ on $x^2+y^2=1$, the equations are $x=\lambda x$ and $2y=\lambda y$. The $x=0$ and $y=0$ branches both matter; dividing by $xy$ would lose every answer.

exercise.prompt: Find the extrema of $x+y$ on $x^2+y^2=1$.
exercise.hint: The equations $1=2\lambda x$ and $1=2\lambda y$ force $x=y$.
exercise.solution: The candidates are $(\pm 1/\sqrt{2},\pm 1/\sqrt{2})$ with matching signs, giving $\pm \sqrt{2}$. Compactness ensures extrema, and Cauchy–Schwarz independently bounds $|x+y|\leq \sqrt{2}$.
rubric: Keep the constraint equation.
Compare all candidates and justify globality.

steps.label: Regularity
steps.text: $\nabla g=(2x,2y)\ne0$ at every feasible point, and both gradients are continuous on $\mathbb R^2$.

steps.label: Condition
steps.text:
At any constrained extremum, tangential derivatives vanish, so $
abla f$ lies in the span of $
abla g$ and $
abla f=\lambda
abla g$.

steps.label: Equations
steps.text: $2x=2\lambda x$ and $4y=2\lambda y$, hence $x=0$ or $\lambda=1$, and $y=0$ or $\lambda=2$.

steps.label: Branches

steps.label: Compare
steps.text: The objective is $2$ at $(0,\pm1)$ and $1$ at $(\pm1,0)$. The circle is compact, so these are the global maximum and minimum.

sections.title: One constraint leaves a tangent plane
sections.text:
On a regular level surface in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$, tangent vectors are perpendicular to $
abla g$. At a constrained extremum the derivative of $f$ vanishes along that entire plane, making $
abla f$ a multiple of $
abla g$.

sections.title: Linear objective on a sphere
sections.text: For $f=x+2y+2z$ on the unit sphere, $\nabla f=(1,2,2)$ and $\nabla g=2(x,y,z)$. The candidates are $\pm (1,2,2)/3$, giving values $\pm 3$. Norm comparison proves these are global extrema.

sections.title: A surface condition is necessary only
sections.text:
For a regular level surface $g=k$ in $\mathbb R^3$, continuous gradients and $
abla g
e0$ make $
abla f=\lambda
abla g$ necessary at a constrained extremum. An open or unbounded feasible set needs a separate global bound.

sections.title: Model the open-top box
sections.text: With positive length $x$, width $y$, and height $z$, the volume is $V=xyz$ and cardboard area is $A=xy+2xz+2yz$. Positivity is part of the domain; a zero dimension is not a feasible box.

sections.title: Solve without losing positivity
sections.text: For $A=12$, the multiplier equations imply $x=y=2z$ and then $(x,y,z)=(2,2,1)$ with volume $4$. This is a candidate, not yet a global maximum.

sections.title: Certify the open-domain maximum
sections.text: The positive feasible set is neither closed nor bounded, so the Extreme Value Theorem does not certify the candidate. AM–GM on $xy$, $2xz$, and $2yz$ gives $(4V^2)^{1/3}\le4$, hence $V\le4$. Equality requires all three area terms equal, giving the unique maximizer $(2,2,1)$.

exercise.prompt: Maximize $2x-y+2z$ on $x^2+y^2+z^2=4$.
exercise.hint: Use Cauchy–Schwarz or solve the multiplier equations.
exercise.solution: The coefficient vector has norm 3 and the sphere radius is 2, so the maximum is 6 at $(4/3,-2/3,4/3)$.
rubric: Scale the maximizing unit vector by the radius.
Check the point satisfies the constraint.

supplementalBlocks.title: Model and check the regular surface
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Check regularity and domain, solve the constraint system, then justify the global conclusion separately.

steps.label: Gradients
steps.text: $\nabla V=(yz,xz,xy)$ and $\nabla A=(y+2z,x+2z,2x+2y)$.

steps.label: Regularity
steps.text: Every component of $\nabla A$ is positive in the domain, so the regular one-constraint condition applies to any attained extremum.

supplementalBlocks.result: At an attained constrained extremum, solve $\nabla V=\lambda\nabla A$ together with $A=12$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: Physical pages 12–14 give the regularity theorem and open-top area model.

supplementalBlocks.title: Solve the positive box equations
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Check regularity and domain, solve the constraint system, then justify the global conclusion separately.

steps.label: System
steps.text: $yz=\lambda(y+2z)$, $xz=\lambda(x+2z)$, and $xy=2\lambda(x+y)$.

steps.label: Eliminate
steps.text: Positivity implies $\lambda>0$. Multiply the first two equations by $x$ and $y$ to get $x(y+2z)=y(x+2z)$, hence $x=y$. Compare with the third equation to get $x=2z$.

supplementalBlocks.result: The only positive multiplier candidate is $(2,2,1)$; its global status still needs proof.
supplementalBlocks.verification: Physical pages 15–16 give this candidate; all divisions use positive quantities.

supplementalBlocks.title: A global bound without compactness
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Check regularity and domain, solve the constraint system, then justify the global conclusion separately.
supplementalBlocks.setup: For every positive feasible box with $xy+2xz+2yz=12$, bound $V=xyz$.

steps.label: Equality
steps.text: $V\le4$. Equality requires $xy=2xz=2yz=4$, giving uniquely $x=y=2$, $z=1$.

supplementalBlocks.result: $V$ has global maximum $4$ at the unique box $(2,2,1)$ despite the noncompact feasible set.
supplementalBlocks.verification: Physical pages 16–17 show nonclosed/unbounded witnesses and this AM–GM certificate.

exercises.outcome: Transfer open-box modeling and global certification.
exercises.prompt: An open-top box has base-material cost $1$ per unit area and side-material cost $3/2$ per unit area. With budget $18$, maximize its volume over positive dimensions. Use multipliers for candidates, then a separate global certificate.
exercises.hint: The budget is $A=xy+3xz+3yz=18$. Solve the positive multiplier equations; then apply AM–GM to $xy$, $3xz$, $3yz$.
exercises.solution: $\nabla A=(y+3z,x+3z,3x+3y)$ is nonzero on the positive domain. The positive multiplier equations are $yz=\lambda(y+3z)$, $xz=\lambda(x+3z)$, and $xy=3\lambda(x+y)$. Multiplying the first two by $x$ and $y$ gives $x=y$; then the third gives $\lambda=x/6$, and the first gives $x=3z$. Thus $3x^2=18$ and the candidate is $(x,y,z)=(\sqrt6,\sqrt6,\sqrt6/3)$. For every feasible box, $(9V^2)^{1/3}=((xy)(3xz)(3yz))^{1/3}\le18/3=6$, hence $V\le2\sqrt6$. Equality requires $xy=3xz=3yz=6$, reached uniquely at that candidate.
rubric: Model the higher side-material cost correctly.
Check regularity and solve every positive candidate.
Use equality in AM–GM to certify the global maximum.

sections.title: Independence matters
sections.text:
For two constraints $g=c$ and $h=d$ in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$, independent gradients give a tangent direction $
abla g	imes 
abla h$. At a constrained extremum, $
abla f$ lies in their span: $
abla f=\lambda 
abla g+\mu 
abla h$. Dependent gradients invalidate this regular argument.

sections.title: Reduce when possible
sections.text: On $x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=1$ and $z=0$, maximizing $x+y$ reduces to the unit circle in the xy-plane. The two gradients $(2x,2y,0)$ and $(0,0,1)$ are independent everywhere on the feasible circle, so the multiplier method is legitimate.

sections.title: Two gradients must have rank two
sections.text:
For two equality constraints in $\mathbb R^3$, the regular theorem needs $
abla g$ and $
abla h$ linearly independent at the feasible extremum. Physical page 18 states only a nonzero-gradient pair; that is insufficient. If the gradients are dependent, inspect the feasible geometry directly before using $
abla f=\lambda
abla g+\mu
abla h$.

sections.title: The source gives a prompt only
sections.text: Physical page 19 asks for extrema of $x^2+y^2+z^2$ on the cone $z^2=x^2+y^2$ intersected with $x+y-z+1=0$. Physical pages 20–23 carry continuation headings but no readable worked solution. The calculation below is an independent derivation, not a transcription of source answers.

exercise.prompt: Find extrema of $x$ on $x^2+y^2+z^2=1$ with $y=z$.
exercise.hint: Either use two multipliers or observe the feasible circle contains $(\pm 1,0,0)$.
exercise.solution: Since $|x|\leq 1$ on the sphere and both $(\pm 1,0,0)$ satisfy $y=z$, extrema are $\pm 1$ at those points. The constraint gradients are independent throughout the intersection.
rubric: Check feasibility of equality cases.
Identify the regularity assumption when using multipliers.

supplementalBlocks.title: Nonzero gradients can still be dependent
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Check regularity and domain, solve the constraint system, then justify the global conclusion separately.

steps.label: Feasible set
steps.text: $x=0$ and $y^2+z^2=0$ leave only the origin, so $f$ has both a constrained minimum and maximum there.

steps.label: Rank failure
steps.text:
At the origin, $
abla g=
abla h=(1,0,0)$: both are nonzero but dependent. $
abla f=(0,1,0)$ is not in their span.

supplementalBlocks.result: The source page’s nonzero condition cannot imply the two-multiplier conclusion; rank two is required.
supplementalBlocks.verification: Independent counterexample to the insufficient condition printed on physical page 18.

supplementalBlocks.title: Derive the cone-plane answer independently
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Check regularity and domain, solve the constraint system, then justify the global conclusion separately.

steps.label: Reduce
steps.text: Put $u=x+1$, $v=y+1$. Eliminating $z=x+y+1=u+v-1$ gives $uv=1/2$ and $f=2(u+v-1)^2$.

steps.label: Compare branches
steps.text: $u,v$ have the same sign. On the positive branch, $u+v\ge\sqrt2$, with equality at $u=v=1/\sqrt2$. On the negative branch, $u+v\le-\sqrt2$, giving larger $|z|$.

steps.label: Global verdict
steps.text: The minimum is $2(\sqrt2-1)^2$ at $x=y=1/\sqrt2-1$, $z=\sqrt2-1$. As $u\to\infty$ with $v=1/(2u)$, $f\to\infty$, so no maximum exists.

steps.label: Regularity
steps.text: For $g=z^2-x^2-y^2$ and $h=x+y-z+1$, dependent $\nabla g$ and $\nabla h$ on the cone would force the apex $(0,0,0)$, which is not on the plane; rank two holds on this feasible set.

supplementalBlocks.result: The source prompt has a unique global minimum and no maximum; this solution is derived here, because source pages 20–23 show none.
supplementalBlocks.verification: Checked algebra and feasible points independently against the page 19 prompt; no source solution claimed.

exercises.outcome: Decide whether nonzero constraint gradients justify two multipliers.
exercises.prompt: At the origin, take $g=x$, $h=2x+y^2+z^2$, and $f=z$, with $g=h=0$. Does the two-multiplier necessary condition apply?
exercises.hint: Find the feasible set and compare the two constraint gradients at the origin.
exercises.solution:
The feasible set is only the origin, so it is a constrained extremum of $f$. Yet $
abla g=(1,0,0)$ and $
abla h=(2,0,0)$ are nonzero but dependent; $
abla f=(0,0,1)$ lies outside their span. The regular two-multiplier theorem does not apply.
rubric: Check linear independence, not mere nonzero status.
Show the feasible geometry and failed span conclusion.

exercises.outcome: Solve a regular two-constraint problem independently.
exercises.prompt: Find both extrema of $f=z$ on $x^2+y^2+z^2=1$ and $x+y=0$, checking regularity.
exercises.hint: Use $x=-y$ and $z^2=1-2x^2$; check the two constraint gradients are independent on the feasible circle.
exercises.solution: $-1\le z\le1$, with maximum $1$ at $(0,0,1)$ and minimum $-1$ at $(0,0,-1)$. The gradients $(2x,2y,2z)$ and $(1,1,0)$ cannot be parallel on the feasible set: parallelism plus $x+y=0$ would force $x=y=z=0$, contradicting the sphere.
rubric: Identify both feasible equality points.
Justify rank two on the full feasible set.

sections.title: Cells contribute value times area
