sections.text: Over a rectangle, a double Riemann sum adds $f(\text{sample})\Delta x\Delta y$. Both widths are essential. Integrability requires independence of increasingly fine tagged partitions; a single sampled mesh is a numerical approximation.

sections.title: Signed volume versus physical volume
sections.text: If $f\geq 0$, the integral is volume under its graph. If $f$ takes both signs, it is signed accumulation. For $f=x$ on $[-1,1]\times [0,1]$, the integral is zero while the volume between graph and plane is $\int |x|=1$.

exercise.prompt: Compute the double integral of constant 3 over $[0,2]\times [0,4]$.
exercise.hint: Every cell contributes three times its area.
exercise.solution: The rectangle area is 8, so the integral is 24. With density units $kg/m^{2}$ and coordinates in metres, the result is kilograms.
rubric: Include both dimensions of area.
Interpret the units of the integrand.

sections.title: A sufficient computational framework
sections.text: For a bounded region with a boundary of area zero and a function continuous on its closure, the double integral can be defined by extending the function by zero to a containing rectangle. The extension may jump at the region boundary but remains Riemann integrable under these sufficient assumptions.

sections.title: Name the stronger theorem
sections.text: The criterion that a bounded function on a rectangle is Riemann integrable when its discontinuity set has area zero is imported here. Lebesgue integration extends beyond Jordan regions and is an optional advanced framework, not a prerequisite silently hidden inside the elementary continuous-rectangle theorem.

exercise.prompt: Why can a continuous density on a disk be extended by zero for integration on a containing square?
exercise.hint: Where can new discontinuities occur?
exercise.solution: Only the circular boundary can acquire jumps. That boundary has area zero, so the bounded zero extension is Riemann integrable by the stated criterion. Its integral equals the disk integral.
rubric: Identify the possible discontinuity set.
Invoke the appropriate extension theorem.

sections.title: Order is a theorem, not typography
sections.text: A continuous function on a closed rectangle has equal double and iterated integrals. For zero extensions over ordinary piecewise smooth regions, a stronger integrability version is required because the extension may have boundary jumps.

sections.title: A sufficient extension for calculations
sections.text: For a bounded Riemann-integrable function whose slices are integrable apart from finitely many exceptional outer values, the iterated integrals agree with the double integral; changing bounded values on those exceptional slices does not affect it. In the Lebesgue setting, absolute integrability permits Fubini and nonnegativity permits Tonelli, but those are separate imported results.

exercise.prompt: Compute $\int_0^1\int_0^2(x+y)\,dy\,dx$ in both orders.
exercise.hint: The rectangle and continuous polynomial satisfy the elementary theorem.
exercise.solution: Integrating in $y$ gives $2x+2$, then total 3. Reversing gives $\int_0^2(1/2+y)\,dy=3$. The domain remains the same rectangle.
rubric: State why the swap is valid.
Keep each variable’s interval attached to it.

sections.title: Bounds describe a set
sections.text: The region $0\leq x\leq 1$, $x^{2}\leq y\leq x$ lies between a parabola and a line. For horizontal slices, $0\leq y\leq 1$ and $y\leq x\leq \sqrt{y}$. Derive these inequalities before changing the integration order.

sections.title: Split when one slice formula fails
sections.text: A region may need several Type I or Type II pieces. Splitting along an internal boundary does not duplicate area if pieces overlap only on boundaries of area zero. Draw or solve each boundary intersection and determine which curve actually limits a slice.

exercise.prompt: Reverse $\int_0^1\int_{x^2}^x f(x,y)\,dy\,dx$.
exercise.hint: Solve $y\geq x^{2}$ and $y\leq x$ in the nonnegative quadrant.
exercise.solution: The reversed integral is $\int_0^1\int_y^{\sqrt{y}}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy$. The conditions give $x\leq \sqrt{y}$ and $x\geq y$.
rubric: Derive both horizontal bounds.
Preserve the region and integrand.

sections.title: Linearity concerns values
sections.text: For integrable $f$,$g$, $\int (af+bg)=a\int f+b\int g$. It does not assert that $\int fg=(\int f)(\int g)$. A product separates only under additional structure, such as independent factors on a product rectangle.

sections.title: Additivity concerns regions
sections.text: If a region is split into pieces overlapping only on negligible boundaries, add their integrals. For signed accumulation, negative contributions remain negative. Overlapping pieces with positive area require subtracting the overlap to avoid double counting.

exercise.prompt: If $\iint_D f\,dA=2$ and $\iint_D g\,dA=-1$, find $\iint_D(3f-2g)\,dA$. Can you infer $\iint_D fg\,dA$?
exercise.hint: Apply linearity only to the linear combination.
exercise.solution: The first integral is $3\cdot 2-2\cdot (-1)=8$. The product integral cannot be determined from these two numbers alone.
rubric: Handle the negative coefficient.
Do not invent multiplicativity.

contentBlocks.title: Keep linearity on one fixed region
contentBlocks.text: For integrable $f$ and $g$ on the same bounded region $D$ and real scalars $a,b$, integration preserves sums and scalar multiples. The region stays fixed; this rule does not make integration multiplicative.

contentBlocks.title: Apply linearity without changing the domain
contentBlocks.strategy: Compute each integral on the common domain, then combine the results with the same coefficients.
contentBlocks.setup: On the unit square $D=[0,1]\times[0,1]$, let $f(x,y)=1+x$ and $g(x,y)=y$.

steps.label: Integrate each function
steps.text: The two component integrals are evaluated on the same unit square.

steps.label: Combine linearly
steps.text: Use the coefficients from the integrand; no product rule is involved.

contentBlocks.result: The common-domain integral is $3/2$.
contentBlocks.verification: Directly, $2f-3g=2+2x-3y$; its integral over the unit square is $2+1-3/2=3/2$.

contentBlocks.title: Restrict the integrand to the subregion
contentBlocks.text: If $D$ is a bounded subregion of an ambient region $R$, the restricted-domain integral uses only the values of $f$ on $D$. The domain restriction preserves the original integrand values wherever the smaller region lies inside the larger one.

contentBlocks.title: Restrict a unit-square integral to a triangle
contentBlocks.strategy: Keep the same function values on the chosen subset and integrate only over that subset.
contentBlocks.setup: Let $D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le1,\ 0\le y\le x\}$ inside $R=[0,1]^2$, with $f(x,y)=1$.

steps.label: Read the restricted domain
steps.text: The triangle occupies half of the ambient unit square.

steps.label: Integrate over the subset
steps.text: Only points in D contribute to the restricted integral.

contentBlocks.result: The integral of one over this triangle is its area, $1/2$.
contentBlocks.verification: The ambient square has area one; the diagonal divides it into two congruent right triangles.

contentBlocks.title: Add pieces when their overlaps have zero area
contentBlocks.text: For finitely many bounded regions, finite additivity requires existing component integrals and pairwise intersections of area zero. A shared boundary is allowed; overlapping interiors would count positive area more than once.

contentBlocks.title: Check a shared edge before adding
contentBlocks.strategy: Verify the intersection has area zero, then sum the integrals on the two pieces.

steps.label: Check the intersection
steps.text: The pieces meet on one vertical segment, which has planar area zero.

steps.label: Add the integrals
steps.text: The boundaries do not contribute a duplicate area term.

contentBlocks.result: The integral over the union is 4.
contentBlocks.verification: Directly, $\int_0^2(1+x)\,dx=4$; the shared edge changes no area integral.

contentBlocks.title: Split a non-simple region into simple pieces
contentBlocks.text: A bounded region that is not Type I or Type II can still be integrated by a finite union of Type I/II pieces, provided every pairwise overlap has area zero and each piece integral exists. Choose cuts that make each piece have a single simple-slice description.

contentBlocks.title: Split a diamond into two Type I regions
contentBlocks.strategy: Use a vertical cut so each half has one lower and one upper graph.
contentBlocks.setup: Let $D=\{(x,y):|x|+|y|\le2\}$. Split at $x=0$ into left and right halves.

steps.label: Write the left fibers
steps.text: For each x from −2 to 0, y runs between the two edges.

steps.label: Write the right fibers
steps.text: For each x from 0 to 2, use the symmetric upper and lower edges.

steps.label: Check the cut and total area
steps.text: The halves share only a line; each triangle has area four.

contentBlocks.result: The split replaces a non-simple description by two Type I integrals.
contentBlocks.verification: The diamond has diagonals of length four, so its area is $(4\cdot4)/2=8$.

contentBlocks.title: Account for all three source pieces
contentBlocks.text: The Lecture 06 example integrates $2x+5y$ over a non-simple region by describing one Type I part and two Type II parts. Its three shared intersections are boundary segments or a point, so finite additivity applies.

contentBlocks.title: Reconstruct the three-piece source calculation
contentBlocks.strategy: List each piece with its own slicing direction, retain the signed component values, and verify the intersections before summing.
contentBlocks.setup: The source example splits the target region into the following pieces.

steps.label: Write the vertical piece
steps.text: The first source component is Type I, with vertical slices below the parabolic boundary.

steps.label: Write the upper horizontal piece
steps.text: The second component uses y as the outer variable.

steps.label: Write the lower horizontal piece
steps.text: The third component has negative y-values and keeps its signed integral.

steps.label: Evaluate the first two pieces
steps.text: The bounds give these component values.

steps.label: Evaluate the lower piece
steps.text: The lower contribution is negative.

steps.label: Check overlaps and sum
steps.text: The pieces meet only on boundary curves or a point, hence on sets of area zero.

contentBlocks.result: The source integral is $1304/105$, or $12\,44/105$.
contentBlocks.verification: The three source values were independently recomputed from the displayed bounds. Their signed sum is $1304/105$.

exercises.outcome: For integrable $f$ and $g$ on the same bounded region $D$ and real scalars $a,b$, integration preserves sums and scalar multiples. The region stays fixed; this rule does not make integration multiplicative.
exercises.prompt: For integrable $f,g$ on the same region, suppose $\iint_Df\,dA=5$ and $\iint_Dg\,dA=-1$. Find $\iint_D(3f+2g)\,dA$.
exercises.hint: Keep both integrals on D and apply the given coefficients.
exercises.solution: The value is $3(5)+2(-1)=13$. No information about $\iint_Dfg\,dA$ follows.
rubric: Use linearity on the common region.
Retain the negative value of the second integral.

exercises.outcome: If $D$ is a bounded subregion of an ambient region $R$, the integral over $D$ uses only the values of $f$ on $D$. A zero extension on $R$ is an equivalent bookkeeping device when the restricted-domain integral is defined.
exercises.prompt: Inside the square $[0,2]^2$, let $D=\{0\le x\le2,\ 0\le y\le x/2\}$. Find $\iint_D1\,dA$.
exercises.hint: Use the restriction to D, then integrate along vertical slices.
exercises.solution: The integral is the triangular area: $\int_0^2\int_0^{x/2}1\,dy\,dx=1$.
rubric: Use the subregion bounds.
Interpret the integral of one as area.

exercises.outcome: For finitely many bounded regions, finite additivity requires existing component integrals and pairwise intersections of area zero. A shared boundary is allowed; overlapping interiors would count positive area more than once.
exercises.prompt: Let two unit squares be $D_1=[0,1]\times[0,1]$ and $D_2=[1,2]\times[0,1]$. Find the integral of $x$ over their union by additivity.
exercises.hint: Their only overlap is the common vertical edge.
exercises.solution: The component values are $1/2$ and $3/2$. Their sum is 2; the shared edge has zero area.
rubric: State why the intersection has zero area.
Add both component integrals.

exercises.outcome: A bounded region that is not Type I or Type II can still be integrated by a finite union of Type I/II pieces, provided every pairwise overlap has area zero and each piece integral exists. Choose cuts that make each piece have a single simple-slice description.
exercises.prompt: Find the area of $\{(x,y):|x|+|y|\le3\}$ by splitting it into left and right Type I pieces.
exercises.hint: Use the cut $x=0$ and write the upper and lower y-bounds on each side.
exercises.solution: The two pieces are congruent triangles of area $9$ each; total area is 18.
rubric: Give bounds for each simple piece.
Note the common cut has zero area.

exercises.outcome: The Lecture 06 example integrates $2x+5y$ over a non-simple region by describing one Type I part and two Type II parts. Its three shared intersections are boundary segments or a point, so finite additivity applies.
exercises.prompt: An L-shaped region is $[0,3]\times[0,2]$ with $[2,3]\times[1,2]$ removed. Split it into $D_1=[0,2]\times[0,2]$ and $D_2=[2,3]\times[0,1]$. Find $\iint_D(x+y)\,dA$.
exercises.hint: These pieces share only one vertical segment. Integrate separately.
exercises.solution: The first contribution is 8 and the second is 3; the union integral is 11.
rubric: Preserve the L-shaped region exactly.
Use additivity after verifying the overlap.

sections.title: Derive the factor geometrically
sections.text: A polar cell has radial thickness $dr$ and transverse length approximately $r\,d\theta$, so area is approximately $r\,dr\,d\theta$. The derivative columns of $(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)$ have determinant $r$, confirming the local scale for $r\ge0$.

sections.title: A coordinate singularity is not a hole
sections.text: At $r=0$ all angles describe one point and the determinant vanishes. For standard disk integrals this point has area zero and can be handled by a limiting argument. Angular endpoints also represent the same ray when using a full $2\pi$ interval.

exercise.prompt: Compute the area of the annular sector $1\le r\le 2$, $0\le \theta\le \pi/3$.
exercise.hint: Integrate the Jacobian $r$, not 1.
exercise.solution: The area is $\int_0^{\pi/3}\int_1^2r\,dr\,d\theta=(\pi /3)(3/2)=\pi /2$.
rubric: Include the radial factor.
Distinguish parameter-rectangle area from physical area.

contentBlocks.title: Separate the parameter rectangle from its image
contentBlocks.text: The polar map is $(r,\theta)\mapsto(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)$ with $r\ge0$. A polar rectangle is the image of $[a,b]\times[\alpha,\beta]$, with $0\le a\le b$ and $0\le\beta-\alpha\le2\pi$; its image is generally an annular sector, not a Cartesian rectangle.

contentBlocks.title: Describe a quarter-annulus from its parameter bounds
contentBlocks.strategy: Map the radius and angle intervals to locate the physical region.

steps.label: Apply the polar map
steps.text: The radial interval sets the inner and outer circles; the angular interval selects the first quadrant.

steps.label: Identify the image
steps.text: Every image point lies in the first-quadrant annular sector.

contentBlocks.result: The image is a quarter of an annulus between radii one and three.
contentBlocks.verification: The angular span is $\pi/2$ and the nonnegative radial interval does not wrap around or repeat positive area.

contentBlocks.title: Derive the polar area weight from one cell
contentBlocks.text: An annular cell from $r_-$ to $r_+$ and angle width $\Delta\theta$ has exact area $\frac12(r_+^2-r_-^2)\Delta\theta=r_*\Delta r\Delta\theta$, where $r_*=(r_-+r_+)/2$. Refining these cells produces the area factor $r$; page 15 separately interprets nonnegative weighted sums as volumes.

contentBlocks.title: Compare equal angular cells at different radii
contentBlocks.strategy: Use the exact annular-sector formula before taking a fine-partition limit.
contentBlocks.setup: Let $\Delta r=0.2$ and $\Delta\theta=0.1$. Compare cells with mid-radii 1 and 4.

steps.label: Factor the exact cell area
steps.text: The area is midpoint radius times radial width and angular width.

steps.label: Compare the two radii
steps.text: The outer cell is four times as wide in area for equal parameter steps.

contentBlocks.result: The local area scale is r, not a constant parameter-rectangle scale.
contentBlocks.verification: The exact difference-of-squares formula gives both cell areas without a small-cell approximation.

contentBlocks.title: Integrate on a polar rectangle with the factor r
contentBlocks.text: For continuous $f$ on the image of a polar rectangle, the double integral becomes an iterated integral of $f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)r$. Either order is permitted under the stated continuity hypothesis.

contentBlocks.title: Integrate x on a quarter-annulus
contentBlocks.strategy: Compose the integrand with the polar map and multiply by the area factor.

steps.label: Transform the integrand
steps.text: The coordinate satisfies $x=r\cos\theta$, and the area measure contributes another $r$.

steps.label: Evaluate either iterated integral
steps.text: The radial and angular integrals separate here.

contentBlocks.result: The integral is $7/3$.
contentBlocks.verification: The radial integral is $7/3$ and the angular cosine integral is one.

contentBlocks.title: Use signed polar contributions on an annular sector
contentBlocks.text: The source region is the left half-annulus $x\le0$ and $1\le x^2+y^2\le4$. Its polar bounds are $1\le r\le2$ and $\pi/2\le\theta\le3\pi/2$. Preserve the sign of $x+y$ when applying the polar area factor.

contentBlocks.title: Recompute the source integral over the left half-annulus
contentBlocks.strategy: Convert both the domain and integrand, then integrate r times the transformed function.

steps.label: Transform the domain and density
steps.text: The half-annulus has fixed radial bounds and a left-facing angular interval.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.text: The cosine term is negative over the left half and the sine term cancels by symmetry.

contentBlocks.result: The source integral equals $-14/3$.
contentBlocks.verification: The radial integral is 7/3; the angular integral of cosine plus sine is −2.

contentBlocks.title: Build volume sums from polar cell areas
contentBlocks.text: For a continuous nonnegative height $f$ over a polar rectangle $R$, approximate the volume between $R\times\{0\}$ and the graph of $f$ by summing sampled heights times physical polar-cell areas. The page 15 Riemann sum uses $\Delta A_{ij}=r_{ij}^*\Delta r\Delta\theta$; continuity and mesh refinement lead to the polar integral.

contentBlocks.title: Turn a sampled polar height into a volume contribution
contentBlocks.strategy: Multiply the sampled height by the physical area of its polar cell before summing.
contentBlocks.setup: Let the height be $f(x,y)=x+3$ above the quarter-disk $0\le r\le2$, $0\le\theta\le\pi/2$.

steps.label: Find the physical cell area
steps.text: At sample radius $r_{ij}^*$, an angular step covers a longer arc farther from the origin.

steps.label: Multiply by the sampled height
steps.text: Compose the height function $f$ with the polar map, then weight the sample by its cell area.

steps.label: Pass from sums to the volume integral
steps.text: The source assumes a continuous, nonnegative height so the Riemann sums approximate volume.

contentBlocks.result: The volume is $3\pi+8/3$.
contentBlocks.verification: The $x$ contribution integrates to $8/3$ over the quarter-disk; the constant height $3$ contributes three times its area, $3\pi$.

exercises.outcome: The polar map is $(r,\theta)\mapsto(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)$ with $r\ge0$. A polar rectangle is the image of $[a,b]\times[\alpha,\beta]$, with $0\le a\le b$ and $0\le\beta-\alpha\le2\pi$; its image is generally an annular sector, not a Cartesian rectangle.
exercises.prompt: Describe the polar image of $2\le r\le5$, $-\pi\le\theta\le0$. State whether it is a full annulus.
exercises.hint: Map the angle interval to the lower half-plane; compare its width with $2\pi$.
exercises.solution: It is the lower half-annulus between radii 2 and 5. The angular width is $\pi$, so it is not a full annulus.
rubric: Translate both radius endpoints.
Use the angle width to distinguish a half-annulus from a full annulus.

exercises.outcome: An annular cell from $r_-$ to $r_+$ and angle width $\Delta\theta$ has exact area $\frac12(r_+^2-r_-^2)\Delta\theta=r_*\Delta r\Delta\theta$, where $r_*=(r_-+r_+)/2$. Refining these cells produces the area factor $r$; page 15 separately interprets nonnegative weighted sums as volumes.
exercises.prompt: Find the area of an annular sector with $1\le r\le4$ and $0\le\theta\le\pi/3$.
exercises.hint: Integrate the radial factor r over the parameter rectangle.
exercises.solution: The area is $\int_0^{\pi/3}\int_1^4r\,dr\,d\theta=5\pi/2$.
rubric: Include the factor r.
Use the actual angular width.

exercises.outcome: For continuous $f$ on the image of a polar rectangle, the double integral becomes an iterated integral of $f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)r$. Either order is permitted under the stated continuity hypothesis.
exercises.prompt: Compute $\iint_D y\,dA$ on the quarter-disk $0\le r\le3$, $0\le\theta\le\pi/2$.
exercises.hint: Under the polar map, $y=r\sin\theta$; multiply by the area factor.
exercises.solution: The integral is $\int_0^{\pi/2}\int_0^3r^2\sin\theta\,dr\,d\theta=9$.
rubric: Compose y with the polar map.
Include the second factor of r from dA.

exercises.outcome: The source region is the left half-annulus $x\le0$ and $1\le x^2+y^2\le4$. Its polar bounds are $1\le r\le2$ and $\pi/2\le\theta\le3\pi/2$. Preserve the sign of $x+y$ when applying the polar area factor.
exercises.prompt: Compute $\iint_D y\,dA$ on the first-quadrant annular sector $1\le r\le2$, $0\le\theta\le\pi/2$.
exercises.hint: Transform y and include the area weight.
exercises.solution: The value is $\int_0^{\pi/2}\int_1^2r^2\sin\theta\,dr\,d\theta=7/3$.
rubric: Use the correct radial bounds.
Check the angular integral of sine.

exercises.outcome: For a continuous nonnegative height $f$ over a polar rectangle $R$, approximate the volume between $R\times\{0\}$ and the graph of $f$ by summing sampled heights times physical polar-cell areas. The page 15 Riemann sum uses $\Delta A_{ij}=r_{ij}^*\Delta r\Delta\theta$; continuity and mesh refinement lead to the polar integral.
exercises.prompt: Over the quarter-disk $0\le r\le2$, $0\le\theta\le\pi/2$, use $f(x,y)=x+3$. Write one polar Riemann-sum volume contribution at sample $(r_{ij}^*,\theta_{ij}^*)$, then give the limiting volume integral.
exercises.hint: The sampled height is $r_{ij}^*\cos\theta_{ij}^*+3$. Multiply it by the physical cell area.
exercises.solution: One cell contributes $\Delta V_{ij}=(r_{ij}^*\cos\theta_{ij}^*+3)r_{ij}^*\Delta r\Delta\theta$. In the limit, $V=\int_0^{\pi/2}\int_0^2(r\cos\theta+3)r\,dr\,d\theta=3\pi+8/3$.
rubric: Compose the height using the polar map.
Use $r_{ij}^*\Delta r\Delta\theta$ for physical cell area.
Retain nonnegativity and continuity as the volume-sum hypotheses.

sections.title: Derive the shifted disk
sections.text: For $(x-1)^2+y^2\le1$, substitute polar coordinates to get $r^2-2r\cos\theta\le0$. With $r\ge0$ and $r>0$ this gives $0<r\le2\cos\theta$, so $\cos\theta\ge0$. Choose $-\pi/2\le\theta\le\pi/2$, with $r=0$ included separately.

sections.title: Verify the area
sections.text: The integral is $\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\int_0^{2\cos\theta}r\,dr\,d\theta=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}2\cos^2\theta\,d\theta=\pi$. This matches a disk of radius one. A centered fixed-radius sector would represent a different region.

exercise.prompt: Write polar bounds for $(x-2)^2+y^2\le 4$.
exercise.hint: Repeat the algebra with center and radius 2.
exercise.solution: The bounds are $-\pi /2\leq\theta\leq\pi /2$ and $0\leq r\leq4\cos\theta$. The area is $4\pi$, matching a disk of radius 2.
rubric: Derive the angular range from nonnegative radius.
Handle the origin without dividing by zero.

contentBlocks.title: Require one radial interval on each ray
contentBlocks.text: A polar region has angles in $[\alpha,\beta]$ and radii between continuous functions $0\le h_1(\theta)\le h_2(\theta)$. Thus each included ray meets the region in one interval. The angle span is at most $2\pi$; for a full turn, each radial boundary must match at its two endpoint values.

contentBlocks.title: Check a variable-bound annular region
contentBlocks.strategy: Check radial ordering, continuity, angular span, and full-turn seam conditions before applying the theorem.

steps.label: Check the radial order
steps.text: The outer bound exceeds the inner bound by one throughout the interval.

steps.label: Find the area
steps.text: Integrating one over each radial interval gives the area of this curved sector.

contentBlocks.result: The region has a single annular interval on every ray in the chosen angle range.
contentBlocks.verification: The area integrand simplifies to $(3+2\cos\theta)/2$, whose integral is $3\pi/4+1$.

contentBlocks.title: Integrate over variable radial bounds
contentBlocks.text: For continuous $f$ on a polar region bounded by $h_1(\theta)$ and $h_2(\theta)$, integrate $f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)r$ first across the radial interval and then over the angle interval. For $f=1$, the formula reduces to one half the integral of the difference of squared radial bounds.

contentBlocks.title: Find the area under a cosine radial bound
contentBlocks.strategy: Use the polar-region theorem with inner radius zero and integrate r exactly.

steps.label: Set up the polar integral
steps.text: The radial upper endpoint depends on angle, while the Jacobian contributes r.

steps.label: Integrate in r
steps.text: The radial integral is half the square of its upper endpoint.

contentBlocks.result: The area is $1+3\pi/8$.
contentBlocks.verification: Expand the square; the cosine and cosine-squared integrals are $1$ and $\pi/4$.

contentBlocks.title: Derive the shifted-disk radial bound before dividing
contentBlocks.text: The source disk $(x-1)^2+y^2\le1$ becomes $r^2-2r\cos\theta\le0$. For $r>0$, division gives $r\le2\cos\theta$ and requires $\cos\theta\ge0$, so one convenient interval is $-\pi/2\le\theta\le\pi/2$. The origin is included separately.

contentBlocks.title: Set up and evaluate the source paraboloid volume
contentBlocks.strategy: Derive the disk domain, transform the height, multiply by the area factor, and integrate.
contentBlocks.setup: Find the volume under $z=4-x^2-y^2$ above the disk $(x-1)^2+y^2\le1$.

steps.label: Derive the radial bound
steps.text: Substitute $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta$; do not lose the origin when dividing by $r$.

steps.label: Transform height and area
steps.text: The vertical height is positive on this disk and the polar area element contributes r.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.text: Integrate the radial polynomial, then use evenness of the cosine powers.

contentBlocks.result: The volume is $5\pi/2$.
contentBlocks.verification: The radial integral is $8\cos^2\theta-4\cos^4\theta$; its integral over a half-turn interval is $4\pi-3\pi/2=5\pi/2$.

exercises.outcome: A polar region has angles in $[\alpha,\beta]$ and radii between continuous functions $0\le h_1(\theta)\le h_2(\theta)$. Thus each included ray meets the region in one interval. The angle span is at most $2\pi$; for a full turn, each radial boundary must match at its two endpoint values.
exercises.prompt: Check whether $1+\cos\theta\le r\le3+\cos\theta$, $0\le\theta\le2\pi$, describes a valid full-turn polar region.
exercises.hint: Check continuity, ordering, and both endpoint values of each radial function.
exercises.solution: The radial bounds are continuous, nonnegative, and ordered. Both have matching values $h_1(0)=h_1(2\pi)=2$ and $h_2(0)=h_2(2\pi)=4$, so they describe one interval on every ray with a compatible full-turn seam.
rubric: Verify $h_1\le h_2$ throughout.
Check both radial functions agree at the angular seam.

exercises.outcome: For continuous $f$ on a polar region bounded by $h_1(\theta)$ and $h_2(\theta)$, integrate $f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)r$ first across the radial interval and then over the angle interval. For $f=1$, the formula reduces to one half the integral of the difference of squared radial bounds.
exercises.prompt: Find the area enclosed by $0\le r\le2+\sin\theta$, $0\le\theta\le\pi$.
exercises.hint: Use one half the integral of the squared outer radius.
exercises.solution: The area is $\frac12\int_0^\pi(2+\sin\theta)^2\,d\theta=4+\frac{9\pi}{4}$.
rubric: Square the variable upper bound.
Integrate the sine and sine-squared terms over the stated angle interval.

exercises.outcome: The source disk $(x-1)^2+y^2\le1$ becomes $r^2-2r\cos\theta\le0$. For $r>0$, division gives $r\le2\cos\theta$ and requires $\cos\theta\ge0$, so one convenient interval is $-\pi/2\le\theta\le\pi/2$. The origin is included separately.
exercises.prompt: Find the volume under $z=9-x^2-y^2$ above the same disk $(x-1)^2+y^2\le1$.
exercises.hint: Reuse the correctly derived disk bounds and replace only the height.
exercises.solution: The polar integral is $\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\int_0^{2\cos\theta}(9-r^2)r\,dr\,d\theta=15\pi/2$.
rubric: Keep the same shifted-disk bounds.
Multiply the transformed height by r.

sections.title: Volume cells need three widths
sections.text: A triple sum adds $f(\text{sample})\Delta x\Delta y\Delta z$. For $f=1$ it approximates volume; for mass density it approximates mass. A display containing only a few columns is a schematic, not a complete three-dimensional partition.

sections.title: Check a separable box
sections.text: For $f=xyz$ on $[0,1]\times [0,2]\times [0,3]$, continuity allows repeated integration and the product structure separates the result into $(1/2)\cdot 2\cdot (9/2)=9$. This separation depends on both the factorized integrand and rectangular domain.

exercise.prompt: Integrate constant density 5 on a box with side lengths 2,3,4.
exercise.hint: Multiply density by the volume.
exercise.solution: The integral is $5\cdot 2\cdot 3\cdot 4=120$. If density is $kg/m^{3}$, this is mass in kg.
rubric: Include all three dimensions.
Interpret the measure and units.

sections.title: Project before setting height bounds
sections.text: The tetrahedron $x,y,z\geq 0$ with $x+y+z\leq 1$ projects onto $x,y\geq 0$, $x+y\leq 1$. Thus $0\leq x\leq 1$, $0\leq y\leq 1-x$, $0\leq z\leq 1-x-y$. The inner bounds depend only on outer variables.

sections.title: Each order describes the same solid
sections.text: A different outer coordinate requires a different projection. Writing all upper limits as 1 would replace the tetrahedron by a cube. Integrating 1 over the correct bounds gives volume $1/6$.

exercise.prompt: Write bounds with $x$ innermost for the same tetrahedron.
exercise.hint: Project onto the yz-plane.
exercise.solution: Use $0\leq z\leq 1$, $0\leq y\leq 1-z$, $0\leq x\leq 1-y-z$. Integrating 1 again yields $1/6$.
rubric: Derive the outer projection.
Keep an inner bound free of its own integration variable.

sections.title: A planar polar map plus height
sections.text: Cylindrical coordinates are $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$, $z=z$ with $r\ge0$. The volume Jacobian is $r$. The angle is measured around the $z$-axis; it does not tilt toward that axis.

sections.title: Identify surfaces by equations
sections.text: $r=2$ is a cylinder, $z=2$ a horizontal plane, and $z=r$ a cone above the plane. The $z$-axis has $r=0$ and nonunique $\theta$; this coordinate singularity does not remove the axis from a solid.

exercise.prompt: Convert $x^2+y^2\le 4$ and $1\le z\le 3$ into cylindrical bounds.
exercise.hint: The planar projection is a full disk.
exercise.solution: $0\leq r\leq 2$, $0\leq \theta \leq 2\pi$, $1\leq z\leq 3$, with volume element $r$ dr $d\theta$ dz in a compatible chosen order.
rubric: Include the full angular range.
Use the factor $r$ for volume.

sections.title: Transform bounds and integrand
sections.text: Between $z=r^{2}$ and $z=4$, the surfaces meet at $r=2$. Volume is $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2\int_{r^2}^4 r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta=8\pi$. An integrand $x^{2}+y^{2}$ becomes $r^{2}$, creating $r^{3}$ after multiplication by the Jacobian.

sections.title: Do not count the Jacobian twice
sections.text: The measure $r$ dr $d\theta$ dz already accounts for geometric stretching. If the physical density is itself $r$, the total factor $r^{2}$ has two different origins: density and volume measure. Label them separately.

exercise.prompt: Find the integral of $x^2+y^2$ over the cylinder of radius 1 and height 2.
exercise.hint: Use density $r^{2}$ and measure $r$.
exercise.solution: The result is $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1\int_0^2r^3\,dz\,dr\,d\theta=\pi$.
rubric: Transform the scalar field.
Multiply by one volume Jacobian.

sections.title: Fix the angle convention
sections.text: Use $\rho\ge0$, azimuth $\theta$ around the $z$-axis, and polar angle $\varphi$ down from the positive $z$-axis: $x=\rho\sin\varphi\cos\theta$, $y=\rho\sin\varphi\sin\theta$, $z=\rho\cos\varphi$. Standard ranges are $0\le\theta<2\pi$ and $0\le\varphi\le\pi$.

sections.title: Distinguish coordinate singularities
sections.text: At $\rho =0$ every angle pair represents the origin. At $\varphi =0$ or $\pi$ the azimuth is nonunique. These failures of coordinates do not imply the sphere or solid is geometrically singular.

exercise.prompt: What spherical coordinates describe $(0,0,-2)$?
exercise.hint: The point lies on the negative polar axis.
exercise.solution: $\rho =2$ and $\varphi =\pi$; any $\theta$ represents the same point. The nonunique azimuth is expected.
rubric: State the polar-angle convention.
Allow nonunique coordinates on the axis.

contentBlocks.title: A sphere centered away from the origin
contentBlocks.strategy: Convert each surface separately, then intersect the allowed angle and radial intervals before integrating.
contentBlocks.setup: Let $E$ lie above $z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ and inside $x^2+y^2+z^2=z$, as posed in MH2100 Lecture 07, physical page 50. Derive its bounds before evaluating the volume.

steps.label: Cone selects directions
steps.text: For $\rho\ge0$, the cone inequality becomes $\rho\cos\varphi\ge\rho\sin\varphi$. Except at the origin this gives $0\le\varphi\le\pi/4$; rotational symmetry gives $0\le\theta\le2\pi$.

steps.label: Sphere sets a variable radial ceiling
steps.text: The sphere inequality is $\rho^2\le\rho\cos\varphi$. The origin is included, and for positive radius the upper bound is $\cos\varphi$, not a constant.

steps.label: Integrate the actual solid
steps.text: Use density $1$ and exactly one spherical volume factor $\rho^2\sin\varphi$. Integrating first in radius gives $\cos^3\varphi/3$.

contentBlocks.result: The exact volume is $\pi/8$; replacing $\cos\varphi$ by a fixed sphere radius changes the region.
contentBlocks.verification: At $\varphi=0$ the radial ceiling is $1$; at $\varphi=\pi/4$ it is $1/\sqrt2$. The sphere is centered at $(0,0,1/2)$ with radius $1/2$, so a constant radial ceiling about the origin cannot describe it.

sections.title: Three scale factors
sections.text: A small spherical cell has lengths approximately $d\rho$, $\rho\,d\varphi$ and $\rho\sin\varphi\,d\theta$. Its volume factor is $\rho^2\sin\varphi$. The signed determinant depends on coordinate order; scalar volume uses its absolute value.

sections.title: Cone and sphere bounds
sections.text: Inside a sphere of radius $R$ and above the cone $\varphi =\pi /4$, use $0\leq \rho \leq R$, $0\leq \varphi \leq \pi /4$, $0\leq \theta \leq 2\pi$. Volume is $(2\pi R^{3}/3)(1-1/\sqrt{2})$, not a cylinder sector.

sections.title: Shifted spheres need variable radial bounds
sections.text: For a sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=cz$ with $c>0$, the interior is $0\leq\rho\leq c\cos\varphi$ where $\cos\varphi\ge0$. An intersecting cone $z\geq\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ restricts directions to $0\leq\varphi\leq\pi/4$. These inequalities specify the same physical solid before any Jacobian is applied.

exercise.prompt: Integrate $x^2+y^2+z^2$ over the ball of radius $R$.
exercise.hint: The integrand is $\rho^2$ and the measure adds another $\rho^2\sin\varphi$.
exercise.solution: The integral is $(R^{5}/5)\cdot 2\cdot 2\pi =4\pi R^{5}/5$. For $R=1$ it is $4\pi /5$.
rubric: Use the full polar range.
Separate the integrand from the Jacobian.

exercises.outcome: Derive a variable spherical radial bound and transform a nonconstant density independently of the Jacobian.
exercises.prompt: Let $D$ lie above $z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ and inside $x^2+y^2+z^2=2z$. Set spherical bounds and compute $\iiint_D z\,dV$.
exercises.hint: The cone still limits $\varphi$ to $[0,\pi/4]$. Divide the sphere inequality by positive $\rho$, then keep the density $z=\rho\cos\varphi$ separate from $dV$.
exercises.solution: The sphere gives $0\le\rho\le2\cos\varphi$, while $0\le\varphi\le\pi/4$ and $0\le\theta\le2\pi$. The density times the volume factor is $\rho^3\cos\varphi\sin\varphi$. Radial integration gives $4\cos^5\varphi\sin\varphi$, so the integral is $8\pi(1-(1/\sqrt2)^6)/6=7\pi/6$.
rubric: Derive the radial bound from the shifted sphere, not a constant-radius ball.
Use the cone for the polar angle and all azimuths.
Transform the density and include the volume factor once.

sections.title: Columns are transformed edges
sections.text: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$, the unit-square edges map to $(2,0)$ and $(1,3)$. The image parallelogram has area $|\det A|=6$. Every cell has the same area scale because the map is linear.

sections.title: Orientation and collapse
sections.text: A negative determinant, such as $\det A<0$, reverses orientation while keeping the ordinary area scale positive. If $\det A=0$, the plane collapses into a line or point, so a two-dimensional inverse does not exist. The matrix $A$ and its determinant $\det A$ are different objects.

exercise.prompt: Find signed and unsigned area factors for $T(u,v)=(u,-2v)$.
exercise.hint: Use the diagonal derivative matrix.
exercise.solution: The signed determinant is $-2$ and the ordinary area scale is $2$. The map reverses orientation.
rubric: Keep the sign for orientation.
Use absolute value for ordinary area.

contentBlocks.title: Read area and orientation from the determinant
contentBlocks.text: A linear map sends the standard basis vectors to its matrix columns, so it sends the unit square to the parallelogram spanned by those columns. The ordinary area scale is $|\det A|$; the sign of $\det A$ records whether orientation is preserved or reversed.

contentBlocks.title: Compute the image parallelogram from its edge vectors
contentBlocks.strategy: Use the images of the two standard basis vectors as adjacent edges; their determinant gives signed area.

steps.label: Read the columns
steps.text: The images of $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ are the adjacent edge vectors.

steps.label: Compute signed area
steps.text: The determinant is positive, so this map preserves the square's orientation.

steps.label: Take ordinary area
steps.text: The image parallelogram therefore has area six.

contentBlocks.result: The unit square maps to a parallelogram of area $6$ with the same orientation.
contentBlocks.verification: The four image vertices are $(0,0)$, $(2,0)$, $(3,3)$, and $(1,3)$; the base and height give area $2\cdot3=6$.

contentBlocks.title: Use absolute determinant for ordinary volume
contentBlocks.text: A linear space map sends a box to a parallelepiped with signed volume scaled by $\det A$. Ordinary volume uses $|\det A|$; a negative determinant records orientation reversal, not negative physical volume.

contentBlocks.title: Scale a box with a diagonal space map
contentBlocks.strategy: The three diagonal entries are the signed scale factors along the coordinate axes.

steps.label: Form the derivative matrix
steps.text: The coordinate directions stay parallel to the axes.

steps.label: Multiply the signed scales
steps.text: One coordinate direction is reversed.

steps.label: Convert to ordinary volume
steps.text: The image cube's physical volume is positive.

contentBlocks.result: The map reverses orientation and multiplies ordinary volume by $24$.
contentBlocks.verification: The image edge lengths are $2$, $3$, and $4$, whose product is $24$.

contentBlocks.title: Transform both the field and the area element
contentBlocks.text: For a linear map $T$ and a bounded source region $D$ with existing area, the transformed density is $f(T(u,v))|\det T|$. In three dimensions, use $f(T(u,v,w))|\det T|$ with volume measure. The determinant factor does not replace composition of the integrand.

contentBlocks.title: Check a linear change of variables on a rectangle
contentBlocks.strategy: Map the region, substitute the transformed coordinates into the density, and include the constant measure factor.

steps.label: Find the image and factor
steps.text: The image is $0\leq x\leq2$, $0\leq y\leq1$, and the area factor is two.

steps.label: Compose the density
steps.text: Replace the physical coordinates by their expressions in the source variables.

steps.label: Evaluate the transformed integral
steps.text: Integrate over the source unit square.

contentBlocks.result: Both the direct and transformed integrals equal $3$.
contentBlocks.verification: Directly, $\int_0^2\int_0^1(x+y)\,dy\,dx=3$.

exercises.outcome: Use the absolute determinant of a linear plane map to find the image area of a unit square, while retaining its sign as orientation information.
exercises.prompt: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$, find the image area of the unit square and say whether orientation is preserved.
exercises.hint: Compute the signed determinant first, then take its absolute value for area.
exercises.solution: $\det A=1-6=-5$, so the image area is $5$ and orientation is reversed.
rubric: Compute the signed determinant as $-5$.
Use absolute value for area and retain the negative sign to describe orientation.

exercises.outcome: Use the absolute determinant of a linear space map as its constant volume scale and distinguish this from signed orientation.
exercises.prompt: Find the ordinary volume scale and orientation behavior of $T(u,v,w)=(u+2v,\,v+w,\,-2w)$.
exercises.hint: Write the triangular derivative matrix in the given input and output coordinate order.
exercises.solution: The matrix is upper triangular with diagonal $1,1,-2$, so $\det DT=-2$. The volume scale is $2$ and orientation is reversed.
rubric: Keep the input coordinate order $(u,v,w)$.
Report both the signed determinant and its absolute value.

exercises.outcome: Transform a double or triple integral under a linear map by composing the integrand with the map and multiplying by the constant absolute determinant.
exercises.prompt: Use $T(u,v)=(u+v,u-v)$ on the unit square to evaluate $\iint_{T[D]}x\,dA$.
exercises.hint: The determinant is $-2$; the composed density is $u+v$.
exercises.solution: The transformed integral is $\int_0^1\int_0^1 2(u+v)\,dv\,du=2$.
rubric: Compose $x$ as $u+v$.
Multiply by $|\det DT|=2$.

sections.title: A nonlinear map with variable scale
sections.text: Let $T(u,v)=(u,(1+u)v)$ on $0\leq u,v\leq1$. Its derivative columns are $(1,v)$ and $(0,1+u)$, so $\det DT=1+u$. The image is $0\leq x\leq1$, $0\leq y\leq1+x$, a trapezoid with area $3/2$.

sections.title: Finite cells versus infinitesimal cells
sections.text: For $T(u,v)=(u,(1+u)v)$, the image area of $[u,u+h]\times[v,v+k]$ is $hk(1+u+h/2)$. Its finite scale approaches $1+u$ as $h\to0$. A separate map $T(u,v)=(u,v+uv^2)$ has exact ratio $1+2(u+h/2)(v+k/2)$ and $\det DT=1+2uv$. With $k$ fixed and $h\to0$, the bias $uk$ remains because the cell diameter does not vanish. Shrinking both $h$ and $k$ makes the diameter $\sqrt{h^2+k^2}$ tend to zero and recovers the local determinant.

exercise.prompt: Compute $\iint_R y\,dA$ over the image trapezoid from $T(u,v)=(u,(1+u)v)$ on the unit square.
exercise.hint: Replace $y$ by $(1+u)v$ and include the Jacobian $1+u$.
exercise.solution: The transformed integrand is $(1+u)^2v$. Integrating $v$ from $0$ to $1$ gives $(1+u)^2/2$, and integrating $u$ gives $7/6$.
rubric: Transform the field as well as the measure.
Use the position-dependent Jacobian.

contentBlocks.title: Build the plane Jacobian from component derivatives
contentBlocks.text: A plane map $T=(X,Y)$ sends parameter points $(u,v)$ to physical points $(x,y)$. Its Jacobian is $J_T=\det\begin{pmatrix}X_u&X_v\\Y_u&Y_v\end{pmatrix}$, with columns ordered by the input variables. For a linear map this is the constant determinant from the area-scaling lesson.

contentBlocks.title: Compute a Jacobian with a nonlinear component
contentBlocks.strategy: Differentiate each output component with respect to each input variable, then take the determinant in the declared order.
contentBlocks.setup: For $T(u,v)=(u^2+v,3u-v)$, compute $J_T$ and evaluate it at $(1,2)$.

steps.label: Differentiate the components
steps.text: Rows correspond to $X$ and $Y$; columns correspond to $u$ and $v$.

steps.label: Take the determinant
steps.text: The result is a position-dependent signed area factor.

steps.label: Evaluate at the requested point
steps.text: Substitute $u=1$; the $v$ coordinate does not enter this determinant.

contentBlocks.result: At $(1,2)$ the local signed area factor is $-5$, so the local ordinary area scale is $5$.
contentBlocks.verification: The determinant formula gives $2(1)(-1)-1(3)=-5$.

contentBlocks.title: Derive the polar area factor
contentBlocks.text: For $T(r,\theta)=(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)$, the ordered Jacobian is $J_T=r$. The change-of-variables application restricts to $r\geq0$, so its ordinary area factor is $r$.

contentBlocks.title: Differentiate the polar coordinate map
contentBlocks.strategy: Place the $r$ derivatives in the first column and the $\theta$ derivatives in the second, then simplify with $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$.

steps.label: Write the derivative matrix
steps.text: The column order matches $(r,\theta)$.

steps.label: Take and simplify the determinant
steps.text: Use the Pythagorean identity.

contentBlocks.result: The signed determinant is $r$; on $r\geq0$ the area factor is $r$.
contentBlocks.verification: For $r=0$, the map collapses the angular coordinate to the origin and the determinant vanishes.

exercises.outcome: Represent a plane transformation by its component functions and compute its Jacobian as the determinant of their ordered first-partial matrix.
exercises.prompt: For $S(u,v)=(u+v^2,2u-v)$, compute $J_S(2,1)$.
exercises.hint: The derivative matrix has first row $(1,2v)$ and second row $(2,-1)$.
rubric: Differentiate both components in input order.
Evaluate the determinant at $(2,1)$.

exercises.outcome: Compute the signed Jacobian of the polar map and use its nonnegative value on the standard radial domain as the area factor.
exercises.prompt: For $S(s,t)=(3s\cos t,3s\sin t)$ with $s\geq0$, find the signed Jacobian and area factor.
exercises.hint: The constant radial scale contributes a factor of three in each planar coordinate.
exercises.solution: $J_S=9s$, which is nonnegative on the stated domain, so the area factor is $9s$.
rubric: Differentiate both output components.
Apply the absolute value and the restriction $s\geq0$.

sections.title: Volume is a triple product
sections.text: For a space map $T(u,v,w)$, the signed determinant of its three derivative columns measures oriented volume scale. Ordinary volume uses its absolute value. Swapping two parameter columns reverses the sign without changing physical volume.

sections.title: Order in spherical coordinates
sections.text: With columns ordered $(\rho,\phi,\theta)$ for $x=\rho\sin\phi\cos\theta$, $y=\rho\sin\phi\sin\theta$, and $z=\rho\cos\phi$, the determinant is $\rho^2\sin\phi$. The order $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ has the negative value. Both give the same positive volume factor on the standard interior range.

exercise.prompt: Find the volume scale for $T(u,v,w)=(2u,-3v,4w)$.
exercise.hint: Multiply the diagonal entries in the given coordinate order.
exercise.solution: The signed determinant is $-24$ and the ordinary volume scale is $24$. The negative sign records orientation reversal.
rubric: State the coordinate order.
Use absolute value for ordinary volume.

contentBlocks.title: Derive the cylindrical volume factor
contentBlocks.text: For $T(r,\theta,z)=(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta,z)$, form a $3\times3$ derivative matrix whose columns follow $(r,\theta,z)$. Its determinant is $r$; when $r\geq0$, this is the ordinary volume factor.

contentBlocks.title: Expand the cylindrical determinant
contentBlocks.strategy: Use the block structure: the $z$ coordinate contributes a final diagonal entry of one, leaving the polar $2\times2$ determinant.
contentBlocks.setup: Compute the Jacobian of the cylindrical map.

steps.label: Differentiate the map
steps.text: The third row is zero except for its final entry.

steps.label: Expand along the final row
steps.text: The remaining determinant is the polar determinant.

contentBlocks.result: The cylindrical volume factor is $r$ on the usual domain $r\geq0$.
contentBlocks.verification: The map leaves height unchanged and scales each horizontal polar slice by the factor $r$.

contentBlocks.title: Keep the spherical parameter order attached to its sign
contentBlocks.text: With $x=\rho\sin\phi\cos\theta$, $y=\rho\sin\phi\sin\theta$, and $z=\rho\cos\phi$, the source orders inputs as $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$. That order gives $J_T=-\rho^2\sin\phi$. Swapping the last two input columns changes the sign; ordinary volume uses $|J_T|$.

contentBlocks.title: Check the spherical determinant sign
contentBlocks.strategy: Use the displayed column order before expanding; do not import a memorized sign from a different coordinate convention.
contentBlocks.setup: Follow the handout's map with inputs ordered $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

steps.label: Write the ordered derivative columns
steps.text: The middle column differentiates with respect to $\theta$, not $\phi$.

steps.label: Evaluate the determinant
steps.text: Cofactor expansion gives the negative signed value for this order.

steps.label: Use the measure factor
steps.text: On $0\leq\phi\leq\pi$ and $\rho\geq0$, the ordinary volume factor is nonnegative.

contentBlocks.result: The order $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ has signed determinant $-\rho^2\sin\phi$, while its ordinary volume factor is $\rho^2\sin\phi$.
contentBlocks.verification: Swapping the $\theta$ and $\phi$ columns changes the determinant sign and leaves the same absolute volume factor.

contentBlocks.title: Separate a space map’s domain, range, and components
contentBlocks.text: A space transformation maps parameter triples $(u,v,w)$ to physical triples $(x,y,z)$. State its domain and range separately, and name its three scalar components $X$, $Y$, and $Z$; page 10 defines this map before the Jacobian calculations.

contentBlocks.title: Read the image of a nonlinear space map
contentBlocks.strategy: Find the input domain from the formula, identify each output component, then characterize which physical triples are reached.

steps.label: State the input domain
steps.text: Every real parameter triple is allowed.

steps.label: Name the component functions
steps.text: Each output coordinate is a scalar function of the parameters.

steps.label: Characterize the range
steps.text: The first output is nonnegative, and every such triple has a preimage.

steps.label: Verify a general image point
steps.text: Choose parameters from the requested physical coordinates.

contentBlocks.result: The map has domain $\mathbb R^3$ and range the half-space $x\geq0$.
contentBlocks.verification: The parameter choice $(\sqrt{x},y-z,z)$ reproduces each physical coordinate for any $x\geq0$.

exercises.outcome: Compute the cylindrical coordinate Jacobian in the ordered variables $(r,\theta,z)$ and obtain the volume factor $r$ on the standard domain.
exercises.prompt: For $S(s,t,z)=(2s\cos t,2s\sin t,z)$ with $s\geq0$, compute its volume factor.
exercises.hint: The planar scale of two contributes a factor of four to area before the radial factor.
exercises.solution: The determinant is $4s$, so the ordinary volume factor is $4s$.
rubric: Keep columns in the order $(s,t,z)$.
Simplify the determinant and use the nonnegative radial range.

exercises.outcome: Compute the signed spherical Jacobian for the stated parameter order and convert it to the nonnegative volume factor without erasing the orientation explanation.
exercises.prompt: Keep the same coordinate formulas but order the inputs as $(\rho,\phi,\theta)$. What is the signed determinant and the standard-domain volume factor?
exercises.hint: This order swaps the last two columns of the handout's matrix.
exercises.solution: The determinant is $+\rho^2\sin\phi$. For $\rho\geq0$ and $0\leq\phi\leq\pi$, the volume factor is also $\rho^2\sin\phi$.
rubric: Track the column swap's sign.
Use an absolute determinant for ordinary volume.

exercises.outcome: State the domain, component functions, and range of a space transformation from its formula.
exercises.prompt: For $S(u,v,w)=(e^u,v-w,w)$ on $\mathbb R^3$, state its domain, its three component functions, and its range.
exercises.hint: The first output is positive; for a target $(x,y,z)$ with $x>0$, solve for $u$, $v$, and $w$.
exercises.solution: The domain is $\mathbb R^3$, with $X=e^u$, $Y=v-w$, and $Z=w$. Its range is $(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^2$: for any $x>0$, take $(u,v,w)=(\ln x,y+z,z)$.
rubric: State the parameter domain and all three output components.
Give the positive-$x$ range and verify a preimage.

sections.title: State the map's scope
sections.text: The handout's sufficient setting requires a bounded region with existing measure, a continuously differentiable coordinate map and inverse on the interiors, and a one-to-one interior restriction. The transformed density must be defined on the image; the integrand uses $f(T(u))|\det DT(u)|$ in two dimensions and the corresponding three-variable form in space.

sections.title: Local invertibility is not global injectivity
sections.text: The map $(u,v)\mapsto(e^u\cos v,e^u\sin v)$ has nonzero determinant $e^{2u}$, but repeats whenever $v$ increases by $2\pi$. Integrating over two full angle turns counts almost every image point twice. Restrict the parameter range or account explicitly for multiplicity.

exercise.prompt: Why does using the polar map over $0\leq\theta\leq4\pi$ count almost every disk point twice?
exercise.hint: Compare the images of $(r,\theta)$ and $(r,\theta+2\pi)$ for $r>0$.
exercise.solution: The coordinates agree for every positive $r$, so almost every disk point is covered twice. Using the usual $r$ factor over two full turns doubles the disk integral.
rubric: Check global coverage, not only the determinant.
Explain multiplicity away from boundary seams.

contentBlocks.title: Check the theorem's map and region hypotheses
contentBlocks.text: The handout's two- and three-variable theorems require a bounded source region with existing measure, continuous first-partial entries for $T$ and its inverse on the relevant interiors, one-to-one behavior of the interior restriction, and a transformed density defined on the image. The formula uses $|J_T|$.

contentBlocks.title: Verify the hypotheses for an invertible linear map
contentBlocks.strategy: Check region, smoothness, injectivity, inverse regularity, and density domain before changing variables.

steps.label: Check the region
steps.text: The source is a bounded rectangle with existing area.

steps.label: Check the map and inverse
steps.text: The constant nonzero determinant makes this linear map globally one-to-one with a smooth inverse.

steps.label: Apply the formula
steps.text: The transformed density is the constant one times the absolute determinant.

contentBlocks.result: All stated hypotheses hold, and the image region has area $2$.
contentBlocks.verification: The linear map has an everywhere-defined inverse and maps the unit square to a parallelogram with area $2$.

contentBlocks.title: Match coordinate bounds with their Jacobian factors
contentBlocks.text: The standard coordinate maps use $r$ for planar polar area, $r$ for cylindrical volume, and $\rho^2\sin\phi$ for spherical volume. The usual ranges $r,\rho\geq0$, $0\leq\theta<2\pi$, and $0\leq\phi\leq\pi$ prevent repeated interior coverage; boundary seams are not extra volume.

contentBlocks.title: Compute a cylinder's volume in cylindrical coordinates
contentBlocks.strategy: Describe the source box, verify the usual one-turn angle range, and multiply by the cylindrical factor.
contentBlocks.setup: Use $0\leq r\leq2$, $0\leq\theta\leq2\pi$, and $0\leq z\leq3$ for a solid cylinder.

steps.label: State the parameter region
steps.text: The radial coordinate is nonnegative and the angular interval covers one turn.

steps.label: Insert the Jacobian
steps.text: The integrand for volume is one, so only the cylindrical measure factor remains.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.text: The radial, angular, and height factors multiply.

contentBlocks.result: The cylinder has volume $12\pi$.
contentBlocks.verification: Its base area is $\pi(2)^2$ and its height is $3$, giving the same volume.

contentBlocks.title: Check global injectivity, not only the Jacobian
contentBlocks.text: The change-of-variables theorem requires the map to be one-to-one on the source-region interior. A nonzero Jacobian gives local information; it does not prevent distinct parameter points from mapping to the same physical point.

contentBlocks.title: Find repeated images despite a nonzero determinant
contentBlocks.strategy: Compute the Jacobian and then test whether distinct inputs can have identical outputs.
contentBlocks.setup: Consider $T(u,v)=(e^u\cos v,e^u\sin v)$ on a region spanning two full angle turns.

steps.label: Compute local scale
steps.text: The determinant never vanishes.

steps.label: Compare separated inputs
steps.text: The angle-period identities make these images equal.

steps.label: Decide injectivity
steps.text: The full two-turn domain is not one-to-one in its interior.

contentBlocks.result: The map is locally nonsingular but globally noninjective on that domain.
contentBlocks.verification: Restricting the angle to a single turn restores one-to-one behavior away from boundary seams.

exercises.outcome: Check bounded-region, differentiability, interior injectivity, inverse regularity, and integrand-domain conditions before applying the multivariable change-of-variables theorem.
exercises.prompt: For $T(u,v)=(u+2v,3u-v)$ on $[0,1]^2$, decide whether the two-variable theorem applies and find the image area.
exercises.hint: A constant nonzero determinant gives global injectivity here; compare the image measure with the source area factor.
exercises.solution: $J_T=-7\ne0$, so the linear map and its inverse are continuously differentiable and one-to-one. The image area is $7\cdot1=7$.
rubric: Verify a nonzero determinant and hence injectivity for this linear map.
Multiply the source area by $|J_T|$.

exercises.outcome: Use the polar, cylindrical, and spherical coordinate formulas only on parameter ranges with the needed interior injectivity, and include their respective measure factors.
exercises.prompt: Use spherical coordinates to find the volume of the ball $0\leq\rho\leq2$ with full standard angle ranges.
exercises.hint: Integrate $\rho^2\sin\phi$ with $0\leq\theta\leq2\pi$ and $0\leq\phi\leq\pi$.
exercises.solution: $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^2\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta=\frac{8}{3}\cdot2\cdot2\pi=\frac{32\pi}{3}$.
rubric: Use the spherical factor $\rho^2\sin\phi$.
Use each standard bound once and evaluate all three factors.

exercises.outcome: Check injectivity before applying change of variables.
exercises.prompt: For $T(r,\theta)=(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)$ on $1\leq r\leq3$, $0\leq\theta\leq3\pi$, identify the multiplicity of almost every image point.
exercises.hint: Angles separated by $2\pi$ have the same image.
exercises.solution: Almost every point in the annulus has two preimages because the angle interval spans one and a half turns. The standard formula over this domain counts the covered annulus twice.
rubric: Compare parameter points separated by $2\pi$.
Check global multiplicity, not just the nonzero determinant.

sections.title: Invert at corresponding points
sections.text: For an invertible differentiable map $S=T^{-1}$, the chain rule gives $DS(T(u))DT(u)=I$. Taking determinants gives $\det DS(T(u))=1/\det DT(u)$. The locations matter: reciprocal determinants are evaluated at corresponding points.

sections.title: A nonlinear example
sections.text: For $u=x$ and $v=y/(1+x)$ with $x>-1$, the forward determinant is $1/(1+x)$. The inverse is $x=u$, $y=(1+u)v$, with determinant $1+u$. When integrating in $u,v$, use the absolute inverse factor $|1+u|$.

exercise.prompt: For $u=2x$ and $v=3y$, what factor converts $du\,dv$ to $dx\,dy$?
exercise.hint: Compute the inverse map or reciprocate the nonzero forward determinant.
exercise.solution: The inverse is $x=u/2$, $y=v/3$, so $dx\,dy=(1/6)\,du\,dv$.
rubric: Identify the direction of substitution.
Do not insert the forward determinant $6$.

contentBlocks.title: Choose coordinates that simplify the boundary
contentBlocks.text: When the handout gives $T^{-1}$, differentiate that inverse and use its absolute determinant to convert physical area or volume to parameter measure. Choose coordinates so the original boundary expressions become simple parameter bounds; still verify the map's coverage and multiplicity.

contentBlocks.title: Straighten four oblique boundaries
contentBlocks.strategy: Use the linear forms that appear in the boundary equations as the new variables, then solve for the inverse map.
contentBlocks.setup: Let $u=x+y$ and $v=x-y$ on the parallelogram $1\leq x+y\leq3$, $-1\leq x-y\leq1$.

steps.label: Read the bounds
steps.text: The chosen variables turn all four oblique sides into constant-coordinate boundaries.

steps.label: Solve for the inverse
steps.text: Add and subtract the defining equations.

steps.label: Compute inverse measure
steps.text: The absolute inverse determinant gives the physical area factor.

contentBlocks.result: A constant density integrates to $\frac12(2)(2)=2$ over this physical parallelogram.
contentBlocks.verification: The same area is base times height in the $(u,v)$ coordinates with the inverse-Jacobian factor.

contentBlocks.title: Turn product and ratio bounds into a rectangle
contentBlocks.text: For positive $x,y$, the variables $u=xy$ and $v=y/x$ turn product-and-ratio bounds into independent intervals. The inverse map is $x=\sqrt{u/v}$, $y=\sqrt{uv}$, and its area factor is $1/(2v)$.

contentBlocks.title: Reconstruct the product-ratio example
contentBlocks.strategy: Map the stated boundaries, solve for $(x,y)$, and compose the density before multiplying by the inverse determinant.
contentBlocks.setup: The handout asks for $\iint_D(x^2+y^2)\,dA$ where $x,y>0$, $1\leq xy\leq4$, and $1\leq y/x\leq4$. Continuation slides 26–27 are blank; the following is a checked guide derivation.

steps.label: Choose and invert
steps.text: The source inequalities become a rectangle in $(u,v)$.
steps.equation: u=xy,\quad v=\frac yx,\quad 1\leq u,v\leq4,\quad x=\sqrt{\frac uv},\quad y=\sqrt{uv}

steps.label: Find the inverse factor
steps.text: Differentiate the inverse map on the positive rectangle.

steps.label: Compose the integrand
steps.text: The two squares become $u/v$ and $uv$.

steps.label: Evaluate the product integral
steps.text: Separate the $u$ and $v$ factors.

contentBlocks.result: The integral is $\frac{225}{16}$.
contentBlocks.verification: The inverse determinant is positive on the rectangle; integrating the two separated factors gives $15/4$ and $15/4$, whose product is $225/16$.

contentBlocks.title: Map the parallelogram's parallel sides to coordinate lines
contentBlocks.text: For an affine parallelogram, select two independent linear forms that are constant on its pairs of parallel sides. Their inverse determinant scales the rectangular parameter area; the density must be composed with the inverse map.

contentBlocks.title: Integrate over the handout's parallelogram
contentBlocks.strategy: Use the two line families in the source diagram to define rectangle coordinates.
contentBlocks.setup: The handout's vertices are $(1,2)$, $(3,4)$, $(4,3)$, and $(6,5)$, with integrand $x-y$. Continuation slide 30 is blank; page 29 supplies the boundary diagram.

steps.label: Define the boundary coordinates
steps.text: The two parallel-side families have constant values of these linear forms.

steps.label: Map the four vertices
steps.text: The parallelogram becomes a rectangle.

steps.label: Invert and scale measure
steps.text: Solving for physical coordinates gives a constant absolute factor.

steps.label: Integrate the odd density
steps.text: The transformed density is $x-y=-u$ on a symmetric interval.

contentBlocks.result: The source integral is zero.
contentBlocks.verification: The rectangle is symmetric in $u$ and the composed integrand is odd in $u$.

contentBlocks.title: Keep the slanted parameter bounds after substitution
contentBlocks.text: For the source trapezoid, $u=x-y$ makes its parallel slanted sides constant and $v=x+y$ simplifies the exponent. The transformed region is $1\leq u\leq2$, $-u\leq v\leq u$; it is not a rectangle.

contentBlocks.title: Evaluate the source trapezoid integral
contentBlocks.strategy: Transform each vertex and boundary before writing the bounds; use the inverse determinant only after finding the actual parameter region.
contentBlocks.setup: The handout asks for $\iint_D e^{(x+y)/(x-y)}\,dA$ over vertices $(1,0)$, $(2,0)$, $(0,-2)$, and $(0,-1)$. Continuation slide 33 is blank; page 32 shows the mapped region.

steps.label: Transform the vertices
steps.text: The four images identify a wedge between two radial lines.

steps.label: Invert the coordinates
steps.text: Solve the two linear equations for $x$ and $y$.

steps.label: Rewrite the exponent and bounds
steps.text: The ratio becomes $v/u$ and the wedge bounds remain dependent.

steps.label: Integrate in the inner variable
steps.text: Substitute $w=v/u$ or integrate the exponential directly.

contentBlocks.result: The integral is $\frac34(e-e^{-1})$.
contentBlocks.verification: The variable substitution $w=v/u$ gives the inner integral $u(e-e^{-1})$, then $\int_1^2u\,du=3/2$.

contentBlocks.title: Use plane equations as space coordinates
contentBlocks.text: When six bounding planes come in three parallel pairs, use their left-hand linear forms as coordinates. The source becomes a box in parameter space, and the absolute determinant of the inverse map converts its volume.

contentBlocks.title: Compute the source solid's volume
contentBlocks.strategy: Map the six planes to a rectangular box, then invert the $3\times3$ linear determinant.
contentBlocks.setup: The handout bounds a solid by $1\leq x+y+z\leq2$, $0\leq x+2y\leq1$, and $2\leq y+z\leq4$. Continuation slide 35 is blank, so these steps supply an independently checked derivation.

steps.label: Choose coordinates
steps.text: Each pair of parallel planes fixes one new coordinate.

steps.label: Read the parameter box
steps.text: The six source planes become the six faces of this box.

steps.label: Compute the inverse factor
steps.text: The forward determinant has absolute value two.

steps.label: Scale the box volume
steps.text: The parameter box has volume two.

contentBlocks.result: The bounded solid has volume $1$.
contentBlocks.verification: Solving gives $x=u-w$, $y=(w+v-u)/2$, and $z=(w-v+u)/2$, confirming the inverse map and factor.

exercises.outcome: Choose parameter coordinates from the physical region's boundary expressions, then compute the inverse-Jacobian factor and transformed bounds.
exercises.prompt: A region is bounded by $2x+y=0$, $2x+y=4$, $x-y=1$, and $x-y=3$. Choose $u,v$ to make it a rectangle and find its area.
exercises.hint: Use the left-hand linear forms as coordinates and compute $\partial(x,y)/\partial(u,v)$.
exercises.solution: Take $u=2x+y$, $v=x-y$. The parameter rectangle has side lengths $4$ and $2$. Since $\left|\partial(x,y)/\partial(u,v)\right|=1/3$, its physical area is $8/3$.
rubric: Use the boundary expressions as coordinate variables.
Include the absolute inverse determinant.

exercises.outcome: Convert the source's positive-quadrant bounds on $xy$ and $y/x$ into a rectangle and use the inverse Jacobian in an integral.
exercises.prompt: For $x,y>0$ with $1\leq xy\leq9$ and $1\leq y/x\leq4$, evaluate $\iint_Dxy\,dA$.
exercises.hint: Use $u=xy$, $v=y/x$ and the inverse area factor $1/(2v)$.
exercises.solution: The transformed integral is $\int_1^9\int_1^4\frac{u}{2v}\,dv\,du=20\ln4$.
rubric: Transform the bounds to $1\leq u\leq9$, $1\leq v\leq4$.
Use the inverse factor and integrate the composed density.

exercises.outcome: Straighten the source parallelogram by two linear boundary coordinates, compute the inverse determinant, and integrate the transformed density.
exercises.prompt: Let $T(u,v)=(u+2v,3u-v)$ on $0\leq u\leq1$, $0\leq v\leq2$. Evaluate $\iint_{T[D]}(x+y)\,dA$.
exercises.hint: Use $|\det DT|=7$ and compose $x+y$ before integrating.
exercises.solution: The composed density is $4u+v$, so the integral is $7\int_0^1\int_0^2(4u+v)\,dv\,du=42$.
rubric: Compute the absolute determinant as $7$.
Compose the density and integrate over the stated rectangle.

exercises.outcome: Choose sum-and-difference coordinates for the source trapezoid, retain its triangular parameter bounds, and transform the exponential density with the inverse determinant.
exercises.prompt: For $1\leq u=x-y\leq3$ and $-u\leq v=x+y\leq u$, evaluate $\iint_E e^{(x+y)/(x-y)}\,dA$.
exercises.hint: Use $\left|\partial(x,y)/\partial(u,v)\right|=1/2$ and integrate $e^{v/u}$ first.
rubric: Keep the bounds $-u\leq v\leq u$.
Include the inverse determinant $1/2$.

exercises.outcome: Use the three plane equations as linear coordinates, invert their map, and apply the inverse determinant to find a bounded solid's volume.
exercises.prompt: Find the volume bounded by $0\leq x+y+z\leq2$, $-1\leq x-y\leq1$, and $0\leq z\leq3$.
exercises.hint: Set $p=x+y+z$, $q=x-y$, and $r=z$, then compute the inverse determinant.
exercises.solution: $\left|\partial(x,y,z)/\partial(p,q,r)\right|=1/2$, and the parameter box has volume $2\cdot2\cdot3=12$, so the volume is $6$.
rubric: Use the three plane expressions as coordinates.
Use the absolute inverse determinant and parameter-box volume.

sections.title: Density accumulates with length
sections.text: For a smooth parametrization $r(t)$, $\int_C f\,ds=\int_a^b f(r(t))|r'(t)|\,dt$. Reversing orientation preserves the value because speed is nonnegative. Repeating a traversal counts each pass, although repeated tracing is outside the handout's nice-parametrization assumption.

sections.title: Non-unit speed is visible
sections.text: For $r(t)=(2\cos t,2\sin t)$, the speed is $2$. With density $f=3$, one traversal gives $\int_0^{2\pi}6\,dt=12\pi$. Using $dt$ alone would underestimate by a factor of two.

exercise.prompt: Integrate density $f(x,y)=x$ along $r(t)=(t,2t)$, $0\leq t\leq1$.
exercise.hint: The speed is constant $\sqrt5$.
exercise.solution: The integral is $\sqrt5\int_0^1t\,dt=\sqrt5/2$. Reversing traversal leaves the scalar line integral unchanged.
rubric: Evaluate the density along the curve.
Include the speed factor.

contentBlocks.title: Accumulate scalar density along arc length
contentBlocks.text: The scalar line integral sums sampled values of $f$ weighted by arc-length increments. Under the handout's nice-curve assumption, its value does not depend on the chosen nice parametrization; reversing direction does not change the unsigned arc-length accumulation. The area-under-a-curve picture on page 41 is an informal interpretation when $f\geq0$.

contentBlocks.title: Accumulate a constant density along a segment
contentBlocks.strategy: Evaluate the density and multiply it by the curve's total arc length.
contentBlocks.setup: Let $r(t)=(3t,4t)$ for $0\leq t\leq1$, with constant density $f=2$.

steps.label: Find the speed
steps.text: The derivative is constant, so the arc-length rate is constant.

steps.label: Integrate density times speed
steps.text: The scalar line integral uses the nonnegative speed.

steps.label: Reverse the parameter
steps.text: Reversing direction changes velocity sign but not speed.

contentBlocks.result: Either orientation gives the scalar line integral $10$.
contentBlocks.verification: The segment has length $5$ and constant density $2$.

contentBlocks.title: Separate existence from the computation formula
contentBlocks.text: A continuous scalar field on a curve of existing finite length has a scalar line integral. If the curve has a smooth nice parametrization $r:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n$, then $\int_C f\,ds=\int_a^b f(r(t))|r'(t)|\,dt$. Continuity and finite length guarantee existence; smoothness supplies this computation formula.

contentBlocks.title: Compute a density integral on a smooth segment
contentBlocks.strategy: Substitute the parametrization into the density and multiply by its speed before integrating.

steps.label: Check the hypotheses
steps.text: The field is continuous and the segment is smooth with finite length.

steps.label: Substitute and compute speed
steps.text: The density along the path is $t$ and speed is constant.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.text: The speed factor remains in the parameter integral.

contentBlocks.result: The integral exists and equals $\sqrt5/2$.
contentBlocks.verification: Directly, the density grows linearly from zero to one along a segment of length $\sqrt5$.

contentBlocks.title: Use the source circle's radius and constant coordinate
contentBlocks.text: The handout's circle lies in $y=4$, has center $(0,4,0)$ and radius $2$, and uses $f(x,y,z)=x^2y^2$. A correct scalar line integral evaluates $f$ on the circle and multiplies by its speed.

contentBlocks.title: Reconstruct the circle example
contentBlocks.strategy: Parametrize the circle once, use its constant speed, and integrate the composed density.
contentBlocks.setup: The source problem is on page 44; continuation slide 45 is blank. Use $r(t)=(2\cos t,4,2\sin t)$ for $0\leq t\leq2\pi$.

steps.label: Evaluate the field

sections.title: Components depend on position
sections.text: A vector field $F$ assigns a vector to each point of its domain. For $F(x,y)=(-y,x)$, arrows are tangent to circles about the origin; for $G(x,y)=(x,y)$, arrows are radial. Arrow normalization improves legibility but hides magnitude unless a scale or readout supplies it.

sections.title: Domain is part of the field
sections.text: The field $F(x,y)=(-y/(x^2+y^2),x/(x^2+y^2))$ excludes the origin. Omitting one arrow from a plot does not add the missing domain point; theorem hypotheses must respect that puncture.

exercise.hint: Substitute the point into each component.
exercise.solution: $F(1,0)=(1,0)$ points outward and $G(1,0)=(0,1)$ is tangent counterclockwise. Their dot product is zero.

contentBlocks.title: Treat domain and component functions as part of the field
contentBlocks.text: An $n$-dimensional vector field maps a subset of $\mathbb R^n$ into $\mathbb R^n$. It is smooth in the handout's sense when every component has continuous first-order partial derivatives throughout its domain. A missing or singular point changes the field's domain; a plot cannot fill it in.

sections.title: Work uses a signed component
sections.text: Work is $\int_C F(r(t))\cdot r'(t)\,dt$. Parallel field and velocity components contribute positively, opposed components negatively, and perpendicular components contribute zero. Unlike a scalar length integral, reversing traversal reverses the sign.

sections.title: A transverse component contributes nothing
sections.text: On $r(t)=(t,0)$ for $0\leq t\leq1$, the field $F=(1,5)$ has dot product $1$ with $r'=(1,0)$. Work is $1$ despite the vertical field component. For $F=(-1,5)$, work is $-1$.

exercise.prompt: Find the work of $F=(2,3)$ along the segment $r(t)=(t,2t)$, $0\leq t\leq1$.
exercise.hint: Use $r'(t)=(1,2)$, not only a unit tangent.
exercise.solution: The dot product $(2,3)\cdot(1,2)=8$ is constant, so the work is $8$. The reverse path gives $-8$.
rubric: Use velocity rather than only a unit tangent.
Retain orientation and sign.

sections.text: The expression $P$ $dx+Q dy+R$ dz becomes $[P(r)x'+Q(r)y'+R(r)z']dt$. Each differential follows the same parameter interval; none is an independent integration variable.

sections.text: For $F=(y,0)$, from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$, traveling horizontally then vertically gives work 0. Traveling vertically then horizontally gives work 1. The same endpoints do not imply the same work without conservativeness.

sections.title: Circulation is work on a closed traversal
sections.text: For $F=(-y,x)$ and the unit circle counterclockwise, $F(r)=r'$ and the dot product is 1, giving circulation $2\pi$. For the radial field $(x,y)$, it is zero because field and velocity are perpendicular.

sections.title: A field can change the sign around a path
sections.text: For constant $F=(1,0)$ on a circle, local work density is $-\sin t$. Some arcs contribute positively and others negatively, with total zero. Zero net work does not mean every local contribution vanishes.

exercise.solution: The dot product is $2R^{2}$, giving circulation $4\pi R^{2}$. Clockwise traversal changes the sign.
rubric: Track both radius factors.

exercises.outcome: Compute constant-force work on a straight displacement by dotting force with displacement.

exercises.solution: The local work rate is $1-t$, so work is $\int_0^1(1-t)dt=\frac12$.

sections.title: Apply chain rule along the curve
sections.text: If $F=\nabla \varphi$ on a domain containing the entire piecewise smooth path, then $F(r)\cdot r'=(\varphi \circ r)'$. Integrating gives $\varphi(\text{end})-\varphi(\text{start})$. A closed path then has zero work.

sections.title: Construct a potential with a missing function
sections.text: For $F=(2xy,x^{2}+2y)$, integrate the first component in $x$ to get $\varphi =x^{2}y+C(y)$. Differentiating in $y$ and matching the second component gives $C'=2y$, hence $\varphi =x^{2}y+y^{2}+\text{constant}$.

exercise.prompt: Find work of that field from $(0,0)$ to $(1,2)$.
exercise.hint: Evaluate the potential at endpoints.
exercise.solution: $\varphi (1,2)=2+4=6$ and $\varphi (0,0)=0$, so work is 6 along every admissible path in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.
rubric: Verify both partials of the potential.
Subtract in endpoint order.
