sections.title: Curl-free needs a domain theorem
sections.text: A $C^1$ field on a simply connected open domain with zero curl is conservative. On an arbitrary domain, zero curl is only a local condition. A potential always forces zero curl when mixed derivatives may be interchanged.

sections.title: The punctured-plane counterexample
sections.text: $F=(-y/r^{2},x/r^{2})$ has zero scalar curl away from zero, yet its circulation around the unit circle is $2\pi$. The loop surrounds an excluded point, so no global single-valued potential exists on the punctured plane. On a suitable cut domain an angle potential is possible.

exercise.prompt: Can Green’s theorem on the full disk justify zero circulation for this vortex?
exercise.hint: Is the field defined on a neighborhood of the whole disk?
exercise.solution: No. It is undefined at the center, violating the theorem’s domain hypothesis. Direct circulation is $2\pi$; an annulus would have both outer and inner boundaries.
rubric: Check the interior as well as the curve.
Account for an inner boundary when using an annulus.

sections.title: Orient the whole boundary
sections.text: For a positively oriented simple closed piecewise smooth curve bounding a suitable planar region, with $P$,$Q$ continuously differentiable on a neighborhood, $\oint P dx+Q dy=\int \int (Q_{x}-P_{y})dA$. Positive orientation keeps the region on the left; inner boundaries of holes therefore run clockwise.

sections.title: Why internal edges disappear
sections.text: Partitioning a region into smaller pieces gives two traversals of every shared edge with opposite directions. Their line integrals cancel, leaving the outer and hole boundaries. This motivates the theorem; a full proof requires controlling the partition and regularity.

exercise.prompt: Find $\oint(-y\,dx+x\,dy)$ around the unit circle counterclockwise using Green.
exercise.hint: Compute $Q_{x}-P_{y}$.
exercise.solution: The scalar curl is $1-(-1)=2$. The disk area is $\pi$, so circulation is $2\pi$.
rubric: Check the field on the entire disk.

sections.title: Choose a field whose curl is one
sections.text: The forms $x\,dy$, $-y\,dx$, and $(x\,dy-y\,dx)/2$ all integrate to area on a positively oriented simple boundary because each corresponding scalar curl equals 1. Reverse orientation and the signed result changes sign.

sections.title: A polygon reduces to endpoint data
sections.text: On a straight edge from $(x_i,y_i)$ to $(x_j,y_j)$, the symmetric form contributes $(x_i y_j-x_j y_i)/2$. Summing edges gives the shoelace formula. Self-intersecting traversals produce signed multiplicity-weighted area rather than automatically the union’s geometric area.

exercise.prompt: Use boundary data to find the area of triangle $(0,0)$, $(3,0)$, $(0,2)$ in that order.
exercise.hint: Sum the three cross-products and divide by two.
exercise.solution: Only the edge $(3,0)\to (0,2)$ contributes 6 before halving. The area is 3 and the ordering is counterclockwise.
rubric: Close the polygon.

Check counterclockwise orientation.

sections.title: Two parameters trace a surface
sections.text: A chart $r(u,v)$ maps a planar parameter region into space. Regularity requires $r_{u}\times r_{v}\ne 0$. To integrate without multiplicity, also check coverage: a regular map can cover the same physical patch more than once.

sections.title: Seams are coordinate artifacts
sections.text: A sphere chart $r(\varphi,\theta)=(\sin\varphi\cos\theta,\sin\varphi\sin\theta,\cos\varphi)$ repeats at the angular seam and degenerates at the poles. Multiple charts or exclusion of negligible boundary sets can handle these defects; they do not make the sphere itself nonsmooth.

exercise.prompt: Parametrize the cylinder $x^2+y^2=4$ for $0\le z\le 3$.
exercise.hint: Use angle and height as independent parameters.
exercise.solution: $r(\theta ,z)=(2cos \theta ,2sin \theta ,z)$, $0\leq \theta \leq 2\pi ,0\leq z\leq 3$. It covers the side once apart from the repeated seam.
rubric: Specify the parameter rectangle.
Explain seam duplication and distinguish the cylinder caps.

contentBlocks.title: A surface chart is one-to-one in its interior
contentBlocks.text: For the source definition, $D^\circ$ is connected and nonempty, $r$ is continuous on $D$, and $r|_{D^\circ}$ is a homeomorphism onto its image. Boundary points may repeat without violating the interior condition.

contentBlocks.title: Verify a graph chart from its first two coordinates
contentBlocks.strategy: Test the domain, continuity, injectivity, and inverse on the interior in that order.

steps.label: Domain
steps.text: The interior $(-1,1)^2$ is nonempty and connected.

steps.label: Injectivity
steps.text: Equal image points have equal first and second coordinates, so their parameters agree.

steps.label: Inverse
steps.text: On the graph image, the inverse is the continuous projection $(x,y,z)\mapsto(x,y)$.

contentBlocks.result: This pair $(r,D)$ parametrizes its graph once on the interior.
contentBlocks.verification: The parameter inverse is explicit and continuous; the boundary of D is not part of the injectivity condition.

contentBlocks.title: Interior and edge belong to the surface
contentBlocks.text: The source tests whether a point of $S$ lies in $r[D^\circ]$ for at least one parametrization of that same surface. The edge is the set of surface points that are not interior; it is not the boundary of the parameter drawing in space.

contentBlocks.title: Locate the edge of a parametrized disk
contentBlocks.strategy: Use the disk graph chart and compare the parameter point with the disk interior.

steps.label: Interior point
steps.text: The origin has parameters strictly inside the disk.

steps.label: Edge point
steps.text: The point $(1,0,0)$ has parameter $(1,0)$ on the disk boundary.

steps.label: Classification
steps.text: The open disk maps to the surface interior; the circle maps to the edge.

contentBlocks.result: The interior is the open planar disk and the edge is its unit circle.
contentBlocks.verification: The chart is injective, so the parameter classification transfers directly to the planar disk.

contentBlocks.title: Angle and height parametrize the source cylinder
contentBlocks.text: The source chart $r(u,v)=(2\cos u,v,2\sin u)$ uses angle $u$ and height $v$. Its image satisfies $x^2+z^2=4$; the endpoints $u=0$ and $u=2\pi$ identify the same seam.

contentBlocks.title: Recover the cylinder and a one-to-one interior
contentBlocks.strategy: Eliminate the angle, then restrict it to an open interval to test the chart interior.

steps.label: Surface equation
steps.text: Square the first and third coordinates and add.

steps.label: Height
steps.text: The second coordinate is the free parameter.

steps.label: Seam
steps.text: On the interior $0<u<2\pi$, each angle is unique; the two outer edges represent one physical seam.

contentBlocks.result: The full source domain traces the radius-two cylindrical side between heights $-1$ and $1$, with a repeated boundary seam.
contentBlocks.verification: The radius equation is independent of $v$ and the angular coordinate wraps once around the circle.

contentBlocks.title: Radial distance and angle chart the top hemisphere
contentBlocks.text: The source uses $u$ as distance from the $z$-axis and $v$ as azimuth. The image satisfies $x^2+y^2+z^2=1$ with $z\ge0$; the pole and angular seam lie on the parameter boundary.

contentBlocks.title: Check the sphere equation and boundary
contentBlocks.strategy: Substitute the three coordinates into the unit-sphere equation and inspect the parameter edges.
contentBlocks.setup: Take the source map $r(u,v)=(u\cos v,u\sin v,\sqrt{1-u^2})$.

steps.label: Sphere equation
steps.text: The squared horizontal radius is $u^2$.

steps.label: Upper half
steps.text: The square root is nonnegative.

steps.label: Boundary
steps.text: At $u=0$ every $v$ gives the north pole; $v=0$ and $2\pi$ give the same seam.

contentBlocks.result: The map covers the unit top hemisphere; repeated values occur on parameter-boundary points, not the open interior.
contentBlocks.verification: On $0<u<1$ and $0<v<2\pi$, the radius determines $u$ and the angle determines $v$.

exercises.outcome: Check that a surface parametrization is continuous on its domain and one-to-one with continuous inverse on the connected, nonempty parameter interior.
exercises.prompt: For $r(u,v)=(u,v,2u-v)$ on $[-2,2]\times[-1,1]$, verify the interior chart conditions and give its inverse.
exercises.hint: Recover $u$ and $v$ from the first two image coordinates.
exercises.solution: The rectangle interior is connected and nonempty; $r$ is continuous. Its first two coordinates recover $(u,v)$, so the inverse on the graph is $(x,y,z)\mapsto(x,y)$ and is continuous.
rubric: Check the connected, nonempty interior and continuity.
Show injectivity and state a continuous inverse.

exercises.outcome: Classify a point as surface interior when some surface chart places it over the parameter interior; classify the remaining surface points as edge.
exercises.prompt: For the graph patch $r(u,v)=(u,v,u+v)$ over $u^2+v^2\le4$, classify $r(0,0)$ and $r(0,2)$.
exercises.hint: Compare each parameter radius with $2$.
exercises.solution: The point $r(0,0)$ lies over the disk interior since $0<4$. The point $r(0,2)$ lies over its edge since $0^2+2^2=4$.
rubric: Use the parameter-domain interior test.
Translate the classification to the surface points.

exercises.outcome: Recognize the image of $r(u,v)=(2\cos u,v,2\sin u)$ on $[0,2\pi]\times\mathbb R$ as the radius-two cylinder and explain its seam.
exercises.prompt: Parametrize the side of $x^2+z^2=9$ between $y=1$ and $y=4$, and identify its repeated seam.
exercises.hint: Replace radius $2$ by $3$ and use $y$ as the height parameter.
exercises.solution: Take $r(u,v)=(3\cos u,v,3\sin u)$ for $0\le u\le2\pi$ and $1\le v\le4$. The edges $u=0$ and $u=2\pi$ coincide.
rubric: Verify $x^2+z^2=9$ and the stated height interval.
Explain the angular seam duplication.

exercises.outcome: Verify the source chart $r(u,v)=(u\cos v,u\sin v,\sqrt{1-u^2})$ covers the unit top hemisphere and locate its parameter-boundary duplications.
exercises.prompt: Use $r(s,\theta)=(3s\cos\theta,3s\sin\theta,3\sqrt{1-s^2})$ to describe the upper hemisphere of radius $3$.
exercises.hint: Compute the squared distance from the origin and note the sign of $z$.
exercises.solution: The image obeys $x^2+y^2+z^2=9$ with $z\ge0$. The pole occurs at $s=0$ for every angle, while $\theta=0$ and $2\pi$ repeat the seam.
rubric: Verify the sphere radius and upper-half condition.
Identify the pole and seam duplications as boundary values.

sections.title: Differentiate one parameter at a time
sections.text: For $r(u,v)=(u,v,u^{2}+v^{2})$, the tangent vectors are $r_{u}=(1,0,2u)$ and $r_{v}=(0,1,2v)$. Their cross product is $(-2u,-2v,1)$, a nonzero upward normal.

sections.title: Tangent plane versus the curved patch
sections.text: At $(u,v)=(1,1)$, the surface point is $(1,1,2)$ and normal ($-2$,$-2$,1), yielding $z=2x+2y-2$. The plane is the affine first-order approximation, not the whole surface.

exercise.prompt: Find tangent vectors and a normal for $r(u,v)=(u,v,uv)$ at $(1,2)$.
exercise.hint: Evaluate derivatives at the parameter pair, not at the 3D point.
rubric: Distinguish parameter pair from physical point.
Verify the normal is perpendicular to both tangents.

contentBlocks.title: A smooth chart has rank two
contentBlocks.text: The source’s regularity test is $r_u\times r_v\ne0$ at each interior parameter point, together with continuous first partials. Nonvanishing makes the two parameter velocities linearly independent.

contentBlocks.title: Test a paraboloid graph chart
contentBlocks.strategy: Differentiate with respect to each parameter, then test whether their cross product can vanish.

steps.label: Tangents
steps.text: Differentiate each coordinate in turn.

steps.label: Rank test
steps.text: Compute the cross product.

steps.label: Nonvanishing
steps.text: Its third coordinate is always $1$.

contentBlocks.result: The chart has continuous first derivatives and rank two everywhere on its interior.
contentBlocks.verification: The cross product cannot be zero because its third component is nonzero.

contentBlocks.title: Piecewise smoothness joins finitely many smooth patches
contentBlocks.text: The source condition has two parts: finitely many smooth parametric patches cover $S$, and any pair intersects only along its edges. A corner between patches does not require one smooth chart for the entire union.

contentBlocks.title: Join a disk to a paraboloid cap
contentBlocks.strategy: Verify the two smooth patches and identify their common circle as an edge.
contentBlocks.setup: Let $S_1$ be $z=0$ over the unit disk and $S_2$ be $z=1-x^2-y^2$ over the same disk.

steps.label: Smooth patches
steps.text: The disk is planar; the paraboloid is a smooth graph.

steps.label: Intersection
steps.text: They meet when $1-x^2-y^2=0$.

steps.label: Finite union
steps.text: The common unit circle is the boundary edge of both patches.

contentBlocks.result: Their union is piecewise smooth under the source definition.
contentBlocks.verification: There are exactly two smooth patches and their intersection is only their shared edge.

contentBlocks.title: Two tangent directions determine two normals
contentBlocks.text: At an interior point of a smooth chart, $r_u$ and $r_v$ span the tangent plane. Their cross product is perpendicular to both, so normalizing it gives one unit normal and changing its sign gives the other.

contentBlocks.title: Normalize the normal to a saddle graph
contentBlocks.strategy: Evaluate both tangent vectors at the parameter, cross them, and divide by the cross-product length.

steps.label: Tangents
steps.text: Differentiate and substitute $(1,2)$.

steps.label: Normal direction
steps.text: Take their cross product.

steps.label: Unit choices
steps.text: The length is $\sqrt6$, giving exactly two signs.

contentBlocks.result: The chart point is $(1,2,2)$ and its two unit normals are $\pm(-2,-1,1)/\sqrt6$.
contentBlocks.verification: The dot products of $(-2,-1,1)$ with both tangent vectors are zero.

exercises.outcome: Test smoothness of a surface parametrization by continuous first partials and a nonzero cross product throughout the parameter interior.
exercises.prompt: Check whether $r(u,v)=(u,v,u^2-3v^2)$ is regular on $[-1,1]^2$.
exercises.hint: The first two coordinates of $r_u\times r_v$ determine whether it vanishes.
exercises.solution: Here $r_u=(1,0,2u)$ and $r_v=(0,1,-6v)$, so $r_u\times r_v=(-2u,6v,1)$; its third component prevents vanishing.
rubric: Compute both parameter derivatives and their cross product.
Use a component that never vanishes to justify regularity.

exercises.outcome: Recognize a surface as piecewise smooth when it is a finite union of smooth patches whose pairwise intersections lie only along patch edges.
exercises.prompt: Join the disk $z=0$, $x^2+y^2\le4$, to the graph $z=4-x^2-y^2$ over the same disk. Verify the source’s piecewise-smooth criterion.
exercises.hint: Solve for the intersection and compare it with each patch boundary.
exercises.solution: Both patches are smooth. They intersect where $4-x^2-y^2=0$, exactly the boundary circle $x^2+y^2=4$, so their union is piecewise smooth.
rubric: Identify each smooth patch.
Show that the intersection lies exactly on both patch edges.

exercises.outcome: Construct the two unit normals to a smooth parametric surface from the cross product of its nonparallel tangent vectors.
exercises.prompt: Find both unit normals to $r(u,v)=(u,v,u^2+2v)$ at $(1,0)$.
exercises.hint: Compute $r_u\times r_v$ before normalizing.
exercises.solution: At $(1,0)$, $r_u=(1,0,2)$ and $r_v=(0,1,2)$. Their cross product is $(-2,-2,1)$ with length $3$, so the normals are its two signs divided by $3$.
rubric: Evaluate the two parameter tangents at the given parameters.
Normalize the cross product and include both signs.

sections.title: A local parallelogram supplies area
sections.text: The parameter cell du dv maps approximately to edges $r_u\,du$ and $r_v\,dv$, giving $dS=|r_u\times r_v|\,du\,dv$. The norm removes orientation but retains stretch; using a unit normal here would lose the area factor.

sections.title: Graphs are a special case
sections.text: For $z=f(x,y)$, $r=(x,y,f)$ gives $dS=\sqrt{1+f_{x}^{2}+f_{y}^{2}}dx$ dy. On the plane $z=x+2y$ over a unit square, the factor is $\sqrt{6}$ and the area is $\sqrt{6}$.

exercise.prompt: Find the area of $z=3x$ over $0\le x\le 2$, $0\le y\le 1$.
exercise.hint: The graph area factor is constant.
exercise.solution: The factor is $\sqrt{1+9}=\sqrt{10}$. Multiplying by projected area 2 gives $2\sqrt{10}$.
rubric: Use surface area rather than projected area.
Keep the factor under the square root.

contentBlocks.title: A nice chart controls both domain and distortion
contentBlocks.text: Before using a surface-integral formula, check that the chart is smooth, $D$ is bounded with boundary of zero area, and both parameter derivatives are bounded on $D^\circ$. These are the source’s stated “nice” conditions.

contentBlocks.title: Check a plane over a square
contentBlocks.strategy: Verify each source condition separately for the chart and its parameter region.

steps.label: Smoothness
steps.text: Both partial derivatives are constant.

steps.label: Parameter region
steps.text: The square is bounded and its boundary has planar area zero.

steps.label: Bounded tangents
steps.text: The constant tangent vectors are bounded on the interior.

contentBlocks.result: This is a nice parametrization under the lecture’s definition.
contentBlocks.verification: Each of the three listed conditions is checked directly.

contentBlocks.title: Surface area is the scalar integral of one
contentBlocks.text: The source defines area by $\operatorname{Area}(S)=\iint_S1\,dS$. In Example 2 the projected disk is $x^2+y^2\le9$ and the graph factor comes from $g_x=2x$, $g_y=2y$; p20 is blank after the prompt.

contentBlocks.title: Independently calculate the source paraboloid area
contentBlocks.strategy: Use polar coordinates on the projected disk and integrate the graph area factor.
contentBlocks.setup: For $z=x^2+y^2$, the plane $z=9$ cuts the graph at $r=3$.

steps.label: Graph factor
steps.text: The gradient is $(2x,2y)$, so in polar coordinates the factor is $\sqrt{1+4r^2}$.

steps.label: Set up area
steps.text: Integrate over $0\le r\le3$ and $0\le\theta\le2\pi$.

steps.label: Substitute
steps.text: Let $w=1+4r^2$, so $r\,dr=dw/8$.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.text: Use the antiderivative $2w^{3/2}/3$.

contentBlocks.result: The guide-derived area is $\pi(37\sqrt{37}-1)/6$; the source does not show the solution.
contentBlocks.verification: The cutoff circle is $r^2=9$ because the graph height equals $9$ there.

exercises.outcome: Check the source’s hypotheses for a nice parametrization: smoothness, a bounded parameter region with zero-area boundary, and bounded parameter tangents.
exercises.prompt: Check whether $r(u,v)=(u,v,3u-v)$ on $D=[-1,1]\times[0,2]$ is a nice parametrization.
exercises.hint: The domain is a bounded rectangle and the partial derivatives are constant.
exercises.solution: The rectangle is bounded with zero-area boundary. The chart is smooth and $r_u=(1,0,3)$, $r_v=(0,1,-1)$ are bounded and have nonzero cross product, so it is nice.
rubric: Check smoothness and nonzero cross product.
Check bounded domain, zero-area boundary, and bounded tangents.

exercises.outcome: Set $f=1$ in the surface integral and evaluate the source’s area problem for $z=x^2+y^2$ below $z=9$.
exercises.prompt: Find the area of the part of $z=x^2+y^2$ below $z=4$.
exercises.hint: The projected disk has radius $2$; keep the same graph factor and change the upper limit.
exercises.solution: The area is $2\pi\int_0^2r\sqrt{1+4r^2}\,dr=\frac\pi6(17^{3/2}-1)$.
rubric: Find the projected radius from the height constraint.
Use the graph area factor and evaluate the integral.

sections.title: Density times area
sections.text: The scalar surface integral is $\int \int f(r(u,v))|r_{u}\times r_{v}|du$ dv. It is unaffected by reversing orientation, although repeating coverage repeats the integral.

sections.title: A plane with variable density
sections.text: On $z=x+y$ over the unit square, density $f=z$ becomes $u+v$ and area factor $\sqrt{3}$. The integral is $\sqrt{3}\int_0^1\int_0^1(u+v)\,du\,dv =\sqrt{3}$. Using only the projected measure would miss the slope factor.

exercise.prompt: Integrate constant density 2 over a sphere of radius $R$.
exercise.hint: Multiply density by surface area.
exercise.solution: The result is $8\pi R^{2}$. It does not change if inward rather than outward orientation is named, because this is a scalar area integral.
rubric: Distinguish scalar integration from flux.
Use area, not enclosed volume.

contentBlocks.title: Scalar density is multiplied by actual area
contentBlocks.text: The source integrates $f(r(u,v))\|r_u\times r_v\|$ over parameter area. The norm is essential and discards orientation sign; reversing the chart order leaves a scalar surface integral unchanged.

contentBlocks.title: Integrate a density on a unit disk
contentBlocks.strategy: For a horizontal graph the cross-product magnitude is one; substitute the density and integrate over the disk.

steps.label: Chart factor
steps.text: Use $r(u,v)=(u,v,0)$, whose cross product has unit length.

steps.label: Polar density
steps.text: Substitute $x=r\cos\theta$ and $dA=r\,dr\,d\theta$.

steps.label: Integrate
steps.text: The radial integral is $1/4$ and the angular integral is $\pi$.

contentBlocks.result: The scalar surface integral is $\pi/4$, with the same value for either orientation.
contentBlocks.verification: Changing $r_u\times r_v$ to its negative leaves its norm unchanged.

contentBlocks.title: Add scalar integrals patch by patch
contentBlocks.text: For the source’s finite patch union, the scalar integral over $S=S_1\cup\cdots\cup S_k$ is the sum over each patch. Shared edges do not supply an extra area term.

contentBlocks.title: Add the area of two joined patches
contentBlocks.strategy: Compute each patch measure separately and add; the common circle has surface area zero.
contentBlocks.setup: Take a unit disk $S_1$ in $z=0$ and a unit-radius graph cap $S_2:z=1-x^2-y^2$. Set $f=1$.

steps.label: Disk
steps.text: Its area is the area of the unit disk.

steps.label: Cap
steps.text: Its graph factor is $\sqrt{1+4r^2}$.

steps.label: Add patches
steps.text: Their intersection is only the rim circle.

contentBlocks.result: The scalar integral of $1$ over the union is $\pi(5+5\sqrt5)/6$.
contentBlocks.verification: The shared circle is one-dimensional and contributes no surface-area integral.

contentBlocks.title: Split the source boundary into three scalar patches
contentBlocks.text: The source problem has a bottom disk, a cylindrical side, and a top graph $z=x+1$. Because this is a scalar integral, each patch uses its positive area factor; the source gives the setup but no displayed calculation on pp14–15.

contentBlocks.title: Independently derive the source Example 1 value
contentBlocks.strategy: Integrate separately on the bottom disk, cylinder, and graph, then add the three scalar contributions.
contentBlocks.setup: Use the exact source boundary: $z=0$, $x^2+y^2=1$, and $z=x+1$.

steps.label: Bottom
steps.text: The density vanishes on $z=0$.

steps.label: Cylinder
steps.text: Parametrize by $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta,z)$ with $0\le z\le1+\cos\theta$; $dS=d\theta\,dz$.

steps.label: Top plane
steps.text: For $z=x+1$, the graph factor is $\sqrt2$ over the unit disk.

steps.label: Add
steps.text: Use symmetry to remove the disk integral of $x$.

contentBlocks.result: The guide-derived value is $\pi(3/2+\sqrt2)$; the source slides do not display this solution.
contentBlocks.verification: The side height is nonnegative on the unit disk, and the top graph density is integrated with its $\sqrt2$ area factor.

contentBlocks.title: A graph stretches projected area by its gradient
contentBlocks.text: For $r(x,y)=(x,y,g(x,y))$, the source graph factor is $\sqrt{1+g_x^2+g_y^2}$. The formula assumes the stated domain and gradient conditions and evaluates the density at $(x,y,g(x,y))$.

contentBlocks.title: Integrate a density over an inclined graph
contentBlocks.strategy: Compute the constant graph factor, substitute the height into the density, and integrate over the projected region.

steps.label: Area factor
steps.text: The gradient is $(2,-1)$, so the factor is constant.

steps.label: Substitute density
steps.text: The scalar density is $x+y+1$ on the graph.

steps.label: Triangle integral
steps.text: On this unit right triangle, $\iint_Dx=\iint_Dy=1/6$ and area is $1/2$.

contentBlocks.result: The surface integral is $5\sqrt6/6$.
contentBlocks.verification: The graph is smooth with bounded constant gradient on the bounded triangular region.

exercises.outcome: Evaluate a scalar surface integral by multiplying the scalar density by the chart’s cross-product magnitude, independent of orientation.
exercises.prompt: Integrate $f=x^2+y^2$ over the horizontal disk $x^2+y^2\le4$.
exercises.hint: In polar coordinates, use density $r^2$ and area element $r\,dr\,d\theta$.
exercises.solution: The integral is $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2r^3\,dr\,d\theta=2\pi(4)=8\pi$.
rubric: Include the surface-area factor.
Use the disk’s radius and integrate the changed density.

exercises.outcome: Add scalar surface integrals over finitely many nice smooth patches that meet only along edges.
exercises.prompt: For density $f=2$, add the integral over a radius-two disk and a separate flat annulus with radii $2$ and $3$, joined only on their boundary circle.
exercises.hint: Multiply the total area of both patches by the constant density.
exercises.solution: The disk and annulus areas add to $4\pi+\pi(9-4)=9\pi$. Thus the integral is $2(9\pi)=18\pi$.
rubric: Compute the integral on each patch.
Add the patch values once and do not add the seam separately.

exercises.outcome: Evaluate the source’s $z$-density integral by splitting the closed boundary into its bottom disk, cylindrical side, and sloped planar top.
exercises.prompt: Repeat the source setup with the top plane $z=x+2$ over the unit cylinder and disk. Find $\iint_S z\,dS$.
exercises.hint: The side height is $2+\cos\theta$; the top graph still has area factor $\sqrt2$.
exercises.solution: The cylinder contributes $\tfrac12\int_0^{2\pi}(2+\cos\theta)^2d\theta=\tfrac{9\pi}{2}$. The top contributes $\sqrt2\iint_D(x+2)dA=2\sqrt2\pi$; the bottom contributes zero.
rubric: Parametrize and integrate over each of the three patches.
Include the top graph factor and use disk symmetry.

exercises.outcome: Convert a scalar surface integral on $z=g(x,y)$ to a planar integral using $\sqrt{1+g_x^2+g_y^2}$ under the source’s boundedness conditions.
exercises.prompt: For $z=3x+4y$ over $0\le x,y\le1$, integrate the density $f=z+1$ over the graph.
exercises.hint: The graph factor is $\sqrt{26}$; then integrate $3x+4y+1$ on the square.
exercises.solution: The factor is $\sqrt{1+3^2+4^2}=\sqrt{26}$. The square integral of $3x+4y+1$ is $3/2+2+1=9/2$, so the surface integral is $9\sqrt{26}/2$.
rubric: Compute the graph area factor from both partial derivatives.
Substitute the density and integrate over the projected domain.

sections.title: Orientation is a continuous choice
sections.text: An orientation chooses one of the two unit normal directions continuously across a regular surface. Reversing parameter order reverses $r_{u}\times r_{v}$. A closed bounding surface usually uses outward normals; open surfaces need an explicit convention.

sections.title: A Möbius strip has no global side
sections.text: Following a local normal around a $M$öbius strip returns it reversed. Thus one global continuous normal cannot be chosen. Local charts and scalar area still make sense; a globally oriented flux or ordinary oriented Stokes surface requires more care.

exercise.prompt: For the graph $z=x^2+y^2$, which cross-product sign gives downward orientation?
exercise.hint: The standard $(x,y)$ order produces a positive $z$ component.
exercise.solution: The upward area vector is $(-2x,-2y,1)$dx dy. Downward uses its negative, $(2x,2y,-1)$dx dy.
rubric: Choose sign from the requested direction.
Do not discard the area magnitude when integrating flux.

contentBlocks.title: Orientation is a continuous global choice
contentBlocks.text: Every smooth interior point has two local unit normals, but orientability requires choosing one continuously over the entire surface interior. The source illustrates that continuity—not a pointwise choice alone—is the condition.

contentBlocks.title: Orient the sphere consistently
contentBlocks.strategy: Use the radial unit vector field and check its norm and continuity on the sphere.

steps.label: Normal length
steps.text: At each sphere point define $n=(x,y,z)/R$.

steps.label: Normal direction
steps.text: The radial vector is perpendicular to tangent directions of the level set.

steps.label: Continuity
steps.text: The formula varies continuously at every point on the sphere.

contentBlocks.result: The sphere admits a continuous outward unit normal, so it is orientable.
contentBlocks.verification: The same formula is defined everywhere on the sphere and has constant norm one.

contentBlocks.title: The Möbius seam reverses a local side
contentBlocks.text: The source parametrizes the Möbius strip over $0\le u\le2\pi$, $-1\le v\le1$. At the seam, $(0,v)$ is identified with $(2\pi,-v)$, reversing the transverse coordinate; a normal transported once around returns with opposite sign.

contentBlocks.title: Track the parameter orientation through the seam
contentBlocks.strategy: Use the seam coordinate change and its Jacobian sign to determine how a local normal changes.
contentBlocks.setup: Compare parameter coordinates $(u,v)$ near $u=0$ and $(u_1,v_1)=(u+2\pi,-v)$ near $u=2\pi$.

steps.label: Seam identification
steps.text: The two boundary points represent the same physical point.

steps.label: Transition determinant
steps.text: The coordinate transition has derivative matrix with diagonal entries $1$ and $-1$.

steps.label: Normal sign
steps.text: A negative transition determinant reverses the ordered tangent pair and its cross product.

contentBlocks.result: One circuit reverses the normal, so no globally continuous unit normal exists.
contentBlocks.verification: A global orientation would have to return to its original sign at the same seam point, contradicting the computed sign reversal.

contentBlocks.title: Choose the cross-product sign on the surface
contentBlocks.text: A chart supplies the local unit normal $\pm(r_u\times r_v)/\|r_u\times r_v\|$. The problem selects the sign. The normal field is a function on the surface points, not on the parameter domain; this is explicitly cautioned on p27.

contentBlocks.title: Orient a cylindrical side outward
contentBlocks.strategy: Compute the ordered cross product, normalize it, and compare its direction with the requested outward side.
contentBlocks.setup: Parametrize a radius-$R$ cylinder by $r(u,v)=(R\cos u,R\sin u,v)$.

steps.label: Tangents
steps.text: Differentiate the angle and height parameters.

steps.label: Cross product
steps.text: Their ordered cross product points radially outward.

steps.label: Normalize
steps.text: Divide by its length $R$.

contentBlocks.result: The chart order gives outward orientation; reversing the parameter order gives inward orientation.
contentBlocks.verification: The dot product of this normal with the radial position $(R\cos u,R\sin u,0)$ is $R>0$.

contentBlocks.title: The third component fixes graph orientation
contentBlocks.text: For a graph, the source’s upward unit normal is $(-g_x,-g_y,1)/\sqrt{1+g_x^2+g_y^2}$. Its area vector is $(-g_x,-g_y,1)\,dx\,dy$; downward uses the negative.

contentBlocks.title: Find both orientations of a sloped graph
contentBlocks.strategy: Differentiate the height function and use the sign of the third component to choose orientation.

steps.label: Gradient
steps.text: Differentiate the height.

steps.label: Upward area vector
steps.text: Insert the derivatives in the source formula.

steps.label: Downward choice
steps.text: Reverse all three components.

contentBlocks.result: The positive third component selects upward orientation; the negative selects downward.
contentBlocks.verification: Each vector is perpendicular to the graph tangents $(1,0,2x)$ and $(0,1,3)$.

contentBlocks.title: Positive boundary orientation points out of the solid
contentBlocks.text: For a piecewise-smooth boundary $S=\partial E$, the source calls the choice with all patch normals pointing outward positive. Reversing every normal gives negative orientation; local choices must not be mixed.

contentBlocks.title: Set orientations on a cylinder boundary
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the solid’s top, bottom, and side, then point each normal away from the interior.

steps.label: Top disk
steps.text: Outward points in the positive vertical direction.

steps.label: Bottom disk
steps.text: Outward points below the solid.

steps.label: Side
steps.text: Outward is radially away from the axis.

contentBlocks.result: The positive orientation uses all three outward choices; the negative orientation reverses all three.
contentBlocks.verification: Each listed direction has nonnegative dot product with a vector from the solid toward the exterior.

exercises.outcome: Decide whether a smooth surface is orientable by the existence of a continuous unit normal field on its surface interior.
exercises.prompt: Give a continuous unit normal field for the plane $2x-y+2z=5$ and verify it is unit length.
exercises.hint: Normalize the constant gradient of the plane equation.
exercises.solution: The normal $(2,-1,2)$ has length $3$, so $n=(2,-1,2)/3$ is a continuous unit normal field.
rubric: Give a normal defined at every surface point.
Verify continuity and unit length.

exercises.outcome: Explain the source’s Möbius-strip example by showing that its seam identification reverses the transverse parameter direction.
exercises.prompt: On the width-one band $-1\le v\le1$, the seam identifies $(0,v)$ with $(2\pi,-v)$. State its transverse effect and orientation.
exercises.hint: The transverse coordinate map is $v\mapsto-v$; compute its derivative and the full transition determinant.
exercises.solution: The interval $[-1,1]$ maps onto itself. The transverse derivative is $-1$, so the transition matrix has determinant $-1$; the seam reverses orientation and a transported normal returns negated.
rubric: State the seam map on the fixed-width interval and its transverse derivative.
Compute the transition determinant and conclude that the normal reverses.

exercises.outcome: Construct either orientation of a smooth surface by normalizing $r_u\times r_v$ and selecting the sign required by the problem.
exercises.prompt: For $r(u,v)=(4\cos u,4\sin u,v)$, find the inward unit normal using the reversed parameter order.
exercises.hint: Use $r_v\times r_u=-(r_u\times r_v)$.
exercises.solution: The outward normal is $(\cos u,\sin u,0)$, so reversing the order gives inward $(-\cos u,-\sin u,0)$.
exercises.solutionTex: \mathbf n_{\rm in}=\frac{r_v\times r_u}{\|r_v\times r_u\|}=(-\cos u,-\sin u,0)
rubric: Compute the cross product in the stated order.
Choose and normalize the sign that points inward.

exercises.outcome: Write upward and downward area vectors for a graph $z=g(x,y)$ using $(-g_x,-g_y,1)$ and its negative.
exercises.prompt: For $z=5x-12y$, give the upward and downward unit normals.
exercises.hint: The graph factor is $\sqrt{1+25+144}=\sqrt{170}$.
exercises.solution: The vector $(-5,12,1)$ has length $\sqrt{25+144+1}=\sqrt{170}$. The upward unit normal is $(-5,12,1)/\sqrt{170}$ and the downward normal is its negative.
rubric: Use both graph partial derivatives with the correct signs.
Normalize and state opposite directions.

exercises.outcome: Assign positive orientation to the boundary of a region by choosing outward normals on each smooth patch; negative orientation reverses them all.
exercises.prompt: State the outward normals on the top, bottom, and side of the cylinder $x^2+y^2\le9$, $-1\le z\le1$.
exercises.hint: Only the side radius changes; the vertical directions do not.
exercises.solution: The top normal is $(0,0,1)$, the bottom is $(0,0,-1)$, and the side unit normal is $(x/3,y/3,0)$.
exercises.solutionTex: \mathbf n_{\rm top}=(0,0,1),\quad\mathbf n_{\rm bottom}=(0,0,-1),\quad\mathbf n_{\rm side}=\left(\frac x3,\frac y3,0\right)
rubric: Choose normals independently on each smooth patch.
Check that each points away from the solid.

sections.title: Flux retains the normal sign
sections.text: Flux is $\int \int F\cdot n$ dS, or $\int \int F(r)\cdot (r_{u}\times r_{v})du$ dv with a compatible parameter orientation. The dot product measures only the normal component; reversing the normal reverses flux.

sections.title: Oblique fields and cancellation
sections.text: For constant $F=(1,0,0)$ on an outward unit sphere, local flux is positive on the right hemisphere and negative on the left, giving total zero. This differs from the radial field $F=(x,y,z)$, which is outward everywhere and has flux $4\pi$.

exercise.prompt: Find upward flux of $F=(1,2,3)$ through the unit square in $z=0$.
exercise.hint: The upward unit normal is $(0,0,1)$.
exercise.solution: The dot product is 3, so flux is 3. Horizontal components contribute zero. Downward orientation gives $-3$.
rubric: Choose the normal.
Multiply normal component by area.

contentBlocks.title: Flux keeps the signed normal component
contentBlocks.text: The source defines flux by $\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,dS$. Components tangent to the surface contribute zero; components along the chosen normal contribute with sign.

contentBlocks.title: Compute flux through a sloped plane patch
contentBlocks.strategy: Use the upward graph area vector so the dot product already includes the area factor.
contentBlocks.setup: Let $z=3x+y$ over the unit square and let $\mathbf F=(2,-1,4)$.

steps.label: Area vector
steps.text: For the graph the upward area vector is $(-3,-1,1)dxdy$.

steps.label: Normal component
steps.text: Take its dot product with the constant field.

steps.label: Integrate
steps.text: The projected square has area one.

contentBlocks.result: The upward flux is $-1$; the field crosses partly against the chosen normal.
contentBlocks.verification: Reversing the orientation changes the answer to $+1$.

contentBlocks.title: Use the ordered cross product in flux
contentBlocks.text: Substituting $\mathbf n=(r_u\times r_v)/\|r_u\times r_v\|$ into the flux definition cancels the normalization against $dS$. The resulting formula uses the signed cross product, so parameter order must respect the chosen orientation.

contentBlocks.title: Check orientation on a sloped square
contentBlocks.strategy: Compute the cross product in parameter order, compare its vertical sign with “upward,” then integrate.
contentBlocks.setup: Let $r(u,v)=(u,v,u+v)$ on the unit square and $\mathbf F=(0,0,1)$.

steps.label: Cross product
steps.text: Differentiate and cross in the stated order.

steps.label: Orientation
steps.text: The positive third component agrees with upward.

steps.label: Flux
steps.text: The dot product is one throughout the square.

contentBlocks.result: The upward flux is $1$. Reversing the parameter order would give $-1$.
contentBlocks.verification: The cross product has positive vertical component, which is the graph’s upward choice.

contentBlocks.title: Split the source paraboloid boundary before integrating
contentBlocks.text: The source boundary has the graph $z=1-x^2-y^2$ and its bottom unit disk. Positive orientation means outward on both patches. Page 32 gives $\mathbf F=(y,x,z)$; the two continuation pages are blank.

contentBlocks.title: Independently derive the source Example 3 flux
contentBlocks.strategy: Use the upward graph area vector on the top and the downward normal on the bottom.
contentBlocks.setup: The solid is $0\le z\le1-r^2$, $0\le r\le1$, with positive boundary orientation.

steps.label: Top graph
steps.text: For $g=1-x^2-y^2$, the outward/upward area vector is $(2x,2y,1)dA$.

steps.label: Top integral
steps.text: The $xy$ term integrates to zero by disk symmetry.

steps.label: Bottom disk
steps.text: On $z=0$, the field has zero vertical component, so its dot product with the downward normal is zero.

steps.label: Sum
steps.text: Add the patch fluxes.

contentBlocks.result: The guide-derived outward flux is $\pi/2$; the source slides do not display a solution.
contentBlocks.verification: The top uses the outward graph area vector and the lower disk contributes zero.

contentBlocks.title: The source hemisphere uses upward orientation
contentBlocks.text: The source asks for the upward flux through the top hemisphere of radius $6$ for $\mathbf F=(0,0,z)$. On this upper hemisphere, upward agrees with outward; the prompt is followed by blank solution slides.

contentBlocks.title: Independently integrate the source hemisphere flux
contentBlocks.strategy: Use spherical coordinates and integrate the field’s normal component over the upper half-sphere.

steps.label: Normal component
steps.text: The upward unit normal is radial, so $\mathbf F\cdot n=z^2/6$.

steps.label: Area element
steps.text: For radius six the element is $36\sin\phi\,d\phi\,d\theta$.

steps.label: Integrate
steps.text: Integrate $216\cos^2\phi\sin\phi$ over the upper hemisphere.

contentBlocks.result: The guide-derived upward flux is $144\pi$; the source does not display the calculation.
contentBlocks.verification: The field is vertical and nonnegative on the top hemisphere, so the flux must be positive.

contentBlocks.title: The source solid has a spherical top and conical side
contentBlocks.text: The cap and cone meet where $r=z$ and $r^2+z^2=8$, hence at $r=z=2$. Positive orientation points outward on the cap and down/outward on the cone. The source’s continuation slides are blank.

contentBlocks.title: Independently sum the source cap and cone flux
contentBlocks.strategy: Parametrize both patches with outward orientation; use symmetry on the cap and a downward area vector on the cone.
contentBlocks.setup: The sphere has radius $\sqrt8$ and cap angle $0\le\phi\le\pi/4$; the cone is $r=z$ for $0\le r\le2$.

steps.label: Intersection
steps.text: Solve the sphere and cone equations.

steps.label: Spherical cap
steps.text: The $y$-component term integrates to zero over a full revolution; the constant vertical component contributes.

steps.label: Cone
steps.text: Use $r(s,\theta)=(s\cos\theta,s\sin\theta,s)$ with outward area vector $(s\cos\theta,s\sin\theta,-s)$.

steps.label: Closed boundary
steps.text: Add the two patch contributions.

contentBlocks.result: The guide-derived outward flux is zero; the opposing patch contributions cancel.
contentBlocks.verification: The field has zero divergence, consistent with the direct cancellation, but the calculation above uses only the source surface integral formula.

contentBlocks.title: Close the cap with a zero-flux base
contentBlocks.text: Lecture 11 opens with the radius-6 upper hemisphere and $\mathbf F=(0,0,z)$. Close it with the disk $z=0$: the field vanishes on the disk, while $\operatorname{div}\mathbf F=1$ in the half-ball. The divergence theorem therefore gives the hemisphere flux as the half-ball volume.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 11 Example 4: radius-6 hemisphere
contentBlocks.strategy: Close the hemisphere by its equatorial disk, whose flux is zero, then use the divergence theorem on the half-ball.
contentBlocks.setup: The source asks for upward flux of $\mathbf F=(0,0,z)$ through the top hemisphere of radius $6$.

steps.label: Check the closure
steps.text: The equatorial disk has $z=0$, so $\mathbf F=\mathbf 0$ there. The hemisphere plus this disk is the closed half-ball, oriented outward.

steps.label: Integrate the divergence
steps.text: The field is smooth on a neighborhood of the half-ball, and its divergence is $1$.

steps.label: Evaluate the volume
steps.text: The requested hemisphere flux equals the half-ball volume because the base contributes zero.

contentBlocks.result: The upward flux through the hemisphere is $144\pi$.
contentBlocks.verification: Directly, $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n=6\cos^2\theta$ and $dS=36\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi$ on $0\leq\theta\leq\pi/2$, giving $144\pi$.

contentBlocks.title: Use zero divergence on a closed cone-and-cap boundary
contentBlocks.text: The source’s Example 5 already gives a closed boundary: the upper sphere and lower cone meet at their common circle. Since $\mathbf F=(y,0,2)$ has zero divergence and is smooth throughout the solid, its outward flux is zero.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 11 Example 5: sphere cap above a cone
contentBlocks.strategy: Check that the two surfaces close the region, then integrate the zero divergence over its volume.
contentBlocks.setup: The upper surface is $z=\sqrt{8-x^2-y^2}$, the lower surface is $z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, and $\mathbf F=(y,0,2)$.

steps.label: Locate the common edge
steps.text: Writing $r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, the surfaces meet when $\sqrt{8-r^2}=r$, so $r=2$. Together they form the complete boundary of a bounded solid.

steps.label: Check the field and divergence
steps.text: The field is smooth on all of $\mathbb R^3$ and has zero divergence.

steps.label: Apply the theorem
steps.text: The entire boundary is oriented outward, so the total flux is the integral of zero over the enclosed solid.

contentBlocks.result: The outward flux is $0$.
contentBlocks.verification: The source specifies the full boundary, not an open cap; no missing side patch has to be added.

contentBlocks.title: Read the solid before setting up a flux integral
contentBlocks.text: The source’s Example 6 is a half-cylinder in the $yz$-plane extruded over $0\leq x\leq2$. For $\mathbf F=(x^2,y^2,z^2)$, integrate $2x+2y+2z$ over that solid; the $2y$ term cancels by symmetry.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 11 Example 6: half-cylinder boundary
contentBlocks.strategy: Use the divergence theorem with bounds copied from the source solid; preserve the symmetric $y$-interval.
contentBlocks.setup: The solid is $0\leq x\leq2$, $-1\leq y\leq1$, $0\leq z\leq\sqrt{1-y^2}$, and $\mathbf F=(x^2,y^2,z^2)$.

steps.label: Differentiate matching components
steps.text: The boundary is closed and piecewise smooth, and the polynomial field is smooth on a neighborhood of the solid.

steps.label: Integrate each term
steps.text: The odd term vanishes; the $x$ and $z$ terms separate over the stated bounds.

steps.label: Simplify
steps.text: The semicircle cross-section has area $\pi/2$ and the last integral is $8/3$.

contentBlocks.result: The outward flux is $2\pi+\frac83$.
contentBlocks.verification: The setup retains the full boundary, including both end caps at $x=0$ and $x=2$.

exercises.outcome: Interpret flux as the surface integral of the vector field’s signed component along the chosen unit normal.
exercises.prompt: Find upward flux of $\mathbf F=(1,3,-2)$ across $z=2x-2y$ over $[0,2]\times[0,1]$.
exercises.hint: Dot the field with $(-2,2,1)$ and multiply by the rectangle area.
exercises.solution: The dot product is $-2+6-2=2$. The projected rectangle has area $2$, so the upward flux is $4$.
rubric: Use the specified orientation and graph area vector.
Multiply the normal component by projected area.

exercises.outcome: Evaluate parametrized flux with $\mathbf F(r)\cdot(r_u\times r_v)$ only when the parameter order respects the chosen orientation.
exercises.prompt: Use $r(u,v)=(u,v,2u+v)$ on $0\le u\le2$, $0\le v\le1$ to find upward flux of $\mathbf F=(0,0,3)$.
exercises.hint: The cross product is $(-2,-1,1)$; integrate its dot product with the field over a parameter rectangle of area two.
exercises.solution: The chart order points upward. The integrand is $3$, so the flux is $3(2)(1)=6$.
rubric: Verify the cross-product sign agrees with upward orientation.
Integrate the signed dot product over the parameter region.

exercises.outcome: Evaluate the source’s positive flux through the boundary of $0\le z\le1-x^2-y^2$ for $\mathbf F=(y,x,z)$ by summing its top and bottom patches.
exercises.prompt: For the solid $0\le z\le4-x^2-y^2$ and $\mathbf F=(y,x,z)$, find outward flux through its entire boundary.
exercises.hint: The base contributes zero. On the top, the graph area vector is $(2x,2y,1)dA$ over $r\le2$.
exercises.solution: The top integrand is $4xy+4-r^2$. Symmetry removes $4xy$, and $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2(4-r^2)r\,dr\,d\theta=8\pi$. The base contributes zero.
rubric: Use outward area vectors on the top and bottom.
Evaluate the disk integral and account for symmetry.

exercises.outcome: Evaluate upward flux of $\mathbf F=(0,0,z)$ through the source’s radius-six top hemisphere.
exercises.prompt: Find upward flux of $\mathbf F=(0,0,z)$ through the top hemisphere of radius $3$.
exercises.hint: Use $\mathbf F\cdot n=z^2/3$ and $dS=9\sin\phi\,d\phi\,d\theta$.
exercises.solution: The integral is $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2}27\cos^2\phi\sin\phi\,d\phi\,d\theta=18\pi$.
rubric: Use the correct hemisphere radius and upward normal.
Integrate the normal component over $0\le\phi\le\pi/2$.

exercises.outcome: Compute positive flux through the source’s closed boundary between a spherical cap and cone by integrating both outward-oriented patches.
exercises.prompt: For the cap $z=\sqrt{18-r^2}$ joined to cone $z=r$ and field $\mathbf F=(y,0,3)$, determine the positive flux through the closed surface.
exercises.hint: The intersection radius is $3$. Compute top-cap and cone contributions with outward orientation.
exercises.solution: The sphere radius is $3\sqrt2$ and the cap angle ends at $\pi/4$. The cap contributes $27\pi$ from the constant vertical field component, and the cone contributes $-27\pi$; the total is zero.
exercises.solutionTex: \iint_{S_{\rm cap}}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf S=27\pi,\quad\iint_{S_{\rm cone}}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf S=-27\pi,\quad\iint_S=0
rubric: Find the cap/cone intersection and choose outward orientations.
Evaluate both patch fluxes and add with their signs.

exercises.outcome: Use a zero-flux closure to evaluate hemisphere flux.
exercises.prompt: For the upper hemisphere of radius $R>0$, oriented upward, find the flux of $\mathbf F=(0,0,z)$.
exercises.hint: Close with the equatorial disk and use $\operatorname{div}\mathbf F=1$.
exercises.solution: The base flux is zero, so the flux is the upper half-ball volume, $\frac23\pi R^3$.
rubric: Close the hemisphere and state the base flux.
Use the divergence theorem with the outward orientation.

exercises.outcome: Evaluate flux through a closed sphere-and-cone boundary.
exercises.prompt: Keep the source’s cone and sphere, but use $\mathbf G=(y,0,1+z)$. Find the outward flux.
exercises.hint: Their edge is at $r=2$. The solid is $r\leq2$ and $r\leq z\leq\sqrt{8-r^2}$.
exercises.solution: $\operatorname{div}\mathbf G=1$. The enclosed volume is $2\pi\int_0^2r(\sqrt{8-r^2}-r)\,dr=\frac{32\pi}{3}(\sqrt2-1)$, so the flux has the same value.
rubric: Check that the cone and cap form the complete boundary.
Use the correct intersection radius and integrate the divergence.

exercises.outcome: Set up the divergence integral from a semicylindrical solid.
exercises.prompt: Change the source bounds to $0\leq x\leq1$, $-2\leq y\leq2$, $0\leq z\leq\sqrt{4-y^2}$, keeping $\mathbf F=(x^2,y^2,z^2)$. Find the outward flux.
exercises.hint: Integrate $2x+2y+2z$; the $y$ term cancels.
exercises.solution: The $2x$ term contributes $2\pi$, the odd term contributes zero, and the $2z$ term contributes $\frac{32}{3}$. The flux is $2\pi+\frac{32}{3}$.
rubric: Use the new interval lengths and semicircle area.
Show why the odd term vanishes.

sections.title: Curl measures oriented circulation density
sections.text: In three dimensions curl $F$ has components $(R_{y}-Q_z,P_z-R_{x},Q_{x}-P_{y})$. Its dot product with a chosen unit normal measures infinitesimal circulation per area in that plane, under smoothness hypotheses.

sections.title: Curved arrows alone are misleading
sections.text: The field $(-y,x,0)$ has curl $(0,0,2)$, while $(-y/r^{2},x/r^{2},0)$ has zero curl away from the $z$-axis despite circular arrows. The latter has an excluded singular axis, so its global circulation behavior needs the domain.

exercise.prompt: Find curl of $F=(0,0,xy)$.
exercise.hint: Only derivatives of the third component are nonzero.
exercise.solution: Curl $F=(x,-y,0)$. At $(1,2,0)$ it is $(1,-2,0)$, describing oriented circulation in corresponding coordinate planes.
rubric: Use the correct component order.
Distinguish curl from the field itself.

contentBlocks.title: Differentiate across components in order
contentBlocks.text: For $\mathbf F=(P,Q,R)$ in three dimensions, the ordered components are $(R_y-Q_z,\,P_z-R_x,\,Q_x-P_y)$. Curl is a three-dimensional operation; it is not the field’s magnitude or a list of matching-coordinate derivatives.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 11 curl Example 1
contentBlocks.strategy: Name $P,Q,R$ first, then use the component order from the determinant.

steps.label: First component
steps.text: Differentiate the third component in $y$ and subtract the second component’s $z$ derivative.

steps.label: Second component
steps.text: Differentiate the first component in $z$ and subtract the third component’s $x$ derivative.

steps.label: Third component
steps.text: Differentiate the second component in $x$ and subtract the first component’s $y$ derivative.

contentBlocks.result: The curl is $\nabla\times\mathbf F=(xz-x,\,x^2-yz,\,z)$.
contentBlocks.verification: The exponential term $e^y$ contributes no partial derivative to curl because none of the required derivatives differentiates it in $y$.

contentBlocks.title: Read curl direction with the loop orientation
contentBlocks.text: The Lecture 11 paddlewheel picture aligns its axis with curl. The component along a chosen unit normal gives oriented circulation density for small loops whose direction is fixed by the right-hand rule.

contentBlocks.title: A curl direction and a reversed normal
contentBlocks.strategy: Differentiate the field, then project curl onto the loop’s chosen normal.
contentBlocks.setup: Use $\mathbf F=(-2y,3x,0)$ and compare small loops oriented by $\mathbf n=\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf n=-\mathbf k$.

steps.label: Compute the curl
steps.text: Only its vertical component is nonzero.

steps.label: Project onto each normal
steps.text: Reversing the loop orientation changes the signed circulation density, not the curl vector.

contentBlocks.result: The upward orientation is positive for counterclockwise travel viewed from above; the downward orientation reverses the sign.
contentBlocks.verification: A circle of radius $a$ has circulation $5\pi a^2$ counterclockwise and $-5\pi a^2$ clockwise.

contentBlocks.title: Use the curl test only with its domain hypothesis
contentBlocks.text: On an open simply connected domain, a smooth three-dimensional field is conservative exactly when its curl vanishes throughout the domain. The open simply connected condition cannot be dropped.

contentBlocks.title: Zero curl on a domain with a hole
contentBlocks.strategy: Test the hypothesis before using the converse from curl-free to conservative.

steps.label: Check the local test
steps.text: The field is smooth on $U$, and direct differentiation gives zero curl there.

steps.label: Check the missing hypothesis
steps.text: The $z$-axis is removed, so $U$ is not simply connected.

steps.label: Measure circulation
steps.text: The unit circle has nonzero circulation, so the field is not conservative on this punctured domain.

contentBlocks.result: Zero curl alone does not imply a global potential when the domain hypothesis fails.
contentBlocks.verification: The loop winds once around the excluded axis; it cannot contract to a point within $U$.

exercises.outcome: Compute curl with the ordered three-dimensional component formula.
exercises.prompt: Find curl of $\mathbf G=(xy,\,x^2z,\,y^2z)$.
exercises.hint: Use $(R_y-Q_z,\,P_z-R_x,\,Q_x-P_y)$.
exercises.solution: The components are $2yz-x^2$, $0$, and $2xz-x$.
rubric: Keep the three curl components in order.
Show each cross-component derivative.

exercises.outcome: Relate the signed curl component to an oriented loop.
exercises.prompt: For $\mathbf F=(-4y,x,0)$, which direction around a small horizontal loop has positive circulation density? What changes when its normal is downward?
exercises.hint: Compute the $z$ component of curl and dot it with the chosen normal.
exercises.solution: $\nabla\times\mathbf F=(0,0,5)$. The upward normal gives positive density for counterclockwise travel viewed from above; the downward normal gives density $-5$ and reverses travel.
rubric: Compute curl rather than inspect arrow magnitude.
Pair the normal with the right-hand-rule direction.

exercises.outcome: Check simple connectedness before using the curl criterion.
exercises.prompt: On $U=\mathbb R^3\setminus\{z\text{-axis}\}$, let $\mathbf F=(-y/(x^2+y^2),x/(x^2+y^2),0)$. Is $\mathbf F$ conservative?
exercises.hint: Its curl vanishes on $U$, but test its integral around the unit circle.
exercises.solution: No. The domain is not simply connected and the unit circle has circulation $2\pi$.
rubric: State whether the domain is open and simply connected.
Use the nonzero loop integral to reject a global potential.

sections.title: Divergence is a signed scalar
sections.text: For $F=(P,Q,R)$, divergence is $P_{x}+Q_{y}+R_z$. Positive divergence means local net outward flux density, not necessarily arrows pointing directly away from the origin.

sections.title: A non-radial example
sections.text: For $F=(x,-y,0)$, divergence is zero: expansion in the $x$ direction balances contraction in $y$. For $F=(x,y,z)$, divergence is 3. Arrow length and direction alone do not supply the derivative balance.

exercise.prompt: Compute divergence of $F=(x^2,yz,z^2)$. Where is it zero?
exercise.hint: Differentiate each component in its matching coordinate.
exercise.solution: Divergence is $2x+z+2z=2x+3z$, zero on the plane $2x+3z=0$.
rubric: Use matching partial derivatives.
Do not add the components without differentiating.

contentBlocks.title: Differentiate each component in its matching coordinate
contentBlocks.text: In $n$ dimensions, divergence is $\sum_{j=1}^n\partial F_j/\partial x_j$. It is a scalar. In three dimensions this becomes $P_x+Q_y+R_z$.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 11 divergence Example 2
contentBlocks.strategy: Differentiate each component only with respect to its corresponding input, then substitute the point.
contentBlocks.setup: The source field is $\mathbf F=(e^x,yz,-yz^2)$; evaluate divergence at $(0,2,-1)$.

steps.label: Compute the derivative sum
steps.text: The matching derivatives are $e^x$, $z$, and $-2yz$.

steps.label: Substitute the point
steps.text: At $(0,2,-1)$ the contributions are $1$, $-1$, and $4$.

contentBlocks.result: The divergence at the source point is $4$.
contentBlocks.verification: Only matching-coordinate derivatives enter the divergence.

contentBlocks.title: Use the derivative sign, not arrow length
contentBlocks.text: The source compares $\mathbf F=(x,y)$, $\mathbf G=(y-2x,x-2y)$, and $\mathbf H=(x,-y)$. Their divergences are $2$, $-4$, and $0$, respectively, giving local net outflow, inflow, and zero first-order net flow.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 11 sign and flow figures
contentBlocks.strategy: Differentiate the vector field components before interpreting the arrow picture.
contentBlocks.setup: Compare the three planar fields shown on Lecture 11 pages 16–18.

steps.label: Positive divergence
steps.text: Both coordinate components expand away from the origin.

steps.label: Negative divergence
steps.text: Both matching derivatives are negative, so a small circle has net inward flow.

steps.label: Zero divergence
steps.text: Stretching in the $x$ direction balances compression in $y$.

contentBlocks.result: The sign gives the local first-order net flow; zero does not mean the field itself is zero.
contentBlocks.verification: These signs agree with the source’s outward, inward, and zero-net-flow captions.

exercises.outcome: Evaluate the n-dimensional divergence at a point.
exercises.prompt: For $\mathbf G=(e^x,yz^2,-yz^3)$, find $\operatorname{div}\mathbf G$ at $(0,2,-1)$.
exercises.hint: Use $\partial_xG_1+\partial_yG_2+\partial_zG_3$.
exercises.solution: The divergence is $e^x+z^2-3yz^2$, so its value is $1+1-6=-4$.
rubric: Differentiate matching components.
Substitute only after forming the derivative sum.

exercises.outcome: Interpret positive, negative, and zero divergence as local net flow.
exercises.prompt: For the planar field $\mathbf G=(2x,-3y)$, determine whether a small circle has net outward or inward flow.
exercises.hint: Compute the two matching partial derivatives.
exercises.solution: $\operatorname{div}\mathbf G=2-3=-1$, so there is local net inflow. The field need not point inward at every point of the circle.
rubric: Compute divergence, not the vector magnitude.
Interpret the sign as local net flow.

sections.title: Write the cancellations
sections.text: For a $C^2$ scalar $\varphi$, $\operatorname{curl}(\nabla\varphi)=0$ because each component is a difference of equal mixed partials. For a $C^2$ vector field, $\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}F)=0$ by the same pairwise cancellations.

sections.title: Converse statements need separate conditions
sections.text: Curl-free does not always mean a global gradient on a punctured domain. Divergence-free does not automatically provide a globally defined vector potential on every domain. These identities are necessary structural checks, not universal converse theorems.

exercise.prompt: Could $F=(x,y,z)$ be the curl of a $C^2$ vector field on an open ball?
exercise.hint: Compute its divergence.
exercise.solution: No: div $F=3$, whereas the divergence of the curl of a $C^{2}$ field must be zero.
rubric: State the smoothness setting.
Use the identity as a necessary condition.

contentBlocks.title: Pair mixed partials in the divergence of curl
contentBlocks.text: Lecture 11 page 21 states that $\operatorname{div}(\nabla\times\mathbf F)=0$ when the component functions have continuous second partial derivatives on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. The identity makes every curl divergence-free.

contentBlocks.title: Expand the source differential identity
contentBlocks.strategy: Expand the component formula and pair equal mixed partial derivatives.
contentBlocks.setup: Let $\mathbf F=(P,Q,R)$ have continuous second-order partial derivatives on open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$.

steps.label: Expand divergence of curl
steps.text: Apply divergence to the three ordered curl components.

steps.label: Cancel by mixed-partial equality
steps.text: Continuous second partials let us exchange the order in each pair.

contentBlocks.result: The divergence of curl is zero, so every such curl field is divergence-free.
contentBlocks.verification: The source places this identity in the gradient–curl–divergence sequence of linear maps.

exercises.outcome: Verify divergence of curl by pairwise cancellation.
exercises.prompt: For $\mathbf F=(xyz,x^2z,y^2z)$, calculate its curl and then its divergence.
exercises.hint: Find the curl components first; differentiate each in its matching coordinate.
exercises.solution: $\nabla\times\mathbf F=(2yz-x^2,xy,xz)$, and $\operatorname{div}(\nabla\times\mathbf F)=-2x+x+x=0$.
rubric: Use the source curl component order.
Differentiate the result and show the cancellation.

sections.title: Boundary and normal are paired
sections.text: Stokes relates $\oint_{\partial S}F\cdot d\mathbf r$ to $\iint_S(\nabla\times F)\cdot n\,dS$ for a suitable oriented piecewise smooth surface and $C^1$ field on a neighborhood. Point the right thumb along the chosen normal: curled fingers give the induced boundary direction. For a surface with an upward normal and a simple projected boundary, this is counterclockwise when viewed from above. Across glued patches, shared edges cancel.

sections.title: Choose the easier surface lawfully
sections.text: For $F=(-y/2,x/2,0)$, curl is $(0,0,1)$. Around a unit horizontal circle counterclockwise, the flat disk gives flux $\pi$. Another admissible spanning surface with the same induced boundary has the same curl flux, provided the field remains smooth near it.

sections.title: A replacement surface needs the same edge
sections.text: A tilted loop can bound its tilted planar disk. Before replacing a curved spanning surface, check that the new surface has exactly the same oriented boundary and that $F$ is smooth on a neighborhood of the whole replacement surface. If the requested traversal is opposite to the disk’s induced direction, reverse the normal or negate the resulting integral.

exercise.prompt: Find circulation of $F=(-y,x,0)$ around the unit circle viewed clockwise from above.
exercise.hint: Use a downward-oriented disk.
exercise.solution: Curl $F=(0,0,2)$. With downward normal, flux is $-2$ times the disk area, giving $-2\pi$.
rubric: Match the boundary to the surface normal.
Check the field on a neighborhood of the spanning surface.

contentBlocks.title: A tilted boundary and a lawful flat spanning disk
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the boundary, choose the planar disk it encloses, check the field and orientation, then integrate curl on that disk.
contentBlocks.setup: MH2100 Lecture 11, physical pages 24–26: $C$ is $x^2+y^2=1$ in the plane $y+z=2$, counterclockwise when viewed from above; $F=(-y^2,x,z^2)$ is defined on $\mathbb R^3$. Evaluate $\oint_C F\cdot d\mathbf r$.

steps.label: Choose an admissible surface
steps.text: The tilted planar disk $S=\{(x,y,2-y):x^2+y^2\le1\}$ is smooth with the required edge $C$. The polynomial field is smooth on a neighborhood of the entire disk; Stokes therefore applies.

steps.label: Match the boundary orientation
steps.text: The parameter order $(x,y)$ gives $\mathbf r_x\times\mathbf r_y=(0,1,1)$, whose vertical component is positive. Seen from above, its induced boundary is counterclockwise, as requested.

steps.label: Integrate the actual curl
steps.text: Here $\nabla\times F=(0,0,1+2y)$. The vertical component of the oriented area vector is $1$, and the $2y$ term integrates to zero by symmetry of the unit disk.

contentBlocks.result: The circulation is $\pi$. A tilted boundary need not use a horizontal disk: the disk must actually have edge $C$.
contentBlocks.verification: Directly, $\mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t,2-\sin t)$ for $0\le t\le2\pi$ gives $F\cdot\mathbf r'(t)=\sin^3 t+\cos^2 t-(2-\sin t)^2\cos t$; only $\cos^2 t$ has nonzero integral, again $\pi$.

contentBlocks.title: Stokes’ Theorem: hypotheses and induced edge
contentBlocks.statement: $\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=\iint_S(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot\mathbf n\,dS$
hypotheses: The compact oriented surface $S$ is piecewise smooth, with finitely many compatible smooth patches; its net boundary is a simple piecewise-smooth loop $C$.
The field $\mathbf F$ is $C^1$ on an open neighborhood of all of $S$.
The direction on $C$ is induced by the chosen normal: point the right thumb along $\mathbf n$ and curl the fingers along $C$.

contentBlocks.title: Match the boundary before changing surfaces
contentBlocks.text: Stokes compares curl fluxes only on surfaces with the same oriented boundary. Reversing the normal reverses the induced loop. The field must be smooth on a neighborhood of every candidate surface, not merely on the boundary curve.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 11 Stokes Example 2: spherical cap
contentBlocks.strategy: Compute curl flux using the cap’s upward vector area; symmetry over the circular projection removes the integrand.
contentBlocks.setup: The source surface is the radius-2 sphere above $z=0$ and inside $x^2+y^2=1$, oriented upward, with $\mathbf F=(xz,yz,xy)$.

steps.label: Differentiate the field
steps.text: The curl has equal first two components and zero third component.

steps.label: Parametrize the cap
steps.text: Write $z=\sqrt{4-x^2-y^2}$ over the unit disk. Its upward vector area is $(x/z,y/z,1)\,dx\,dy$.

steps.label: Integrate with the induced orientation
steps.text: The disk is symmetric under swapping $x$ and $y$, so the integrand integrates to zero.

contentBlocks.result: The upward curl flux and the induced counterclockwise boundary circulation are both $0$.
contentBlocks.verification: Directly, the boundary circle is $z=\sqrt3$, and $\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=0$ for its counterclockwise parametrization.

exercises.outcome: Choose a lawful tilted spanning disk and match its induced boundary orientation before using Stokes.
exercises.prompt: Let $C$ be $x^2+y^2=4$ in the plane $z=1+x$, traversed clockwise when viewed from above, and let $F=(-y,x,z^2)$ on $\mathbb R^3$. Decide whether its tilted planar disk is an admissible Stokes surface; choose its normal orientation and evaluate $\oint_C F\cdot d\mathbf r$. Explain why the horizontal disk $z=1$ cannot simply be substituted.
exercises.hint: Parametrize the tilted disk by $\mathbf r(x,y)=(x,y,1+x)$ over $x^2+y^2\le4$. Determine the upward cross product, then reverse it for the requested traversal. Check the field on the whole disk.
exercises.solution: The tilted disk has edge $C$ and the polynomial field is smooth on all of $\mathbb R^3$. Its upward area vector is $(-1,0,1)\,dx\,dy$, inducing counterclockwise travel viewed from above; use $(1,0,-1)$ for the requested clockwise direction. Since $\nabla\times F=(0,0,2)$, the flux is $-2$ times the disk area $4\pi$, hence $-8\pi$. The horizontal disk has a different boundary, so Stokes does not equate its flux directly with this circulation.
rubric: Verify the replacement disk has exactly the given edge and that the field is smooth on it.
Relate the upward area vector to counterclockwise travel and reverse for clockwise travel.
Use the actual curl and account for the disk area; reject the horizontal disk as a different boundary.

exercises.outcome: Use the Stokes curl flux on a changed spherical-cap radius.
exercises.prompt: Keep the radius-2 sphere and field $\mathbf F=(xz,yz,xy)$, but let the cap project to $x^2+y^2\leq a^2$ for $0<a<2$. Find its upward curl flux.
exercises.hint: The upward area vector is $(x/z,y/z,1)\,dx\,dy$.
exercises.solution: The integrand is $(x^2-y^2)/\sqrt{4-x^2-y^2}$. The disk is symmetric under exchanging $x$ and $y$, so the flux is zero for every allowed $a$.
rubric: Use the field’s curl and the correct upward vector area.
Explain the symmetry cancellation on the changed disk.

exercises.outcome: Reject Stokes when the field is not defined near the candidate surface.
exercises.prompt: Can Stokes be applied to $\mathbf F=(-y/(x^2+y^2),x/(x^2+y^2),0)$ on the unit circle $z=0$ using its flat disk?
exercises.hint: Check whether the field is defined on an open neighborhood of the whole disk.
exercises.solution: No. The field is undefined on the $z$-axis, which crosses the disk. Although its curl is zero along the punctured disk, the theorem’s field-domain hypothesis fails for this spanning surface.
rubric: Check the field on the full disk, not just its edge.
Identify the failed neighborhood hypothesis.

sections.title: The surface must close the region
sections.text: For a suitable bounded solid $V$ with outward-oriented boundary and $C^1$ field near its closure, total flux equals $\iiint_V\operatorname{div}F\,dV$. An open cap or side surface needs its missing pieces included and then subtracted.

sections.title: Singularities and holes
sections.text: The field $r/|r|^{3}$ is singular at zero, so the theorem cannot be applied to a ball containing zero despite vanishing divergence away from it. On a shell the inner boundary points toward the center as an outward normal from the shell, and its flux cancels the outer contribution.

exercise.prompt: Find outward flux of $F=(x,y,z)$ through a sphere of radius $R$.
exercise.hint: Use divergence 3 and the enclosed volume.
exercise.solution: The flux is $3\cdot (4\pi R^{3}/3)=4\pi R^{3}$. Directly, $F\cdot n=R$ and surface area is $4\pi R^{2}$, giving the same answer.
rubric: Use outward orientation on a closed surface.
Check with the direct area calculation.

contentBlocks.title: Gauss–Ostrogradsky: closure and outward orientation
contentBlocks.statement: $\iint_{\partial E}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,dS=\iiint_E\operatorname{div}\mathbf F\,dV$
hypotheses: The solid $E$ is bounded and closed, with a volume and a piecewise-smooth boundary $S=\partial E$ that has no exposed edge.
The field $\mathbf F$ is $C^1$ on an open neighborhood of all of $E$.
Every boundary component is oriented outward from $E$; cavity components point into the cavity.

contentBlocks.title: Translate every face into bounds
contentBlocks.text: The source solid is bounded by a parabolic cylinder and three planes. Use $-1\leq x\leq1$, $0\leq z\leq1-x^2$, and $0\leq y\leq2-z$; these bounds include the complete closed boundary.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 11 Gauss Example 1: parabolic solid
contentBlocks.strategy: Replace the closed-surface flux by a triple integral of divergence over the exact source region.
contentBlocks.setup: Let $E=\{(x,y,z):-1\leq x\leq1,\ 0\leq z\leq1-x^2,\ 0\leq y\leq2-z\}$ and $\mathbf F=(xy,\,y^2+e^{xz^2},\,\sin(xy))$.

steps.label: Verify the boundary and field
steps.text: The cylinder and planes close a bounded region; the field is smooth on all of $\mathbb R^3$ and the normal is outward.

steps.label: Differentiate
steps.text: Only the $x$ derivative of the first component and the $y$ derivative of the second contribute.

steps.label: Integrate over the source bounds
steps.text: Integrate first in $y$, then $z$, then $x$.

contentBlocks.result: The outward flux through the parabolic solid boundary is $184/35$.
contentBlocks.verification: The bounds make $y\geq0$, so a positive integral of $3y$ is consistent with the result.

exercises.outcome: Change the vector field while preserving the source solid.
exercises.prompt: On the source solid $-1\leq x\leq1$, $0\leq z\leq1-x^2$, $0\leq y\leq2-z$, find outward flux for $\mathbf G=(x,y,z)$.
exercises.hint: Its divergence is $3$; integrate the volume over the source bounds.
exercises.solution: The volume is $\int_{-1}^1\int_0^{1-x^2}(2-z)\,dz\,dx=32/15$. Therefore the flux is $3(32/15)=32/5$.
rubric: Check the complete boundary and outward orientation.
Use divergence 3 and evaluate the triple integral.

exercises.outcome: Decide whether an open surface satisfies the divergence theorem.
exercises.prompt: Can the divergence theorem evaluate flux through only the parabolic side $z=1-x^2$ of the source solid?
exercises.hint: List the faces that meet it along an edge.
exercises.solution: No. That side has exposed edges and is not the complete edgeless boundary. Include the planar faces at $y=0$, $z=0$, and $y+z=2$, with outward normals, before applying the theorem.
rubric: State the closure requirement.
Identify the missing boundary pieces and orientation.

sections.title: Keep the original review data
sections.text: The two Stokes tasks use outward curl flux for $F=(y,-x,z)$ on the cone $z=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$, $0\leq z\leq 1$, joined to the cylinder $x^{2}+y^{2}=1$, $1\leq z\leq 4$; and upward curl flux for $F=(x+y^{2},y+z^{2},z+x^{2})$ on the first-octant triangle $x+y+z=3$. The original Green task from Lecture 12, physical page 7, asks for clockwise circulation of $P\,dx+Q\,dy$ around the triangle $(0,0)$,$(0,12)$,$(3,0)$, where $P=y\cos x-xy\sin x$ and $Q=xy+x\cos x$. The original potential task on physical page 10 gives $(2xy+e^{-x^2})\,dx+(x^2+y\cos(\pi y^2/2))\,dy$ along the oriented curve whose parametrization $r(t)=(e^{t^2-t}-\cos(2\pi t),2\sin(\pi t^2/2)-t^9)$, $0\leq t\leq 1$, runs opposite to the requested orientation. These original tasks are distinct from the simplified scaffolds below.

sections.title: Work the Stokes setups
sections.text: For the cone and cylinder, the top boundary is clockwise under the outward side orientation; $r=(\cos t,-\sin t,4)$ gives integrand 1 and answer $2\pi$. Excluding a tiny cone-tip cap and taking its limit handles the apex. For the first-octant triangle, $\operatorname{curl}F=(-2z,-2x,-2y)$; its dot product with the upward area vector $(1,1,1)$ is $-6$, so the flux is $-27$. Check the induced boundary orientation before using Stokes instead.

sections.title: Original Green task: cancellation before integration
sections.text: Differentiate both components of the original field: $Q_x=y+\cos x-x\sin x$, while $P_y=\cos x-x\sin x$. Thus $Q_{x}-P_{y}=y$; the trigonometric terms cancel only after the full source field has been used. The triangle has $0\leq x\leq 3$ and $0\leq y\leq 12-4x$. Green’s theorem with clockwise orientation gives $-\int_0^3\int_0^{12-4x}y\,dy\,dx=-72$. As a simpler, separately labelled scaffold, $F=(0,xy)$ on the same triangle has the same curl and answer but does not teach that derivative cancellation.

sections.title: Original potential task: endpoints and reversed orientation
sections.text: The original field has potential $\varphi (x,y)=x^{2}y+\int_0^xe^{-s^2}\,ds +\sin(\pi y^{2}/2)/\pi$. Its derivatives reproduce both field components. The supplied complicated parametrization has $r(0)=(0,0)$ and $r(1)=(0,1)$, opposite to the requested curve orientation. Hence the requested integral is $\varphi (0,0)-\varphi (0,1)=-1/\pi$; no elementary antiderivative of $e^{-x^2}$ or direct path integration is needed. The straight segment $r(t)=(0,1-t)$, $0\leq t\leq 1$, is a separately labelled scaffold with the desired direction, not the original parametrization.

exercise.prompt: For the original Green field $P=y\cos x-xy\sin x$, $Q=xy+x\cos x$, reverse the triangle direction and compute the new circulation by Green’s theorem.
exercise.hint: Differentiate the full $P$ and $Q$ before cancelling terms; reversing clockwise orientation changes the sign.
exercise.solution: $Q_x=y+\cos x-x\sin x$ and $P_y=\cos x-x\sin x$, so $Q_{x}-P_{y}=y$. Counterclockwise circulation is $\int_0^3\int_0^{12-4x}y\,dy\,dx=72$. The simplified scaffold $F=(0,xy)$ gives the same result, but skips the cancellation in the original field.
rubric: Use both components of the original source field.
Match orientation before integrating.
Show the curl cancellation and bounds.

sections.title: Map every boundary
sections.text: For the first-quadrant region bounded by $y=x^{3},y=2x^{3},xy=1,xy=3$, take $u=y/x^{3}$ and $v=xy$. The new rectangle is $1\leq u\leq 2,1\leq v\leq 3$. The inverse $x=(v/u)^{1/4}$, $y=u^{1/4}v^{3/4}$ maps its four edges to the actual curved boundaries.

sections.title: Check sign, scale, and bounds
sections.text: The inverse determinant is $-1/(4u)$, so scalar area uses $1/(4u)$. Integrating gives $(\ln 2)/2$. Since the factor lies between $1/8$ and $1/4$ on a rectangle of area 2, the result must lie between $1/4$ and $1/2$; this catches a mistaken forward determinant.

exercise.prompt: Compute $\iint_D xy\,dA$ over the same region.
exercise.hint: The integrand xy becomes $v$.
exercise.solution: The integral is $\int_1^2\int_1^3\frac{v}{4u}\,dv\,du=(ln2)/4\cdot 4=ln2$.
rubric: Transform both region and field.
Use the absolute inverse determinant.
Compare with the area-scaled bounds.

sections.title: Why the box is centered
sections.text: For an axis-aligned box whose eight vertices lie on $2x^{2}+72y^{2}+18z^{2}=288$, compare vertices differing in only one coordinate. Their squared endpoints must agree, so a nondegenerate box has opposite coordinate pairs. Its positive half-lengths $x$,$y$,$z$ give volume 8xyz.

sections.title: Global bound without multipliers
